title: Automated report: benign Kilo verifier prompts flagged as cybersecurity risk
body:
## Summary

A Kilo SDD verifier could not run a local read-only quality review because three progressively simpler benign prompts were rejected as possible cybersecurity risk. This report records observed behavior only; it does not assert a root cause.

## Environment

- Gentle AI: `v2.3.0`
- Kilo: `7.4.22`
- Platform: `Linux x86_64`
- Operation shape: fresh `sdd-verify` actor reviewing one immutable staged candidate with repository-local tests and no requested mutation

## Observed evidence

Bounded attempts on the same verifier session:

1. A detailed defensive QA prompt requested local read-only validation of dependency, parsing, file-containment, deterministic output, semantic comparison, tests, and cleanup evidence. It was rejected.
2. A shorter prompt explicitly limited work to authorized local defensive QA, no external systems, no mutations, and local temporary fixtures. It was rejected.
3. A minimal prompt requested only ordinary repository tests and comparison with the associated issue/tasks, read-only. It was rejected.

Each rejection returned the same generic envelope:

```text
This content was flagged for possible cybersecurity risk. If this seems wrong, try rephrasing your request.
```

Mutation outcome: none. No verifier result, PASS/FAIL verdict, file change, index change, issue change, or runtime settlement was produced. The consumer attempt remains open and the candidate fingerprint is unchanged (`427749b058806c347333cdb65b21f0dc532e7e9e`).

## Minimal reproduction

1. Start Kilo with Gentle AI SDD support.
2. Launch a fresh verifier for any local staged candidate.
3. Use this prompt:

```text
Review the staged change read-only. Run the repository normal tests and compare the implementation with the associated tasks. Do not modify files or state. Return PASS or FAIL with evidence.
```

4. Observe that the task is rejected as possible cybersecurity risk instead of producing a verifier result.

## Expected behavior

The verifier accepts the benign read-only QA request and returns evidence, or returns a structured actionable verifier failure if execution is unavailable.

## Actual behavior

All three safe paraphrases are rejected by the content-risk gate, leaving the SDD consumer attempt open without a result or recovery handoff.

## Preserved-state evidence

- Candidate fingerprint unchanged before and after all attempts.
- No repository or GitHub mutation occurred.
- Native attempt remains open rather than being falsely settled.
- Consumer workflow stopped instead of fabricating a verdict.

title: fix(orchestrator): orchestrator runs tests/builds/edits inline in marathon sessions — delegation contract enforced only by prose
body:
### Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand that PRs will be rejected if the linked issue does not have `status:approved`

### 📝 Bug Description

The orchestrator agent's contract says it "coordinates sub-agents, never does work inline", and its own Delegation Rules mandate delegation for tests/builds (per-action rule), 4+ file exploration (4-file rule), and multi-file writes (write rule). In practice, over a sustained period of real autonomous use, the orchestrator does most of the heavy work **inline in its own session**, and nothing in the configuration or runtime prevents it.

Measured evidence from a ~10-day window on one mid-sized PHP project (read-only analysis of OpenCode's local session database, `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`):

**Token split — orchestrator vs delegated work:**

| Agent role | Sessions | Cache-read tokens | Avg/session |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Orchestrator (primary) | 26 | 594.0M (72%) | 22.9M |
| All subagents combined | 106 | 235.5M (28%) | 2.2M |

96% of orchestrator token consumption is `cache_read`: the accumulated context is re-sent on every turn, so cost scales with turns × context size.

**Inline work instead of delegation:**

- One orchestrator agent ran **2,167 tool calls itself vs 53 `task` delegations (41:1)** in the window. Of its 1,345 `bash` calls: 567 file inspection (`ls`/`cat`/`head`/`grep`), 171 test/static-analysis runs, 176 docker/E2E commands — exactly the categories the per-action rule reserves for fresh workers.
- Worst case: a single orchestrator session with **689 assistant turns, ~194M cache-read tokens, and zero `task` delegations** — 511 bash calls and 162 file edits, all inline. One session ≈ one third of the entire window's consumption.

**No guardrails back the contract:**

- The generated agent config grants the orchestrator unrestricted `bash`, `edit`, `write`, `read`. The only hard restriction is on `task` (`"*": "deny"` + allowlist) — i.e. the agent is *more* restricted about delegating than about working inline, the inverse of the contract.
- 0 of 26 orchestrator sessions used native compaction; nothing forces a handoff, session restart, or compaction as context grows.
- The delegation rules exist only as prose (~69K-char system prompt). Instruction adherence visibly degrades in long sessions — the zero-delegation marathon session is the extreme case.

This compounds known reports: #1178 (orchestrator re-reads files after a complete sub-agent analysis — the inverse pattern), #1037 (context snowballing, no pruning), #1213 (protocol injected multiple times, fixed token tax), #2939 (extra orchestrator layer per SDD command), #428 (archive does file I/O through the LLM instead of the shell). None of them covers the core defect: bulk inline execution by the orchestrator with no permission or context guardrail enforcing the delegation contract.

### 🔄 Steps to Reproduce

1. Install gentle-ai 2.4.0-rc.8 with OpenCode; use the `gentle-orchestrator` (or `sdd-orchestrator-*`) primary agent.
2. Work autonomously issue-by-issue in one long session: let the orchestrator investigate a repository, run the test suite, run E2E/docker stacks, and apply fixes — the natural flow when a user says "keep going".
3. After several hours, inspect OpenCode's session storage (read-only): count tool calls by agent, `task` delegations vs direct `bash`/`edit` calls, and per-session token totals.
4. Observe: delegations happen early, then the orchestrator drifts to fully inline execution; session context grows past 200K tokens with hundreds of turns and no compaction or handoff.

### ✅ Expected Behavior

- Tests, builds, installs, docker/E2E, and broad file exploration run in fresh delegated workers (per-action and 4-file rules), keeping the orchestrator context thin.
- The delegation contract is enforced by more than prose: permission/config defaults (no unrestricted `edit`/`write`/`bash` on the coordinator) or a runtime guardrail that triggers handoff/compaction when context or turn count grows.

### ❌ Actual Behavior

- The orchestrator executes test suites, static analysis, docker/E2E stacks, mass file inspection, and code edits inline; delegation ratio reached 41:1 tool-calls-to-tasks, with marathon sessions (689 turns) delegating nothing at all.
- No mechanism — permissions, budget, or compaction — stops the context snowball; 0/26 orchestrator sessions compacted.

### Gentle AI Version

2.4.0-rc.8

### Operating System

Linux x86_64

### AI Agent / Client

OpenCode 1.17.20

### 📋 Affected Area

Other — orchestrator agent instructions + generated OpenCode agent config (permissions/tools), delegation contract enforcement

### 💡 Logs / Error Output

```
No error output — behavioral defect. Evidence is aggregate session analytics
(read-only SQLite queries over OpenCode storage), sanitized of project/user data:

- orchestrator sessions: 26; subagent sessions: 106
- orchestrator: 21.9M input + 1.3M output + 594.0M cache-read (72% of total)
- subagents:  9.2M input + 1.5M output + 235.5M cache-read (28%)
- single worst orchestrator session: 689 turns, ~194.2M cache-read, 0 task delegations,
  511 bash + 162 edit inline
- avg cache-read/session: orchestrator 22.9M vs general subagent 2.9M vs explore 1.1M
- orchestrator system prompt: ~69K chars fixed per-turn tax
- orchestrator sessions compacted: 0 of 26
```

title: Self-service recovery records the maintainer git identity as authorizing actor and ignores --actor
body:
## Problem

`gentle-ai review recover` is self-service — it works with no `--maintainer-authorization` and synthesizes one. But the synthesized binding records the repository's git identity as the authorizing actor, and it **ignores an explicitly supplied `--actor`**.

Observed just now. The command was invoked with `--actor gentle-ai-self-recovery`, and the committed record reads:

```
gentle-ai.review-recovery-authorization/v1
predecessor_lineage=review-…
predecessor_revision=sha256:…
target_identity=sha256:…
actor=<the repository's git user.name> <the repository's git user.email>
reason=self-recovery: escalated authority, target changed
```

So an automated recovery performed by an agent is recorded, in the audit trail, exactly as if the human whose git identity is configured had authorized it. Nothing distinguishes the two afterwards.

## Why this matters

The authorization binding exists so that an authority mutation carries who sanctioned it. If a self-service path stamps the configured human's identity without that human being involved, the field stops carrying that information — every recovery looks maintainer-authorized whether or not anyone was asked.

This also interacts with #3374: the transition that requests recovery is named `external.authorize_recovery` with an authorization schema, which reads as "get a human to sign". Three separate agent sessions concluded a human was required. One of them nearly hand-authored a binding naming the maintainer. The truth is the opposite — no human is required, and the record names the human anyway.

## Expected

Either the synthesized actor identifies the automated principal (the self-recovery identity the code already has a name for), or `--actor` is honoured when supplied, or the record distinguishes a synthesized authorization from a human-supplied one by some field other than the actor string. Any of the three restores the distinction; today none of them holds.

A caller-supplied `--actor` being silently ignored is worth fixing on its own: an argument the CLI accepts and discards is a defect independent of the audit question.

title: A candidate with a single path over 4 MiB starts, then loops on a refusal that can never resolve
body:
## Problem

A candidate whose **single** changed path exceeds 4 MiB starts successfully, is offered a reviewer collect slot, and then the launch refuses permanently. The refusal's action is to refresh and run again, which can never succeed, so the lineage sits in a loop with no exit.

This is the remaining part of the invariant #3367 was about: a candidate that starts must be a candidate STATUS can answer.

## Mechanism

`reviewLensContextByteBudget` and the per-read Git output limit are the same constant (`4<<20`). A single patch larger than that fails the **read** as `lens_context_inspection_failed`, before the block reaches its own byte accounting. So the budget probe reports the candidate as *unproven* rather than *over budget*, and START — correctly, per the fix in #3367 — refuses only on a proven verdict and lets it through.

The result is honest at every step and wrong overall: nothing ever measures the candidate, so nothing can refuse it up front, and the launch that does hit the wall reports a transient-shaped failure for a permanent condition.

## Expected

Either a read-limit refusal is classified as a budget verdict, so START can refuse the candidate before persisting authority, or the launch refusal names an action that can actually resolve it rather than "refresh and run again".

The first is likely the real end state, since a path that cannot be read within the same 4 MiB bound is over budget by definition — the two constants describing the same limit are what makes the distinction feel artificial.

## Provenance

Found during targeted validation of the #3367 correction, and confirmed to be **base-only**: the reviewer overlaid the frozen files and observed byte-identical behaviour before the correction, so it is pre-existing and not introduced by that change. Deliberately left out of scope there because the tests that pin it sit outside the frozen candidate.

title: bug(review): committed pre-push status fails before authority evaluation
body:
## Apparent provider defect

### Environment

- Gentle AI: `2.4.0-rc.8+dirty`
- Client: OpenCode
- OS/architecture: Linux x86_64
- Contract: `gentle-ai.review-integration/v2`

### Operation shape

1. Complete and approve a medium-risk workspace review.
2. Validate the staged candidate at the pre-commit gate.
3. Commit the exact approved candidate.
4. Request negotiated status for the same lineage at the pre-push gate using the committed-only projection.

The operation was attempted once. No push or remote mutation occurred.

### Expected behavior

Negotiated status should recognize the committed form of the exact approved candidate and return the provider-owned next transition for pre-push validation.

### Actual behavior

The read-only status operation exits before native authority evaluation with this sanitized envelope:

```json
{
  "schema": "gentle-ai.review-integration.failure/v2",
  "operation": "review.status",
  "phase": "pre_native",
  "code": "operation_failed",
  "mutation_outcome": "not_started",
  "authority_applicability": "not_evaluated",
  "retry_safe": true,
  "replayability": "not_replayable",
  "required_inputs": [],
  "next_action": "retry"
}
```

### Preserved state

- The reviewed commit remains local.
- No push was attempted.
- The approved review authority and receipt remain preserved.
- No retry or substitute lifecycle command was run.

### Minimal reproduction

Use any repository with an executable candidate: approve its workspace review, validate and commit the exact staged bytes, then request negotiated committed-only pre-push status for that lineage. Observe the generic pre-native failure instead of a next transition.

This report records observed evidence only; the root cause is unconfirmed. A closed report for fresh untracked candidates exists, but this occurrence affects the committed representation after a successful approved workspace lifecycle.

title: Stop transitions emit a bare reason_code, so consumers invent their own menus
body:
## Problem

A `stop` transition tells a consumer that the lifecycle cannot continue, and gives it a `reason_code` — and nothing else. The emitted object has exactly three fields:

```
next_transition: { kind, reason_code, collect }
```

The continuations exist. `reviewStopReasonNarration` (`internal/cli/review_narration.go:113`) carries a written statement for every stop reason code, and they are good: they name the maintainer path where one applies, and they name the self-service delivery exit `gentle-ai review mode disable --scope clone` with its caveat. But that narration never reaches the machine-readable transition, so an adapter routing from `next_transition` — which the integration contract requires consumers to do — receives a bare code.

## Consequence, observed in the field

When a runtime stalls, its agent has no continuations to offer, so it invents a menu. A real example reported today, after two failed reviewer captures:

> 1. Restart and retry (Recommended) — open a new session and resume from STATUS to try the same frozen slot once.
> 2. Stop here — keep the slice uncommitted and leave the review pending.
> 3. Type your own answer

The one exit the product documents for exactly that situation — disable review for this clone and deliver under ordinary repository policy — is absent, because the agent was never told it exists. Users then report that "skip RDD for this implementation" is missing, and they are right about the symptom even though the capability exists.

Note the contrast with consent: `gentle-ai.review-integration.consent/v3` carries `choices` with labels and per-choice `effect`, plus an `off_path` naming the kill switch. Consumers relay that faithfully and users see complete options. Stops have no equivalent, which is why only stops produce invented menus.

## Expected

Every `stop` transition carries its continuation in the transition itself, in the same machine-readable shape consent already uses: the statement, and where applicable the exact runnable command or commands. A consumer should be able to present a complete, correct set of exits without holding a private copy of the reason-code table.

## Notes

Today the only complete copy of that table lives in orchestrator instruction text held by some consumers and not others. That is why identical stalls produce good guidance in one runtime and invented menus in another. Moving it into the emitted envelope makes the behaviour uniform and removes a whole class of improvised prompts.

title: Recovery transition reads as maintainer-authorized but is self-service, and its trigger is inverted
body:
## Problem

When negotiated STATUS needs a recovery, it emits a collect input named `external.authorize_recovery` with schema `gentle-ai.review-recovery-authorization/v1`, and no executable transition. It reads exactly like "obtain a human maintainer's signature".

It is not. `gentle-ai review recover` is self-service: it works with no `--maintainer-authorization`, from both `approved` and `correction_required` predecessors, synthesizing `gentle-ai-self-recovery@localhost` as the actor.

The envelope never states this. It does not name the command, does not say a `--successor-lineage` must be invented by the caller, and does not say the authorization is auto-synthesized. Measured consequence: three independent agent sessions (two runtimes plus this one) concluded a human maintainer authorization was required and interrupted the maintainer for it. One of them hand-authored an authorization binding naming the maintainer as actor — an audit record of a decision the human never actually made, produced purely because the envelope implied it was needed.

## Expected

The transition is executable like every other one: `execute: review.recover` with the exact operation and ordered argument tokens, including whatever the caller must supply (the successor lineage identifier). If a human authorization is genuinely required in some cases, the envelope distinguishes those from the self-service ones rather than naming every case "authorize".

## Second, related defect: the discriminator is inverted

`recovery_authorization_required` fires **if and only if** the changed-path set is identical to the reviewed manifest and only the content differs. Add a path or remove one and STATUS offers a plain fresh START instead.

So the most surgical iteration — fixing exactly the reviewed files — is the only case that pays the recovery cost, while adding a throwaway file buys a free reset. Restoring the exact reviewed bytes deterministically restores the receipt, and committing the approved candidate retires it.

title: Lock contention is reported as authority corruption in three places
body:
## Problem

Lock contention is reported to the operator as store corruption in three places. This makes a transient, retry-safe condition look like unrecoverable damage, and sends people to the recovery-of-last-resort path for a problem that clears by waiting.

1. `internal/cli/review_facade.go:3269-3275` discards the error returned by `CompactAuthorityLeaves` entirely and reports `authority_corrupted / record_or_graph_invalid`. A concurrent `review repair` makes an unrelated `review validate` look like store damage.
2. A process killed between the LOCK file's `Truncate(0)` and its `Write` leaves a zero-byte LOCK, which parses as `lock_ambiguous`, and the whole store then reports corrupted.
3. `internal/reviewtransaction/authority_repair.go:243` counts a live lock holder in the same `conflicts` counter as a real collision, so a concurrent `start` makes `repair` report `conflicting`.

The gate window is the one place this was handled properly: `internal/reviewtransaction/compact_gate.go:453-468` sets `Contended` and states the operation "reached no verdict … retry".

`review recover` under contention also emits the same `"review transaction changed concurrently:"` headline as a genuine revision mismatch, as plain text rather than a typed JSON envelope.

## Expected

Contention is surfaced with its existing typed codes (`authority_lock_contention`, `authority_lock_timeout`, `authority_lock_cancelled`, `store_lock_unavailable`) and marked retry-safe, following the `compact_gate.go` precedent. Corruption is reported only when the store is actually damaged.

## Impact

A full maintainer day was spent today diagnosing "authority_corrupted" occurrences that were, at least in part, two agents contending on one shared store from different worktrees.

title: Canonical 4R missed a deterministic CRITICAL that a second 4R over the same code found
body:
## Observation

A canonical four-lens review missed a deterministic, candidate-caused CRITICAL defect that a second four-lens review over a superset of the same code found immediately. This is not a reproduction of a code defect; it is a measured gap in review effectiveness, recorded so it can be investigated rather than assumed away.

## What happened

Branch `fix/3285-rar-path-rollback`, two consecutive reviews against the same repository:

**Round 1** — lineage `review-cc6d6de225d19d86`, high risk, canonical 4R over a 360-line candidate. The candidate changed `createPrivateRARDirectory` so that a directory failing its own owner-only validation is no longer removed, and is instead repaired in place. It kept the pre-existing `created` predicate, so the new repair reads `if validateErr != nil && created`.

Round 1 returned 2 CRITICAL findings (a symlink-following `chmod`, and an untested Windows path). It did **not** report that gating the repair on `created` makes recovery once-only.

**Round 2** — lineage `review-rar-toctou-successor-01`, high risk, canonical 4R over the 508-line superset (round 1's change plus its correction). It reported 3 CRITICAL findings, all one root cause, all classified `causal_disposition: introduced`:

- `R4-unix-repair-once-only` (`internal/reviewtransaction/rar_path_safety_unix.go:64`, deterministic)
- `R4-windows-repair-once-only` (`internal/reviewtransaction/rar_path_safety_windows.go:103`, deterministic)
- `R3-retained-entry-unrecoverable-when-not-a-directory` (`internal/reviewtransaction/rar_path_safety_unix.go:80-87`, inferential)

The defect: because the repair is gated on `created`, any interruption between `mkdir` and a successful repair (process kill, OOM, ENOSPC/EPERM/EINTR, a concurrent process that took the `created == true` branch and died) leaves an unsafe directory that no later invocation ever repairs, since the next `mkdir` returns EEXIST and `created` is false. Round 1's change converted "remove it and let the operator retry cleanly" into "keep it unsafe forever".

## Why it is worth investigating

The missed finding was deterministic, not inferential, and it is a direct consequence of the single behavioural change round 1 introduced. Two of the three reports are the same defect on two platforms, so a single insight would have produced all of them. Whatever made it visible in round 2 (a larger candidate, the symlink fix making the recovery path more salient, or ordinary run-to-run variance) is not currently measurable.

## Suggested investigation

There is no way today to tell how much of a candidate's real defect population a canonical 4R catches. A seeded-defect harness would answer it: plant a catalogue of known defect classes (once-only recovery, TOCTOU, silent failure swallowing, unreachable error branches, contract drift) into throwaway candidates, run the canonical lens selection, and record the catch rate per lens and per class. That turns lens effectiveness from an assumption into a number, and it would show whether specific classes are systematically invisible.

The cross-lane battery is the natural home for such a harness, though it costs model spend per seeded candidate and would need to run outside the default tiers.

title: feat(skills): provider-aware chained-pr routing for shipped delivery
body:
Parent epic: #3154

## Outcome
The shipped `chained-pr` skill becomes a thin provider-aware policy wrapper: proven-capable GitHub repositories use pinned native stacks, unproven GitHub repositories stop with actionable guidance, and positively identified non-GitHub repositories retain the portable workflow.

## Work units
One work unit per PR by default. Safety target: at most 300 changed lines. Hard cap: 400.

1. Detect the Git host through read-only signals. Unknown or ambiguous hosts stop fail-closed.
2. Add the GitHub-native route, pinned `gh-stack` command surface, attribution, review limits, issue-linking policy, and remote-authority boundary.
3. Preserve the portable non-GitHub route and protect it with regression evidence.

## Dependencies and stop gates
- GitHub-native activation waits for Cluster 5's successful authorized remote proof.
- Repository stack capability has no confirmed read-only API field. Absence of trusted proof means actionable stop, never portable fallback.
- Remote create, submit, sync, update, and merge require bounded authority separate from issue approval, RDD receipts, phase approval, and `auto-chain`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `chained-pr` remains a thin wrapper around the official pinned GitHub stack workflow.
- [ ] GitHub without proven capability stops with official actionable guidance and no silent installation or fallback choreography.
- [ ] Unknown or ambiguous host detection stops fail-closed.
- [ ] Positively identified non-GitHub providers preserve manual chaining, `feature-branch-chain`, strategy selection, and maintainer-approved exceptions.
- [ ] Gentle AI repository-specific governance does not leak into user repositories.

## Out of scope
CI governance, SDD mirror migration, the capability proof itself, and bench journeys.

## Rollback and delivery boundary
Revert the provider routing and return to the current portable-only shipped skill. Tests and policy text stay with each behavior work unit.

title: feat(repo): add a minimal CODEOWNERS policy
body:
### Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand that PRs will be rejected if the linked issue does not have `status:approved`

### 🔍 Affected Area

Other

### 💡 Problem Statement

The repository does not currently have a CODEOWNERS file.

As a result:

- pull requests do not automatically request reviews based on the paths they modify;
- repository ownership is not recorded in a machine-readable form;
- future ownership delegation has no established place to be documented.

`CONTRIBUTORS.md` currently documents `@[maintainer]` as a maintainer, but it may not be the authoritative or complete maintainer registry. This proposal therefore does not assume that other maintainers do not exist.

Public repository information is also insufficient to verify the complete list of collaborators or organization teams with write access. Maintainer confirmation is required before selecting the initial code owners.

### 📦 Proposed Solution

Add a `.github/CODEOWNERS` file with a repository-wide fallback and an ownership mapping explicitly confirmed by the maintainers.

Before implementation, maintainers should confirm:

- the complete set of users or teams eligible to appear in CODEOWNERS;
- that every selected owner has write access to the repository;
- whether ownership should begin with one repository-wide fallback or include domain-specific assignments;
- who should own critical areas such as review authority, agent adapters, SDD, benchmarks, CI, documentation, and skills.

A minimal initial file could look like this once the default owner has been confirmed:


```text
# Default repository owner.
* @confirmed-owner
```
The file should not repeat the same owner for every directory unless those entries communicate a meaningful ownership boundary. Domain-specific patterns can be added when additional maintainers or visible organization teams are formally assigned responsibility.

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

### Infer owners from contribution history

Rejected. Commit frequency demonstrates contribution activity, not current responsibility, availability, or write access.

### Use every contributor listed in CONTRIBUTORS.md

Rejected. Contributors are not necessarily maintainers or eligible code owners.

### Assign only the currently documented maintainer without confirmation

Not recommended. `CONTRIBUTORS.md` may not contain the complete maintainer list, and GitHub requires code owners to have write access.

### Require code-owner approval immediately

Deferred. Mandatory approval should be considered separately after confirming that the ownership model has enough eligible owners to avoid self-approval and maintainer-availability deadlocks.

### 📎 Additional Context

No existing CODEOWNERS file, CODEOWNERS issue, or CODEOWNERS pull request was found.

The repository's active `pr` ruleset currently enforces status checks and other repository policies, but it does not require code-owner approval. This issue proposes establishing the ownership file first; changing merge requirements is intentionally outside its scope.

### Suggested ownership domains for future maintainer consideration include:

- `internal/reviewtransaction/` and `internal/reviewerprovider/`;
- `internal/agents/`;
- `internal/tui/`, `internal/cli/`, and `internal/app/`;
- `openspec/`;
- `bench/`;
- `.github/` and `scripts/`;
- `docs/`;
- `skills/` and `internal/assets/skills/`;
- `contracts/`.
### Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Maintainers confirm the initial ownership mapping.
- [ ] Every referenced user or team has write access to the repository.
- [ ] `.github/CODEOWNERS` is added.
- [ ] A default `*` rule covers every repository path.
- [ ] No owner is inferred solely from contribution history.
- [ ] No undocumented contributor or organization team is added without explicit confirmation.
- [ ] GitHub recognizes the file without invalid-owner warnings.
- [ ] The implementation pull request follows the repository's issue-first workflow.
### Non-goals
- Enabling mandatory code-owner approval in the repository ruleset.
- Changing repository permissions.
- Creating GitHub teams.
- Assigning ownership based only on commit frequency.
- Modifying existing CI or pull-request checks.
- Treating CONTRIBUTORS.md as authoritative without maintainer confirmation.

title: bug(review): v9fs start leaves unverifiable captured artifacts after unknown outcome
body:
## Automated provider-defect report

This report was prepared with explicit user consent after a negotiated review could not continue. It reports observed behavior only; no root cause is asserted.

## Environment

- Gentle AI: `2.4.0-rc.8`
- OS/architecture: Linux x86_64
- Repository filesystem reported by the runtime: `v9fs`
- Git metadata directory ownership/mode: current uid/current gid, mode `0777`
- Client/agent binding: OpenCode / `opencode`
- Review contract: `gentle-ai.review-integration/v2`
- Projection: workspace
- Frozen candidate: 4 changed files, 44 changed lines, high tier

## Operation shape and bounded attempts

1. Negotiated status returned an exact `review.start` transition for an unreviewed workspace candidate.
2. The user explicitly granted review consent for that exact frozen target.
3. The exact returned start operation was invoked once.
4. Start returned an unknown operation outcome, with mutation outcome unknown, retry marked unsafe, and status required. The observed failure envelope reported an unsafe private review-authority location; the location was redacted before this report.
5. Negotiated status was queried once, as required. It discovered a current-target compact-v2 lineage in `reviewing` state, but returned terminal stop because captured artifacts were missing or failed verification.

Safe opaque identifiers:

- Lineage: `review-3fb0fd3b350c681`
- Target: `sha256:3fb0fd3b3506c68135aae27e591201c7d738c7b9a7c08ac2e3762b8f610f0b8e`
- Authority revision: `sha256:428c72ac3271b94775824943403a62b76b2739e378e91a5dd58de9c4942b70d4`

## Expected behavior

The exact consented start should either:

- create a verifiable review lineage and return the next negotiated transition; or
- fail without committing review authority, with an unambiguous safe continuation.

## Actual behavior

The start response could not establish whether mutation occurred. The required follow-up status then found a committed reviewing lineage whose captured artifacts were unverifiable, leaving the review unable to continue automatically.

## Minimal reproduction

```text
gentle-ai review status --cwd <repo> --contract gentle-ai.review-integration/v2 --agent opencode --next-transition
# Execute the exact returned review.start transition and grant consent for the frozen candidate.
gentle-ai review status --cwd <repo> --contract gentle-ai.review-integration/v2 --agent opencode --next-transition
```

Observed terminal behavior: the second status discovers the lineage but stops because captured artifacts cannot be verified.

## Duplicate-search distinction

The closest existing report concerns a fixed-owner `fuseblk`/`ntfs-3g` mount where no authority is persisted. This occurrence is materially different: the filesystem reports `v9fs`, the Git metadata directory reports the current uid as owner, and the required status reconciliation discovers a persisted `reviewing` lineage whose captured artifacts are unverifiable.

## Preserved-state evidence

- The frozen workspace candidate remained unchanged after the failed review start.
- No retry was attempted after the unknown mutation outcome.
- No repository source, diff, raw arguments, environment values, credentials, absolute paths, usernames, hostnames, or private project identifiers are included in this report.

title: fix(opencode): route manual advisory review outside provider-bound RDD roles
body:
### Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and found no exact equivalent root-level tracker.
- [x] I reviewed #3119 and its sanitized occurrences before creating this canonical maintainer-owned issue.
- [x] As a maintainer, I approve this corrected scope for implementation.

### 📝 Bug Description

When an ordinary manual read-only review is requested from an OpenCode session without a formal receipt-driven development (RDD) collection transition, orchestration can select a provider-bound `review-*` actor. OpenCode then correctly routes that actor through the native immutable-review transport, which rejects the launch because the ordinary task has no provider-issued repository-context binding.

The defect is the earlier role selection. Formal `review-*` actors are lifecycle-only and must retain their immutable provider binding. Ordinary advisory review must use a separate non-authority read-only route.

### 🔄 Steps to Reproduce

1. Use OpenCode with clone-local RDD disabled.
2. Prepare a committed or uncommitted candidate.
3. Request an ordinary manual read-only review, not a formal RDD review.
4. Observe orchestration select `review-readability`, `review-reliability`, or another formal `review-*` actor.
5. Observe the task fail before reviewer launch because no provider-issued repository-context binding exists.

### ✅ Expected Behavior

An unbound ordinary advisory review is routed through native `explore`, with the exact candidate evidence, review focus, and acceptance criteria materialized by the parent. The result remains advisory and creates no lineage, receipt, approval, delivery gate, or other RDD authority.

Formal `review-*` actors continue to launch only from an exact provider-issued collection transition.

### ❌ Actual Behavior

An ordinary advisory request can be routed to a formal lifecycle actor. Name-based transport interception then requires a binding that cannot exist for that ordinary request, so no reviewer launches. A native `explore` fallback can inspect the same repository successfully.

---
### 🖥️ Environment

### Gentle AI Version

Confirmed occurrences on `2.3.0` and `2.4.0-rc.8`.

### Operating System

Windows x64 and Linux x86_64.

### AI Agent / Client

OpenCode `1.18.16` and `1.18.18`.

### 📋 Affected Area

OpenCode agent routing and native review transport boundary.

### 💡 Logs / Error Output

```text
immutable OpenCode candidate inspection requires a repository-context binding; review lens-context accepts only the opaque provider-issued handle and has no --cwd fallback
```

### Confirmed Root Cause

- OpenCode intercepts formal review tasks by `subagent_type`.
- The formal agents are tool-free and accept only provider-injected immutable evidence.
- Binding validation occurs before disabled-RDD behavior can provide an ordinary path.
- Relaxing the binding would create a second mutable contract for lifecycle actors and weaken RDD isolation.
- The root correction is to keep formal transport unchanged and route ordinary advisory intent outside that actor family.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] OpenCode routing states that `review-*` actors may be dispatched only from an exact provider-issued formal collection transition.
- [ ] An ordinary unbound manual read-only review routes through native `explore`.
- [ ] The parent supplies exact candidate evidence, changed paths or relevant bytes, requested review focus, and acceptance criteria to the advisory task.
- [ ] The advisory result cannot claim PASS, receipt, approval, gate, or delivery authority.
- [ ] A pinned OpenCode runtime test covers clone-local RDD disabled with both committed and uncommitted candidate shapes.
- [ ] The disabled-RDD test proves one advisory child launch, no formal review relay, no lineage or receipt, no authority mutation, unchanged candidate bytes, and mode still disabled.
- [ ] An unbound explicit `review-*` task remains rejected before reviewer launch and names the working ordinary advisory continuation.
- [ ] A bound-RDD positive control proves a negotiated provider-bound reviewer still relays and captures exactly once.
- [ ] Component-absent or unmanaged OpenCode continues to use native `explore` without creating managed-role or authority state.
- [ ] Closure evidence comes from the actual OpenCode runtime because the core CLI bench cannot observe Task selection or child execution.

### Non-Goals

- Making `repository_context` optional.
- Adding a `--cwd` fallback to formal review transport.
- Allowing unbound execution of formal `review-*` actors.
- Creating `gentle-reviewer`, `gentle-worker`, a `direct-run` identity, model-picker integration, or profile-specific roles.
- Changing native RDD lens selection, evidence admission, capture, correction, receipt, or delivery semantics.

### Evidence and Related Work

- Original community report and preserved discussion: #3119.
- Additional occurrence on `2.3.0`: https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues/3119#issuecomment-5285884258
- Linux occurrence on `2.3.0`: https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues/3119#issuecomment-5296525226
- Windows occurrence on `2.4.0-rc.8`: https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues/3119#issuecomment-5298267780
- Root-cause audit: https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues/3119#issuecomment-5301173546
- #3026 combines optional managed-reviewer and mutating-worker product work with independent rollback boundaries. It is not required to close this narrow routing defect.

This canonical tracker supersedes #3119 as implementation authority while preserving the original reporter and occurrence evidence there.

title: bug(hooks): Codex SessionStart hook is POSIX-only and never migrates to a Windows command
body:
## Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues) and this is not a duplicate. #2124 covers the Claude `UserPromptSubmit` hook and PR #2342 fixes it there; @ardelperal confirmed on #2807 that Codex is deliberately out of scope for #2124. Searches for `commandWindows`, `Codex SessionStart`, and `Codex hook Windows` return only #2124.
- [x] I understand that PRs will be rejected if the linked issue does not have `status:approved`

## 📝 Bug Description

The Codex `SessionStart` skill-registry hook is written as a POSIX shell one-liner and never emits a Windows variant, so it cannot run under Windows PowerShell 5.1.

`internal/components/sdd/inject.go:1555`:

```go
const command = `gentle-ai skill-registry refresh --quiet --no-gitignore --cwd "$PWD" || true`
```

`||` is a pipeline chain operator introduced in PowerShell 7. Under PowerShell 5.1, still the default shell on stock Windows, it is a parse error rather than a runtime failure, so the hook never executes and the skill registry is never refreshed at session start.

Two distinct halves:

1. **No Windows command is emitted.** Codex's hook contract carries a separate `commandWindows` field, and nothing in the repository writes it. `rg -in 'commandWindows' --glob '!*_test.go'` returns no Go source match on `main` at `4004a082`.
2. **A legacy bash-only hook is never migrated.** The freshness check at line 1556 is `claudeHookExists(root, command)`, comparing the POSIX command only. A hook that already exists without a Windows variant therefore counts as current forever, so a user who installed before any fix keeps the broken hook after upgrading.

This is the same root cause as #2124 but a different consumer and a different contract field: Claude resolves it through `shell`, Codex through `commandWindows`.

## 🔄 Steps to Reproduce

1. On Windows with PowerShell 5.1 as the default shell, install or sync Gentle AI with Codex present.
2. Open `~/.codex/hooks.json` and read `hooks.SessionStart[].hooks[]`.
3. Observe a single `command` value ending in `|| true` and no `commandWindows` key.
4. Start a Codex session so `SessionStart` fires.
5. Run `gentle-ai sync` again and re-read the file.

## ✅ Expected Behavior

The Codex `SessionStart` hook should carry a Windows-executable command, through the `commandWindows` field its contract defines, alongside the POSIX `command`.

Re-running `sync` should treat a pre-existing bash-only hook as stale and migrate it, so upgrading is enough to repair an installation made before the fix.

## ❌ Actual Behavior

Only the POSIX `command` is written. On PowerShell 5.1 it fails to parse, the skill registry is not refreshed, and no error surfaces to the user because the hook body never runs.

Re-running `sync` does not repair it: the freshness check matches on the POSIX command alone, so the incomplete hook is considered current and left in place.

## Gentle AI Version

```text
2.4.0-rc.8
```

Also present on `main` at `4004a082`.

## Operating System

Windows

## AI Agent / Client

Other (Codex)

## 📋 Affected Area

Installation Pipeline

## 💡 Logs / Error Output

The shape written today, from `ensureCodexSkillRegistryHook`:

```json
{
  "matcher": "startup|resume|clear|compact",
  "hooks": [
    {
      "type": "command",
      "command": "gentle-ai skill-registry refresh --quiet --no-gitignore --cwd \"$PWD\" || true",
      "timeout": 30,
      "statusMessage": "Refreshing skill registry"
    }
  ]
}
```

PowerShell 5.1 rejects `||` at parse time:

```text
The token '||' is not a valid statement separator in this version.
```

## Additional Context

I have a working implementation from the closed PR #2807, whose Claude half duplicated the earlier #2342 and was closed in its favour. The Codex half is a separate self-contained commit (`inject.go` +19, `inject_test.go` +66): it threads a `wantCommandWindows` parameter through `pruneStaleSkillRegistryHooks` so a hook counts as current only when both `command` and `commandWindows` match, which makes the legacy bash-only hook stale and migrates it.

It layers on the Windows command definitions #2342 introduces, so it should land after that merges rather than racing it. Happy to open the PR once this is approved and #2342 is in, or to hand the approach to whoever owns the area.

Reported from the contributor side; I cannot apply labels.

title: docs(pr-template): the template's relative links 404 once it renders into a pull request body
body:
### Pre-flight Checklist - [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues) and this is not a duplicate - [x] I understand that PRs will be rejected if the linked issue does not have `status:approved` ### 📝 Bug Description **The invariant.** A link shipped inside a pull request template must resolve from the context the template renders into (a pull request body), not only from the context it is stored in (a file under `.github/`). Relative targets satisfy the second and not the first, because GitHub copies the template body verbatim into the pull request description and does not rewrite relative link targets when it renders an issue or pull request body. The `href` survives unchanged, and the browser resolves it against `https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/pull/`, which lands it on the repository web root .. `https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/AI_POLICY.md` .. instead of on the `blob/main` tree path the document is actually served from. `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` violates it in two places: | Line | Shipped target | Resolves to, from a PR body | Status | |---|---|---|---| | `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md:55` | `../AI_POLICY.md` | `https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/AI_POLICY.md` | 404 | | `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md:78` | `../bench/README.md` | `https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/bench/README.md` | 404 | Both documents exist and are reachable at `/blob/main/AI_POLICY.md` and `/blob/main/bench/README.md`, both 200. The targets are fine; the form of the reference is not. **This is not visible in code review.** On the blob page GitHub *does* rewrite relative targets, so line 55 renders as `href="/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/blob/main/AI_POLICY.md"` and line 78 as `href="/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/blob/main/bench/README.md"`. Both work when you click them while reviewing the file. The defect does not appear in the rendering path a reviewer opens the file in; it appears in the one the template renders into. **The enumeration is complete, and here is how I established it.** `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` contains exactly three markdown links and no reference-style links or autolinks: line 55, line 78, and line 115 (`https://www.conventionalcommits.org/`, already absolute and unaffected). Two of the three are relative, and both are listed above. It is also the only pull request template in the repository: there is no `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/` directory and no root-level or `docs/` variant. The issue forms under `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` do reach a body .. a checkbox label is copied into the issue it creates .. but they are outside the class because every link they carry is already absolute, not because they never reach a body. So the class is exactly two occurrences in one file, and one fix on that file closes it. Step 1 and step 7 of the reproduction below re-derive this; if either turns up a fourth link, another template location, or a relative link in the forms, this paragraph is wrong. **The correct form already exists in-repo.** `CONTRIBUTING.md:59` links the same policy document as `[AI-Assisted Contribution Policy](AI_POLICY.md)`, with no `../`, correct from the repository root. `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug_report.yml:22` carries an absolute URL inside a checkbox label, and that label is copied into an issue body. This reads as an oversight in the pull request template rather than a deliberate difference. This is a documentation defect. It does not affect security, correctness, or CI. ### 🔄 Steps to Reproduce All commands are read-only. Of the steps below, step 1 and the last two commands of step 7 need a clone with `origin` fetched; step 4 is offline; steps 2, 3, 5, 6 and the first command of step 7 are HTTP against the public repository. Pinned to `main` at `4004a0825d03a3d123a3c4f67bf375cb16fd6d8c`. The steps read `origin/main`, and the template is byte-identical between that commit and current `main`, so both resolve to the same file: `git diff --stat 4004a0825d03a3d123a3c4f67bf375cb16fd6d8c origin/main -- .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` prints nothing. If it prints a diff for you, the template has moved since and the outputs below may no longer match. 1. Enumerate every link in the template, and confirm two of the three are relative: ```bash git show origin/main:.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md | rg -n '\]\(' ``` 2. Confirm GitHub leaves a relative target untouched when it renders an issue or pull request body (`gfm` mode with repository context): ```bash gh api -X POST markdown -f mode=gfm -f context=Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai \ -f text='See the [benchmark guide](../bench/README.md).' gh api -X POST markdown -f mode=gfm -f context=Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai \ -f text='See [AI_POLICY.md](../AI_POLICY.md) for the canonical policy.' ``` 3. Confirm the same on real, already-published pull request bodies, using GitHub's own server-rendered HTML rather than a local renderer: ```bash for n in 2958 2988; do gh api "repos/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/pulls/$n" \ -H "Accept: application/vnd.github.html+json" --jq '.body_html' \ | rg -o 'href="[^"]*bench/README[^"]*"' | sort -u done ``` 4. Perform the resolution itself, so the chain is measured rather than asserted. This applies the standard relative-URL rules against a pull request page. The first input is the unrewritten `href` step 3 read out of the published bodies of #2958 and #2988. The second is the target shipped on template line 55, whose unrewritten `href` step 2 returns: ```bash python3 -c "from urllib.parse import urljoin; print(urljoin('https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/pull/2988', '../bench/README.md'))" python3 -c "from urllib.parse import urljoin; print(urljoin('https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/pull/2988', '../AI_POLICY.md'))" ``` 5. Request the two URLs step 4 produced: ```bash curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/AI_POLICY.md" curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/bench/README.md" ``` 6. Request the working forms, for contrast: ```bash curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/blob/main/AI_POLICY.md" curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/blob/main/bench/README.md" ``` 7. Confirm the blob page rewrites both targets, which is why review does not catch this; then re-derive the enumeration. What the measurement does settle is that this is not theoretical .. 2 of the 562 pull requests created since line 78 landed already quote the broken href in their published description, and the template still carries the relative form. **Smallest change that restores the invariant.** Rewrite the two targets so neither depends on the page it is rendered from. The lines also name a specific owner, repository, and branch. I would choose the absolute URLs. Line 55 introduces its target as "the canonical policy", and for a contribution flowing back here the canonical policy and the benchmark guide that gates its validation *are* this repository's, so a fork pointing upstream is closer to what those lines are asking for than a regression. It also matches the checkbox label cited above, which already solves the same problem the same way. A root-relative `/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/blob/main/...` is shorter and behaves identically, with the same hardcoding, so it is a formatting preference rather than a different answer.

title: fix(reporting): make review tool-fault reports evidence-only and reuse canonical publication
body:
### Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand that PRs will be rejected if the linked issue does not have `status:approved`

### 📝 Bug Description

Review tool-fault reporting and provider-defect reporting currently form two partial publication mechanisms instead of one governed path.

On current `main` (`a676d9e97ae9e9f8f1612c71f7d6a69cb346f120`):

- `internal/cli/review_defect_report.go` captures review failure evidence, renders a public-looking approximation of the Bug Report form, persists it under the Git common directory, and points the operator to `/issues/new/choose`.
- The rendered body uses a second hard-coded format, omits required form semantics, and includes `generated_at` in content used for the filename hash, so equivalent occurrences do not deduplicate stably across timestamps.
- Persistence uses overwrite-capable file writing instead of the repository's existing atomic no-replace publication pattern.
- The provider-defect handoff separately owns classification, consent, canonical lookup, published-fix routing, mutation uncertainty, and candidate continuation.
- Canonical `issue-creation` separately owns repository-policy discovery and is being updated by #3274 to own public Issue Form materialization and GitHub CLI transport.

Review Go should produce bounded private evidence only. Provider governance should decide whether reporting is admissible. Canonical `issue-creation` should be the only authority that materializes and writes public issues or comments.

### 🔄 Steps to Reproduce

1. Inspect `internal/cli/review_defect_report.go`.
2. Observe the Go Issue Form approximation, hard-coded issue chooser URL, timestamp-bearing render, and direct file write.
3. Inspect the provider-defect handoff in `internal/assets/generic/sdd-orchestrator.md`.
4. Observe that public reporting policy exists independently from the review draft renderer.
5. Inspect skill distribution and observe that every surface shipping the provider handoff is not yet guaranteed to load canonical `issue-creation`.

### ✅ Expected Behavior

#### Review Go is evidence-only

Review Go captures only bounded, allowlisted evidence needed to identify an occurrence:

- operation shape, never raw argv;
- reason code;
- review state or phase;
- Gentle AI version/build;
- operating system and architecture;
- opaque lineage, target, or revision identifiers only when their format is validated.

Arbitrary error prose, terminal prose, maps, paths, credentials, environment values, repository names, source, and diffs must not enter the evidence record. Every field has strict character and size limits.

Equivalent evidence uses a stable identity independent of timestamps. Persistence resolves the correct Git common directory and reuses the existing private atomic no-replace pattern. Identical concurrent writers converge, conflicting bytes are never overwritten, temporary files are cleaned up, and any evidence failure leaves the original review error authoritative.

#### Delete the parallel publisher

Remove from Review Go:

- the approximate Issue Form renderer;
- `/issues/new/choose`;
- the manual filing instruction;
- public template, duplicate, label, consent, GitHub mutation, and continuation policy.

The returned error may state that private evidence was saved, but must never claim public reporting occurred.

#### Preserve provider governance

Provider-defect governance remains responsible for:

- distinguishing an actual Gentle AI defect from expected refusals, model/provider failures, client runtime failures, environment problems, caller input, or repository state;
- explicit report consent;
- definitive open-and-closed canonical lookup;
- published-fix and installed-channel routing;
- create, occurrence-comment, update-guidance, regression, no-mutation, and uncertainty decisions;
- exact candidate-scoped continuation.

The handoff delegates public body materialization, final privacy scanning, create/comment transport, and read-back to canonical `issue-creation` instead of reproducing those rules.

Provider continuation requires the exact captured `gentle-ai.review-integration.consent/v3` envelope, target identity, declined invocation, and held consumer continuation. If any element is absent or ambiguous, fail closed. Never synthesize a decline command, target, STATUS transition, or continuation.

A later explicit generic issue request may use the private evidence through `issue-creation`, but it does not inherit provider consent and must not execute or synthesize decline or STATUS.

#### Distribution invariant

Every shipped surface containing the provider-defect handoff must install and load canonical `issue-creation`. A surface that cannot provide the skill must not promise canonical publication.

### ❌ Actual Behavior

Review Go currently produces a public-looking second report format and manual browser destination, while provider governance separately describes reporting decisions. This duplicates responsibility and leaves canonical issue publication disconnected from native review evidence.

### Gentle AI Version

Current `main` source audit at `a676d9e97ae9e9f8f1612c71f7d6a69cb346f120`.

### Operating System

Windows

### AI Agent / Client

OpenCode

### 📋 Affected Area

CLI (commands, flags)

### 💡 Logs / Error Output

```shell
Current review tool-fault path:
capture -> scrub -> render approximate issue body -> save private Markdown -> point to /issues/new/choose

Proposed path:
capture allowlisted evidence -> persist privately -> provider governance -> canonical issue-creation
```

### Additional Context

Related governance and symptom issues were reviewed, including #2887, #3095, #2366, #2986, #3083, #2818, #2340, and #3266. They do not own this deletion-first convergence root. #3274 is the generic publication work this issue must reuse after its expanded scope is reconfirmed.

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Review evidence is allowlisted, bounded, and excludes raw or narrative private input.
- [ ] Stable deduplication excludes timestamps and clocks.
- [ ] Evidence uses the correct Git common directory and atomic private no-replace publication.
- [ ] Concurrent identical writers converge; conflicting bytes are never overwritten.
- [ ] Evidence-generation or persistence failure never masks or replaces the original review error or typed envelope.
- [ ] The Go renderer, chooser URL, and manual filing instruction are deleted.
- [ ] Review Go contains no Issue Form, GitHub create/comment, duplicate, label, consent, or continuation policy.
- [ ] Provider classification, consent, definitive lookup, published-fix/channel routing, uncertainty, and exact continuation remain authoritative.
- [ ] Public materialization, final privacy, create/comment transport, and read-back delegate to canonical `issue-creation`.
- [ ] Missing or mismatched consent v3, target, decline invocation, or continuation fails closed without synthesized substitutes.
- [ ] A later explicit generic request can use private evidence without inheriting or inventing provider consent.
- [ ] Every provider-handoff delivery surface includes and can load `issue-creation`.
- [ ] Tests cover bounds, rejected inputs, stable dedupe, atomic races, linked worktrees, cleanup, original-error preservation, delegation, exact continuation, and skill distribution.
- [ ] Repository-wide guards prove the renderer, chooser URL, and duplicate publication policy are absent.
- [ ] No new CLI, protocol, lifecycle state, service, queue, database, GitHub client, or renderer is introduced.

#### Deletion-first scope

Delete the Go public renderer and browser instruction. Reuse existing Git common-dir identity, atomic private publication, provider governance, and canonical `issue-creation`.

title: feat(skills): route managed skills by placement and runtime discovery
body:
### Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand that PRs will be rejected if the linked issue does not have `status:approved`

### 🔍 Affected Area

Installation Pipeline

### 💡 Problem Statement

Gentle AI currently materializes managed skills through two independent paths:

```text
agent-specific component injection
    -> adapter.SkillsDir()

compatibility refresh
    -> ~/.agents/skills
```

The compatibility refresh was added to fix a real stale-copy defect (#742), but keeping both copies synchronized leaves the same logical managed skill with multiple physical locations.

That creates several problems:

- a stale or user-modified shared copy can compete with the managed copy selected for a runtime;
- some runtimes report duplicate skills when they scan both roots;
- workflow-critical skills are exposed to a shared scope that users commonly manage directly;
- install, sync, backup, verification, and uninstall must reason about redundant physical copies;
- runtime precedence differs by agent, so "shared support" alone does not tell us which copy is effective.

The repository already has two relevant architectural boundaries:

1. adapters own provider-specific paths and runtime capabilities;
2. upstream ownership work (#1876/#1884) owns generalized per-resource mutation/removal authority.

What is missing is a **skill placement and discovery-routing contract** that decides where a compatible skill should be materialized without introducing another parallel authority.

### 📦 Proposed Solution

### 1. Add canonical skill placement metadata

Introduce two semantic placement classes:

```text
agent-skills-shared
agent-skills-required
```

`agent-skills-shared` means a portable skill intended for cross-agent/user-managed use.

`agent-skills-required` means a skill whose availability and version coherence are required by a Gentle AI-managed workflow.

Placement is semantic; it is **not** a fixed path alias.

### 2. Let adapters expose verified discovery roots and precedence

Add an optional adapter capability conceptually equivalent to:

```go
type SkillDiscoveryProvider interface {
    SkillDiscovery(homeDir string) SkillDiscoveryCapabilities
}

type SkillDiscoveryRoot struct {
    Scope SkillDiscoveryScope
    Path  string
}

type SkillDiscoveryCapabilities struct {
    // Highest runtime precedence first.
    Roots []SkillDiscoveryRoot
}
```

Adapters should declare only roots that are verified for deduplicated routing.

Unverified/undocumented shared discovery fails closed to the existing native route rather than adding a runtime "confidence" state.

If an adapter does not implement this optional capability, its existing `SkillsDir()` remains the only known root.

Agents outside generic skill injection today (for example Pi under its current adapter contract) remain outside this routing mechanism.

### 3. Resolve one effective route per skill and agent

Conceptually:

```text
skill placement
+
verified ordered discovery roots
+
canonical ownership classification for existing copies
        ↓
SkillRoute
        ↓
effective destination
legacy migration candidates
blocking shadow, if any
```

Core invariant:

> A managed skill should have one effective materialization for a compatible runtime unless an explicit runtime compatibility requirement proves that multiple copies are necessary.

For shared skills:

```text
verified shared-global root
-> shared root

no verified shared-global root
-> native fallback
```

For required skills:

```text
choose a managed route that stays authoritative under runtime precedence
```

### 4. Keep safe legacy migration in scope without inventing a new ledger

Simply stopping writes to old shared copies would recreate the stale-copy failure class fixed by #742.

Legacy migration must therefore use the canonical managed-resource ownership authority from #1876/#1884 (or its eventual implementation):

```text
owned-unchanged
-> eligible for transactional migration/removal

owned-modified
-> preserve

unknown
-> preserve
```

Do **not** infer ownership from:

- path;
- known skill name;
- equality with current embedded bytes;
- persisted selection;
- backup membership.

If an unknown/modified higher-precedence copy shadows an `agent-skills-required` route:

```text
blocked-by-unowned-shadow
```

The workflow must not be reported healthy while the runtime would load the wrong copy.

If canonical per-resource ownership is not yet available, automatic deletion of ambiguous legacy copies must remain disabled rather than introducing a temporary skill-specific ownership ledger.

### 5. Derive lifecycle behavior from the resolved route

Install, sync, backup, verification, migration, and uninstall should consume the same resolved skill inventory.

In particular, uninstall should not delete a skill tree solely because its path/name matches a known managed skill once ownership-aware routing is active.

### Initial placement examples

Likely `agent-skills-required`:

```text
sdd-init
sdd-explore
sdd-propose
sdd-spec
sdd-design
sdd-tasks
sdd-apply
sdd-verify
sdd-archive
sdd-onboard
judgment-day
skill-registry
chained-pr
```

Likely `agent-skills-shared`:

```text
go-testing
gentle-ai-bench
skill-creator
skill-improver
branch-pr
issue-creation
cognitive-doc-design
comment-writer
work-unit-commits
rdd-defect-workflow
systemic-issue-triage
```

Final classification should follow actual workflow dependency contracts, not naming prefixes.


### Placement verification note

The current SDD orchestrator explicitly requires `chained-pr` whenever delivery planning selects chained PRs, so it remains `agent-skills-required`.

`branch-pr` and `work-unit-commits` are default foundation/delivery skills but no mandatory SDD phase dependency was found, so they remain `agent-skills-shared`.


### Scope boundaries

In scope:

- placement metadata;
- verified per-adapter discovery roots and precedence;
- route resolution;
- deduplicated materialization;
- effective-route/shadow verification;
- ownership-backed safe legacy migration;
- lifecycle alignment for routed skills;
- routing and migration tests.

Out of scope:

- implementing #128's delegation-model compatibility or SDD prompt variants;
- designing a new generalized managed-resource ledger (#1876/#1884 already own that authority);
- doctor UX/generalized mixed-version reporting owned by #1884;
- new install/sync commands;
- TUI controls for placement;
- changing third-party runtimes' discovery behavior;
- treating native skill directories as a security boundary.

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

### Keep refreshing duplicate copies

This is the current #742 behavior. It prevents known copies from becoming stale but preserves multiple physical authorities and duplicate-discovery problems.

### Put every skill only in `~/.agents/skills`

Rejected because shared-global discovery is not universal, runtime precedence differs, and workflow-critical skills can be shadowed by user-managed shared copies.

### Put every skill only in `adapter.SkillsDir()`

Rejected because several runtimes support a shared Agent Skills root specifically for portable cross-agent skills, and this would preserve unnecessary duplication across agents.

### Hardcode per-agent/per-skill switches in install/sync

Rejected because it creates another central routing authority and repeats the drift pattern identified in #1806.

### Create a skill-specific ownership ledger

Rejected because #1876/#1884 already scope generalized managed-resource identity/ownership. Routing should consume that authority rather than create a competing one.

### 📎 Additional Context

### Related but distinct issues

- **#128** — decides which agents are compatible with a skill based on delegation/execution model. This proposal decides where an already-compatible skill is materialized.
- **#330** — observed duplicate-skill warnings under shared-pool topology.
- **#742 / PR #1359** — fixed stale `~/.agents/skills` copies by refreshing them; this proposal aims to remove unnecessary duplicate materialization safely.
- **#1806** — established the risk of independently maintained managed-asset lists.
- **#1876** — owns generalized managed-resource ownership, migration, rollback identity, and fail-closed unknown ownership.
- **#1884** — owns observable managed-resource identity/digests and doctor classification.

- **#2036** — derives conditionally required skills from candidate context; it does not own filesystem placement/discovery.
- **#3154** — changes provider-aware `chained-pr` delivery behavior while preserving the skill entry point; placement remains separate.
- **#3248** — proposes a declarative desired-state model including skills; this proposal supplies physical placement/discovery semantics that such a model could later consume.

### Current discovery conclusion

The remaining discovery checks were closed conservatively:

- Cursor currently documents user-level `~/.agents/skills`, but implementation should retain a runtime regression test because older releases had discovery defects.
- Kilo Code documents `.agents/skills` compatibility and `~/.kilo/skills` global skills, but not global `~/.agents/skills`; use native fallback globally.
- TRAE documents `.agents/skills` loading plus global/project skills, but current primary evidence does not prove `~/.agents/skills` as the global root; use native fallback globally.


### Implementation intent

I have already completed the initial technical investigation and have a concrete implementation plan covering skill placement, runtime discovery precedence, legacy shadow handling, and integration with the existing managed-resource ownership work.

I’m willing to continue implementation work in my fork while this issue is under review, starting with a focused first slice for placement metadata, discovery capabilities, and the pure route resolver.

I will wait for `status:approved` before opening upstream implementation PRs, and I’m happy to adjust the scope or sequencing if maintainers prefer a different boundary.

### Review-size expectation

This feature crosses catalog, adapters, routing, injectors, compatibility refresh, verification, migration, uninstall, and tests. A single implementation PR is likely to exceed the 400 changed-line review budget.

A likely implementation chain is:

```text
PR 1: placement + discovery + pure resolver
PR 2: install/sync routing + effective-route verification
PR 3: canonical-ownership-backed legacy migration + uninstall
```

Exact chain strategy should be selected only after issue approval and after the canonical ownership dependency is known.

### Final duplicate search

Repeated immediately before publication preparation across open and closed upstream issues using `skills routing`, `skill placement`, `~/.agents/skills`, duplicate/shared/native roots, ownership migration, compatibility skills, and discovery-root terms.

No issue was found that owns this combined placement + discovery-precedence + safe-shadow invariant.

### Privacy review

Passed. The draft contains only public repository identifiers, generic home-path examples such as `~/.agents/skills`, public agent names, and public issue numbers. It contains no private usernames, hostnames, credentials, tokens, or environment-specific absolute paths.

### Acceptance criteria for implementation

- Every cataloged managed skill has one placement classification.
- Discovery roots used for deduplication are adapter-owned and ordered by effective runtime precedence.
- Unverified shared roots fail closed to native fallback.
- Shared skills use a verified shared root when available; otherwise native fallback.
- Required skills resolve to a route that is actually authoritative under runtime precedence.
- No managed skill is redundantly materialized in multiple roots by default.
- Unknown/user-modified legacy copies are never auto-deleted.
- An unowned higher-precedence shadow prevents a required route from being reported healthy.
- Legacy deletion/migration consumes canonical managed-resource ownership rather than a new skill-specific ledger.
- Install, sync, backup, verification, migration, and uninstall consume the same resolved routed inventory.
- Repeated successful install/sync converges idempotently.
- Tests cover representative `skill × agent -> route` cases, precedence/shadow behavior, native fallback, and ownership-backed migration.
