title: docs(security): add a private vulnerability disclosure path
body:
## Problem

Gentle AI currently has no documented private path for reporting suspected security vulnerabilities.

At main commit `4004a0825d03a3d123a3c4f67bf375cb16fd6d8c`:

- no `SECURITY.md` exists in a GitHub-supported location;
- GitHub private vulnerability reporting is disabled;
- the live Community Profile reports no security policy.

Reporters are therefore not told how to disclose a potential vulnerability without exposing sensitive details in a public issue or Discussion. Do not post vulnerability details, proof-of-concept material, credentials, personal data, private repository information, or other sensitive evidence in this issue or its comments.

## Proposed scope

1. Enable GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting.
2. Add `.github/SECURITY.md` as the canonical disclosure policy.
3. Direct suspected vulnerabilities to GitHub's private **Report a vulnerability** flow and explicitly away from public Issues and Discussions.
4. Support the latest stable release and the current published prerelease. Older releases and `main` are not supported release channels.
5. Explain what a useful private report should contain using privacy-safe guidance.
6. State that maintainers coordinate remediation and advisory publication with the reporter, without promising a response SLA.
7. Add a short link from `CONTRIBUTING.md` to the security policy.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Private vulnerability reporting is enabled and the API reports `enabled: true`.
- [ ] `.github/SECURITY.md` is recognized by GitHub as the repository security policy.
- [ ] The policy identifies GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting as the only canonical reporting channel.
- [ ] The policy says not to disclose suspected vulnerabilities through public Issues or Discussions.
- [ ] The latest stable release and current published prerelease are documented as supported.
- [ ] Report guidance is actionable and privacy-safe.
- [ ] Maintainer coordination and advisory publication behavior are documented without an SLA or bounty commitment.
- [ ] `CONTRIBUTING.md` links to the security policy.

## Non-goals

- Disclosing or investigating a specific vulnerability in this public issue.
- Adding vulnerability scanning or Codex Security integration; that is tracked separately by #3226.
- Creating an enterprise compliance framework or SDD security layer.
- Establishing a bug bounty program.
- Publishing personal email addresses or inventing an unverified security contact.
- Adding unrelated automated security gates.

## Alternatives considered

- **Public Issues or Discussions:** rejected because details may expose users before remediation.
- **A fallback email address:** rejected because no verified, monitored private address is established.
- **Only enabling the GitHub setting:** insufficient because reporters also need supported-version and disclosure guidance.
- **Folding this into #1002 or #3226:** rejected because those issues cover broader security architecture and scanning, not vulnerability intake.

## Evidence

- The live Community Profile reports 62% health and no security policy.
- `GET /repos/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/private-vulnerability-reporting` returns `{"enabled":false}`.
- Searches across open and closed issues and pull requests found no canonical tracker or merged fix for this scope.

title: feat(workflow): derive the PR type label from the checkbox contributors already fill
body:
## Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand that PRs will be rejected if the linked issue does not have `status:approved`

## 🔍 Affected Area

Other (CI / contribution workflow)

## 💡 Problem Statement

`Check PR Has type:* Label` fails for any PR whose author cannot apply labels, which is every external contributor. The check's own failure message says so:

```
❌ PR must have exactly one type:* label.
...
Ask a maintainer to add the appropriate label.
```

A required check whose only remedy is "ask someone else" is not a quality gate. It is a queue that needs a maintainer to drain by hand, and it is currently not draining.

**Measured on the open PR queue today:**

| | Count |
|---|---|
| Open non-draft PRs | 147 |
| With a `type:*` label | 117 |
| **Without one** | **30** |
| Of those 30, authored by a maintainer | **0** |

All thirty are external contributions. The oldest has been waiting since 2026-08-04. Every one of them is red on a check that its author is structurally unable to turn green, and several are otherwise fully passing.

**The information the check wants already exists in the PR.** `.github/pull_request_template.md` collects it at lines 15-25:

```markdown
## 🏷️ PR Type

- [ ] `type:bug` — Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)
- [x] `type:feature` — New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality)
...
```

Contributors are already declaring the type. `check-type-label` in `.github/workflows/pr-check.yml` (lines 146-182) reads `pr.labels` instead and never looks at the box the contributor ticked.

**Compounding factor:** on fork PRs the workflow run itself sits at `action_required` with zero jobs until a maintainer approves it, so the check often has not even executed. The result reads as "pending" rather than "waiting on you", which makes the backlog easy to miss.

Worth stating plainly: this is a throughput problem, not a complaint about review speed. Anyone triaging thirty PRs by hand while cutting a release is going to fall behind, and that is exactly the work this check creates.

## 📦 Proposed Solution

Read the declaration that already exists instead of requiring a second, permission-gated copy of it.

Two shapes, either works:

1. **Derive the label.** Have `check-type-label` parse the ticked `type:*` box from the PR body and apply that label itself via `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Contributors keep zero label permissions, the label still lands, and maintainers can override by relabelling. Ambiguity stays an honest failure: zero or multiple boxes ticked fails with a message the author can actually act on.

2. **Check the box, not the label.** Validate exactly one ticked `type:*` checkbox in the PR body and drop the label requirement from the gate, leaving `type:*` labels as maintainer-owned metadata rather than a merge blocker.

Option 1 is preferable because it preserves the labels other tooling and reporting may rely on.

Either way the failure message should name a remedy the author can perform. Today it names one they cannot.

## 🔄 Alternatives Considered

- **Grant contributors label permissions.** Rejected: it hands write access to `status:approved`, `size:exception`, and `priority:*`, which are deliberately maintainer-owned. The whole point is that the contributor should not be trusted to self-approve.
- **Keep asking maintainers to label each PR.** This is the status quo and produced the thirty-PR backlog above.
- **Drop the check.** Loses the taxonomy that changelog and reporting depend on.

## 📎 Additional Context

`CONTRIBUTING.md` lists type labels under "Type Labels (applied to PRs)" without naming who applies them, and the "Automated PR Checks" table lists `Check PR Has type:* Label` alongside checks a contributor can satisfy alone. Whichever fix lands, that section is worth a sentence making the ownership explicit.

I hit this on three PRs across two repositories and assumed I had missed a step before checking the queue and finding twenty percent of it in the same state. Filing it as a workflow issue rather than commenting on my own PRs, since the individual PRs are not the problem.

Reported from the contributor side. I cannot apply the `enhancement` or `status:needs-review` labels this template would normally add automatically.

title: sync emits invalid __replace__ permission artifact and rollback remains unverifiable
body:
## Automated provider-defect report

### Environment

- Gentle AI: `v2.4.0-rc.8`
- OpenCode: `1.18.18`
- Claude Code: `2.1.221`
- OS/architecture: Linux amd64
- Client shape: managed Gentle AI wrapper delegating to the published release binary

### Operation shape

A managed sync targeted `opencode` and `claude-code` with OpenCode background subagents enabled. A dry run completed successfully and reported the background runtime ready. One real sync attempt was then executed.

### Observed evidence

The real sync reported 44 managed files changed. Post-sync validation then failed because the generated OpenCode configuration contained a runtime merge artifact at:

```text
agent.gentle-orchestrator.permission.task.__replace__
```

OpenCode configuration validation rejected that value because a permission action was expected. The wrapper attempted its automatic rollback, but rollback validation also failed and ended with a manual-restore-required result. No second sync or manual repair was attempted.

Mutation outcome:

- Published release binary installation: succeeded.
- Dry-run sync: succeeded.
- Real sync mutation: reported 44 changed managed files.
- Post-sync validation: failed.
- Automatic rollback: attempted, but final state could not be validated.
- Consumer repository/worktrees: unchanged; the consumer experiment was halted.

### Expected behavior

Managed sync should materialize a schema-valid OpenCode permission map. If post-validation fails, automatic rollback should restore and verify the exact pre-sync configuration.

### Actual behavior

Sync materialized an internal merge directive into the runtime configuration. Post-validation rejected it, and the rollback path did not recover to a verifiably valid state.

### Minimal reproduction

1. Install the published Linux amd64 binary for `v2.4.0-rc.8`.
2. Use an existing managed OpenCode installation with a `gentle-orchestrator` task permission map.
3. Dry-run a sync for OpenCode and Claude Code with OpenCode background subagents enabled.
4. Execute the same sync once.
5. Observe post-validation reject `permission.task.__replace__`; observe rollback finish without a valid configuration.

### Notes

This report records observed behavior only. It does not claim an unverified root cause. Raw configuration, source contents, diffs, environment values, credentials, usernames, hostnames, and absolute paths are intentionally omitted.

title: bug(review): status exhausts aggregate timeout after rejected capture
body:
## Automated provider-defect report

### Summary
A negotiated review became unrecoverable after a reviewer capture invocation was rejected during local argument validation. The immediately following read-only negotiated STATUS call exhausted its aggregate time budget before authority applicability was evaluated. This report contains observed evidence only; the root cause is unconfirmed.

### Environment
- Gentle AI: `2.3.0`
- Client: OpenCode `1.18.18`
- OS/architecture: Windows AMD64
- Review contract: `gentle-ai.review-integration/v2`
- Candidate risk: medium; one reliability lens

### Operation shape
1. Start a negotiated workspace review for a medium-risk executable candidate.
2. Complete the selected reviewer inspection.
3. Invoke the bound reviewer capture with a result artifact; local argument validation rejects an unsupported result-file flag before persistence.
4. Query negotiated review STATUS once to recover the provider-owned continuation.

### Actual behavior
The capture invocation failed before persisting the reviewer result. The single subsequent STATUS attempt returned:

- schema: `gentle-ai.review-integration.failure/v2`
- operation: `review.status`
- phase: `pre_native`
- code: `operation_timeout`
- message: negotiated review operation exceeded its aggregate time budget
- mutation outcome: `not_started`
- authority applicability: `not_evaluated`
- retry safe: `false`
- replayability: `manual_action_required`
- required inputs: empty
- next action: `stop`

No provider-owned execute, collect, or documented stop continuation was returned.

### Expected behavior
After a capture command fails before persistence, negotiated STATUS should rediscover the unchanged reviewing authority and return the current collect transition or a typed actionable stop. A read-only recovery query should not consume the remaining aggregate budget and strand the exact frozen candidate before authority evaluation.

### Minimal reproduction
1. In a disposable repository, create a medium-risk workspace candidate and start negotiated review.
2. Complete its selected reviewer lens without mutating the candidate.
3. Invoke reviewer capture with an invalid local result-input flag so argument validation fails before persistence.
4. Immediately request negotiated review STATUS with next-transition.
5. Observe `operation_timeout` in `pre_native`, with no mutation started, applicability not evaluated, and automatic replay prohibited.

### Bounded attempts and preserved state
- Capture attempts: one; rejected locally before persistence.
- STATUS attempts after rejection: one.
- The reviewer result was not admitted.
- The candidate bytes, paths, modes, index intent, and test results remained unchanged.
- No correction, commit, push, delivery action, authority repair, reset, or manual authority edit was attempted.

### Related but not equivalent reports
- #2248: advertised `capture-evidence` transition omitted required parameters.
- #2411: valid `capture-result` failed after successful binding preflight.
- #2132: STATUS failed after a bounded correction with a retry-safe envelope.
- #1793: STATUS timeout involved multiple compact-v2 lineages and stale authority state.
- #2918: the same timeout class occurred during pre-push validation of an approved receipt.

### Privacy
This report excludes raw argv, absolute paths, private repository names, usernames, hostnames, credentials, diffs, source contents, environment values, and private payloads.

`RegisteredRuntimeIdentities` documents a stable lexical order, and `validateEntries` compares the decoded manifest inventory order-sensitively with `slices.Equal` — but the only guard test sorts both sides before comparing. title: feat(opencode): add an optional cost-aware GPT-5.6 model preset for SDD/JD/review roles
body: ### Pre-flight Checklist - [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues) and this is not a duplicate - [x] I understand that PRs will be rejected if the linked issue does not have `status:approved` ### 🔍 Affected Area TUI (terminal UI) ### 💡 Problem Statement Gentle AI already supports per-phase model assignment, which is one of its strongest features. However, with the GPT-5.6 family (`Sol`, `Terra`, `Luna`) the difference between reasoning-effort variants is large enough that choosing a model only by capability can produce a poor cost/latency trade-off. For example, the benchmark snapshot used for this proposal shows cases where: - a more expensive model/effort gives only a very small intelligence gain while multiplying end-to-end latency; - two configurations have the same measured Intelligence Index but one costs several times more; - some `max` variants provide relatively small intelligence gains but introduce very high latency, which compounds badly in multi-agent workflows; - the most efficient choice depends on the role: reasoning/architecture, coding/execution, or exploration/mechanical work. The goal is not "always use the cheapest model". The goal is: 1. choose the **minimum model/effort that preserves the quality required by the role**; 2. among configurations with similar measured quality, prefer the **lower-cost option**; 3. use latency as a secondary optimization, except for roles on the critical interactive path. This would provide a practical OpenAI-specific preset for users who want strong output quality without unnecessarily spending Sol-level tokens or `max`-level reasoning on every phase. ### 📦 Proposed Solution Add an **optional OpenAI GPT-5.6 cost-aware preset** (or an equivalent documented reference preset) for OpenCode model assignments. It should remain opt-in and should never overwrite explicit user assignments. ### Proposed grouped matrix #### GPT-5.6 Luna — `high` Use for low-risk, exploration-heavy, passive, or mostly mechanical work where cost efficiency matters more than shaving a few seconds from latency. | Roles | |---| | `explore` | | `sdd-init` | | `sdd-explore` | | `sdd-archive` | | `sdd-onboard` | Benchmark reference from the supplied snapshot: - Luna `high`: Intelligence Index **47**, cost/task **$0.02**, E2E **18.48 s** - Terra `medium`: Intelligence Index **47**, cost/task **$0.12**, E2E **6.61 s** For this preset, equal measured intelligence makes Luna `high` preferable for these roles because it is approximately **6× cheaper**, accepting the higher latency. --- #### GPT-5.6 Terra — `high` Use as the main implementation/workhorse tier. | Roles | |---| | `general` | | `sdd-spec` | | `sdd-tasks` | | `sdd-apply` | | `jd-judge-b` | | `jd-fix-agent` | | `review-readability` | | `review-resilience` | Benchmark reference: - Terra `high`: Intelligence Index **50**, cost/task **$0.22**, E2E **8.45 s** This tier is intended for roles where coding/tool-use quality and execution reliability matter enough to justify moving above Luna, while avoiding Sol for routine implementation. Using Terra for `sdd-spec` and `sdd-tasks` also aligns with the direction already discussed in issue #1820: these phases have downstream impact and should not be treated as purely cheap/mechanical work. --- #### GPT-5.6 Sol — `medium` Use for important reasoning and adjudication where Sol's higher intelligence materially affects downstream quality, but where `high`/`xhigh` are not justified on every invocation. | Roles | |---| | `gentle-orchestrator` | | `sdd-propose` | | `sdd-verify` | | `review-risk` | | `review-reliability` | Benchmark reference: - Sol `medium`: Intelligence Index **56**, cost/task **$0.37**, E2E **11.61 s** - Sol `high`: Intelligence Index **57**, cost/task **$0.55**, E2E **19.10 s** Sol `medium` appears to be a particularly strong quality/cost/latency point: moving to `high` gains only one Intelligence Index point in this snapshot while increasing both cost and latency. --- #### GPT-5.6 Sol — `high` Reserve for roles where a wrong decision is expensive and the extra reasoning quality is more valuable than the additional cost. | Roles | |---| | `sdd-design` | | `jd-judge-a` | | `review-refuter` | These roles are architecture/adversarial-decision heavy: - `sdd-design` defines technical architecture and decisions that propagate downstream. - `jd-judge-a` acts as the stronger adversarial judge. - `review-refuter` decides whether severe findings survive adversarial refutation. For Judgment Day, using **Sol `high` for judge A** and **Terra `high` for judge B** also introduces useful model diversity instead of paying twice for the same Sol configuration. --- ### Matrix summary | Model / effort | Agents | |---|---| | **Luna `high`** | `explore`, `sdd-init`, `sdd-explore`, `sdd-archive`, `sdd-onboard` | | **Terra `high`** | `general`, `sdd-spec`, `sdd-tasks`, `sdd-apply`, `jd-judge-b`, `jd-fix-agent`, `review-readability`, `review-resilience` | | **Sol `medium`** | `gentle-orchestrator`, `sdd-propose`, `sdd-verify`, `review-risk`, `review-reliability` | | **Sol `high`** | `sdd-design`, `jd-judge-a`, `review-refuter` | Conceptually: ```text Luna -> explore / collect / mechanical Terra -> specify / implement / fix Sol -> reason / design / verify / adjudicate ``` ### What I would deliberately NOT use in this preset, and why This means **"not selected as a default in this cost-aware preset"**, not "the model/effort is useless in every possible workload". | Configuration | Why it is not selected by default | |---|---| | **Sol `max`** | Intelligence 61, $1.23/task, 165.35 s E2E. Compared with Sol `xhigh` (59, $0.81, 46.65 s), the marginal intelligence gain is small relative to the cost and especially the latency increase. | | **Terra `max`** | Intelligence 57, $0.51/task, 199.34 s E2E. In the snapshot it reaches the same Intelligence Index as Sol `high`, while taking roughly an order of magnitude longer end-to-end. | | **Luna `max`** | Intelligence 52, $0.05/task, 142.88 s E2E. Still cheap in absolute dollars, but the latency is difficult to justify inside multi-agent chains. | | **Terra `xhigh`** | Intelligence 53, $0.31/task, 26.38 s E2E. When Sol is available, Sol `medium` scores higher (56) for only $0.06 more and responds much faster (11.61 s). **However, Terra `xhigh` remains a useful fallback for users/accounts without access to Sol.** | | **Sol `low`** | Intelligence 51, $0.23/task, 11.43 s E2E. Sol `medium` raises the measured score to 56 for only $0.14 more with almost identical E2E time in this snapshot. | | **Terra `medium`** | Intelligence 47, $0.12/task, 6.61 s E2E. Luna `high` has the same measured Intelligence Index (47) for $0.02/task. For cost-first auxiliary roles, the ~6× price difference matters more than the latency advantage. | | **Luna `xhigh`** | Intelligence 50, $0.03/task, 49.21 s E2E. It is extremely cost-efficient and may be a good optional asynchronous tier, but for implementation-critical roles Terra `high` has the same measured Intelligence Index with much lower latency and is a better coding-oriented workhorse. | | **Sol `xhigh`** | Not assigned permanently. It should remain an escalation/manual option for exceptionally difficult architecture, security, concurrency, debugging, or irreversible design decisions. | ### Expected behavior / acceptance criteria - The preset is **optional** and does not replace existing custom assignments. - Existing user-selected model/variant assignments are preserved. - The preset is only offered when the relevant OpenAI GPT-5.6 models/variants are actually available through the active provider/runtime. - Generic role guidance remains **capability-based**, consistent with #2301; this proposal is a provider-specific convenience preset/reference. - `general` and `explore` use their own assignments when exposed/configurable, consistent with #2104 and #2197. - Judgment Day assignments remain independently configurable. - Users can still override any single role after applying the preset. - The UI should make clear that benchmark values are external measurements and can change over time. ### 🔄 Alternatives Considered ### Keep only generic capability guidance This is the most future-proof approach and is already being pursued in #2301. However, users still have to translate "strong reasoning", "cheap exploration", or "coding reliability" into concrete GPT-5.6 model/effort selections themselves. An optional provider-specific preset can complement generic guidance without replacing it. ### Use one model for every phase Simpler configuration, but it wastes budget on exploration/mechanical tasks or reduces quality in architecture/review roles. ### Use Sol everywhere Maximizes consistency but spends the most expensive model on tasks where the benchmark suggests much cheaper configurations preserve enough quality. ### Optimize primarily for latency This would favor Terra `medium` over Luna `high` in several auxiliary roles. For this proposed preset, cost is intentionally prioritized when measured intelligence is equal or very similar, because multi-agent workloads multiply per-call cost. ### Make these mappings universal defaults Not proposed. Model catalogs, benchmarks, prices, provider access, and role behavior change over time. This should be an **opt-in OpenAI-specific preset/reference**, not a permanent universal rule. ### 📎 Additional Context ### Benchmark screenshot The following screenshot is the benchmark snapshot used to derive the proposed ratios. ### External benchmark source - [Artificial Analysis — GPT-5.6 benchmarks across Intelligence, Speed and Cost](https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/gpt-5-6-has-landed) - [Artificial Analysis — model benchmark/comparison data](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models) The screenshot should be treated as a point-in-time snapshot. Artificial Analysis updates its Intelligence Index and measurements, so exact values may change. ### Gentle AI references / related issues This proposal builds on existing project direction rather than replacing it: - [#1066 — prepare GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna defaults](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues/1066) established the GPT-5.6 family direction and intentionally deferred `max`. - [#1820 — dedicated `sdd-spec` profile and move `sdd-tasks` to `sdd-mid`](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues/1820) argues that spec/task planning deserve stronger-than-cheap models. - [#2104 — bind OpenCode `general`/`explore` instead of silently inheriting an expensive primary model](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues/2104). - [#2197 — expose OpenCode `general`/`explore` in the TUI model picker](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues/2197). - [#2301 — adaptive model assignment lists and capability-based role guidance](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues/2301). That issue explicitly prefers generic capability guidance over hard-coded model recommendations; this proposal is therefore scoped as an **optional, benchmark-backed OpenAI preset/reference**, not a replacement for that guidance. - [OpenCode SDD Profiles documentation](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/blob/main/docs/opencode-profiles.md). ### Why this may be useful The GPT-5.6 family creates a useful role specialization: ```text Luna -> lowest cost for auxiliary/passive work Terra -> efficient implementation/coding tier Sol -> high-value reasoning and adjudication ``` A curated optional preset can make that specialization immediately usable without forcing every user to manually benchmark and map every Gentle AI role.

title: feat: Add a first-class declarative configuration contract
body:
### Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand that PRs will be rejected if the linked issue does not have `status:approved`

### 🔍 Affected Area

CLI (commands, flags)

### 💡 Problem Statement

Gentle AI currently has no first-class, machine-readable way to describe the complete desired configuration of an installation.

Configuration semantics are distributed across interactive CLI flows, internal assets, provider-specific renderers, generated agent definitions, and runtime state. As a result:

- A complete Gentle AI setup cannot be reliably stored, reviewed, and recreated from one declarative source.
- Non-interactive provisioning requires reproducing internal Gentle AI behavior.
- External integrations must understand implementation details such as agent names, cross-references, prompt transformations, permissions, and provider-specific output.
- Those integrations can silently drift when Gentle AI changes its internal assets or rendering rules.
- The interactive CLI and external configuration systems cannot share a single semantic source of truth.

This is broader than supporting a particular package manager or configuration system. Gentle AI needs an upstream declarative contract that every frontend can consume.

The requested outcome is a versioned declarative configuration model representing the desired state of a Gentle AI installation. The interactive CLI, non-interactive automation, provider adapters, and external integrations should all consume the same semantic model instead of maintaining independent configuration logic.

The declarative path should eventually cover every stable configuration choice supported by Gentle AI. Delivery may be phased, but partial provider-specific configuration should not become a separate competing source of truth.

A user should be able to define a complete Gentle AI installation once, validate it before activation, render provider-specific output for inspection, compare it with the currently managed installation, and reproduce the same result in another environment.

This enables configurations that are:

- Reproducible.
- Reviewable before activation.
- Suitable for source-controlled environments.
- Usable in CI and other non-interactive workflows.
- Safer to integrate with external configuration systems.
- Less likely to drift from the behavior implemented by Gentle AI itself.

The same contract should also improve the existing interactive experience. Interactive setup should become another frontend over the shared desired-state model, so interactive users and automation receive the same validation, defaults, reference handling, and provider rendering semantics.

This would also enable integrations such as Nix and Home Manager to consume an upstream-supported model instead of independently recreating Gentle AI's rendering semantics. That is one enabled integration, not the core motivation for the feature.


### 📦 Proposed Solution

Introduce a documented, versioned declarative configuration model and a deterministic renderer from desired state to provider-specific output.

The exact storage format is a design decision. The important public contract is the versioned semantic model, not whether its first human-authored representation is YAML, JSON, TOML, or another format. A normalized machine-readable representation should also be available so renderers and external integrations do not need to implement format-specific behavior.

## Configuration domain

The declarative model should be capable of representing at least:

- Target client or provider adapters.
- Model and profile selection.
- Logical agent roles.
- Enabled agent sets.
- User-facing agent names.
- Model assignments by logical role.
- Workflow modes and Gentle AI capabilities, including SDD and RDD configuration.
- Skills and their assignment to agents.
- MCP configuration.
- Agent permissions and capabilities.
- Provider-specific configuration and supported extensions.
- Additional client configuration that must be merged into generated output.

## Logical identities and rendered names

Agent identity should be modeled independently from the name rendered for a specific client.

Renaming an orchestrator or phase agent must update every semantic reference to that agent, including delegation targets, permission rules, agent-to-agent references, generated prompts, provider configuration, and any other generated asset that refers to the logical role. External consumers should not need to perform textual replacement across generated files.

## Required operations

The public contract should support these capabilities, without prescribing their final CLI names:

1. **Validate**
   - Validate schema and semantic constraints without mutating the system.
   - Reject unresolved logical references, incompatible options, and unsupported adapter configuration.
   - Return machine-readable diagnostics.
2. **Render**
   - Produce provider-specific files without installing or activating them.
   - Support rendering into an explicit destination.
   - Produce stable output suitable for automated comparison.
3. **Plan or diff**
   - Compare desired state with the currently managed configuration.
   - Report files and managed resources that would be created, changed, or removed.
   - Distinguish managed changes from unrelated user-owned configuration.
4. **Apply or reconcile**
   - Bring managed configuration to the declared state.
   - Preserve unrelated user-owned configuration where the adapter supports composition.
   - Avoid leaving partially rewritten cross-references.
5. **Export**
   - Export the stable configuration currently known to Gentle AI into the declarative model where a lossless representation is possible.
   - Report values that cannot be represented rather than silently dropping them.

## Proposed CLI API

The following CLI is illustrative. Exact command and flag names can be refined during design, but the final API should preserve these operation boundaries.

```console
# Validate syntax, schema compatibility, references, and adapter options.
gentle-ai config validate --file gentle-ai.yaml

# Render managed output without installing or activating it.
gentle-ai config render \
  --file gentle-ai.yaml \
  --target opencode \
  --output ./rendered

# Compare the desired state with the currently managed installation.
gentle-ai config diff --file gentle-ai.yaml

# Preview initial installation from declarative state.
gentle-ai install --config gentle-ai.yaml --dry-run

# Install the declared configuration.
gentle-ai install --config gentle-ai.yaml

# Preview reconciliation of an existing installation.
gentle-ai sync --config gentle-ai.yaml --dry-run

# Reconcile an existing installation with the declared state.
gentle-ai sync --config gentle-ai.yaml

# Export representable configuration from the current installation.
gentle-ai config export --output gentle-ai.yaml
```

Read-only operations should support machine-readable output:

```console
gentle-ai config validate --file gentle-ai.yaml --format json
gentle-ai config diff --file gentle-ai.yaml --format json
```

`--config` should be mutually exclusive with flags that modify semantic configuration, such as `--agent`, `--component`, `--skill`, `--persona`, `--preset`, and `--sdd-mode`.

Operational flags such as `--dry-run`, `--output`, and `--format` may still be combined with declarative configuration. Rejecting ambiguous combinations is preferable to establishing hidden precedence rules between individual flags and the declarative file.

The existing interactive and flag-based commands should remain supported. Internally, they should normalize their inputs into the same desired-state model consumed by the declarative path.

## Illustrative YAML

This example is not intended to finalize the schema. It demonstrates the expected boundaries and the level of configuration that the declarative model should eventually represent.

```yaml
schemaVersion: 1

installation:
  scope: global
  channel: stable

profile:
  preset: full-gentleman
  persona: neutral

targets:
  opencode:
    enabled: true
    config:
      merge:
        theme: system

  claude-code:
    enabled: false

components:
  permissions:
    enabled: true

  theme:
    enabled: true

skills:
  include:
    - comment-writer
    - cognitive-doc-design

workflows:
  sdd:
    enabled: true
    mode: single
    strictTdd: true

    roles:
      orchestrator:
        renderedName: gentle-orchestrator
        model: provider/model-name

      explore:
        renderedName: gentle-explore
        model: provider/model-name

      apply:
        renderedName: gentle-apply
        model: provider/model-name

      verify:
        renderedName: gentle-verify
        model: provider/model-name

  rdd:
    enabled: true

mcp:
  servers:
    example:
      command: example-mcp
      arguments:
        - serve

      environment:
        API_TOKEN:
          fromEnvironment: EXAMPLE_API_TOKEN
```

In this model:

- `targets` identifies client applications for which Gentle AI produces configuration.
- `workflows.*.roles` identifies logical Gentle AI agents rendered inside those targets.
- `renderedName` changes the provider-facing name without changing the logical role.
- References between roles use logical identities such as `orchestrator` or `apply`, never rendered names.
- `targets.*.config.merge` represents adapter-owned composition with existing client configuration.
- `fromEnvironment` represents a runtime environment reference, not an embedded value.
- Unknown fields, invalid role references, unsupported targets, and incompatible options fail validation.
- Omitting an optional section uses documented defaults rather than depending on previously executed commands.

## Deterministic rendering

Given the same Gentle AI version, configuration schema version, declarative input, selected adapters, and relevant source assets, the renderer should produce the same files, paths, permissions, and content.

Rendering should be available as a non-mutating operation so consumers can inspect, test, cache, or package its result before applying it.

## State ownership

The declarative contract must distinguish desired configuration from runtime-owned operational state. It should describe what Gentle AI is expected to configure, while transient execution state remains owned by the corresponding runtime subsystem.

This boundary should be explicit and versioned. External integrations must not need to replace or reconstruct Gentle AI's entire internal state to configure it declaratively.

Reconciliation must also distinguish Gentle AI-managed resources from unrelated user-owned configuration. Managed resources may be created, changed, or removed to reach the declared state, while unrelated content should be preserved where the adapter supports composition.

## Composition and precedence

The design should define how these sources compose:

- Defaults shipped by Gentle AI.
- Selected profiles.
- Declarative user configuration.
- Provider-specific extensions.
- Existing user-owned client configuration.
- Explicit runtime or CLI overrides, if supported.

Precedence must be deterministic and inspectable. The effective configuration should not depend on incidental command ordering.

## Versioning and migration

The configuration schema should have an explicit version. When its semantics change, Gentle AI should migrate older configurations, provide a migration operation, or reject them with actionable diagnostics.

Schema compatibility should not depend only on the Gentle AI binary version. Consumers need a stable way to determine whether a configuration can be safely interpreted.

## Adapter contract

Provider adapters should consume the normalized declarative model rather than independently deciding Gentle AI semantics.

An adapter may define provider-specific options, but it should not redefine logical agent identity, workflow behavior, or common configuration rules. This lets new providers and integrations reuse Gentle AI's semantic model while implementing only output-specific behavior.

## Backward compatibility

The existing interactive experience should remain supported. Interactive setup should become another frontend that produces or updates the same normalized desired state.

Users should not be required to adopt declarative files, but choosing the declarative path must not create a parallel, less capable configuration system.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Gentle AI exposes a documented, versioned declarative configuration schema.
- [ ] The schema represents the stable configuration domain supported by the CLI.
- [ ] Logical agent roles are independent from rendered provider names.
- [ ] Renaming an agent updates every generated reference consistently.
- [ ] Configuration can be validated without modifying the environment.
- [ ] Provider output can be rendered into an explicit destination without activation.
- [ ] Identical inputs produce identical rendered output.
- [ ] Invalid references and unsupported combinations produce actionable, machine-readable diagnostics.
- [ ] Provider adapters consume a normalized common model.
- [ ] Provider-specific configuration has an explicit extension boundary.
- [ ] Configuration precedence and composition rules are documented and deterministic.
- [ ] Desired configuration is explicitly separated from transient runtime state.
- [ ] Schema compatibility and migration behavior are defined.
- [ ] Existing interactive workflows remain supported through the same semantic model.
- [ ] At least one existing provider adapter proves the complete end-to-end contract.
- [ ] Tests cover validation, deterministic rendering, renaming, reference integrity, composition, and schema migration.


### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

## Keep interactive commands and individual flags as the only configuration interface

This preserves the current behavior but does not provide a complete machine-readable desired state. Automation would still need to reproduce command ordering and internal rendering behavior, and external integrations would continue to drift independently.

## Add a provider-specific declarative path

A declarative renderer or manifest for one provider would solve only a narrow integration problem. It would create a second source of truth unless it consumed the same normalized model as the interactive CLI and every other adapter.

## Let each external configuration system reproduce Gentle AI semantics

This avoids adding an upstream contract, but forces integrations to understand logical agent references, prompt transformations, permissions, assets, merge behavior, and provider output. Every internal Gentle AI change could then require coordinated downstream updates.

## Expand one existing related issue

Existing issues cover useful foundations such as managed-resource observation, desired agent sets, model configuration, MCP manifests, fallback roles, or a narrower renderer. None defines the complete declarative configuration boundary, and expanding one would mix distinct root scopes.

## Standardize a storage syntax before defining the semantic model

YAML, JSON, TOML, or another representation can carry the contract. Selecting syntax first would not resolve identity, ownership, composition, migration, or adapter semantics, so the semantic model should be the primary design decision.

## Allow declarative files and semantic CLI flags to override each other

Hidden precedence between `--config` and flags such as `--agent`, `--skill`, or `--preset` would make effective configuration depend on invocation details. Ambiguous combinations should be rejected; operational flags such as `--dry-run`, `--output`, and `--format` can remain composable.


### 📎 Additional Context

## Implementation ownership

I am willing and able to take ownership of the design and implementation of this feature.

If maintainers agree with the proposed direction, I can prepare the technical design, split the work into reviewable increments, implement the schema and rendering contract, add the required tests and documentation, and follow through on the initial adapter integration.

I would wait for maintainers to approve the issue and confirm the intended scope before starting implementation, following the repository's issue-first contribution workflow.

## Related issues

Several existing issues cover parts of this problem, but none appears to define the complete declarative configuration contract:

- #2214 addresses declarative reconciliation for workspace MCP manifests.
- #1884 addresses managed-resource observation and version manifests.
- #2766 addresses the desired installed agent set.
- #838 and #393 discuss model configuration and sources of truth.
- #2197 covers configurable fallback roles.
- #882 explored a narrower declarative renderer.
- #110 and PR #975 concern NixOS installation rather than declarative Gentle AI configuration.

These can provide implementation foundations, but expanding any one of them would mix distinct root scopes.

## Open design questions

- What is the smallest schema version that still establishes the complete semantic boundary?
- Which current CLI choices are stable configuration and which are operational commands?
- How should declarative configuration interact with later interactive changes?
- What ownership metadata is required to reconcile managed resources without removing user-owned content?
- Should plan, apply, and export ship together, or follow the initial schema and renderer?
- How should adapter-specific schema extensions be versioned?
- What compatibility guarantees should external consumers receive across Gentle AI releases?

title: feat(skills): let systemic-issue-triage assign cluster labels, so root classification survives the run
body:
### Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand that PRs will be rejected if the linked issue does not have `status:approved`

### 🔍 Affected Area

Other

### 💡 Problem Statement

`systemic-issue-triage` ships with Gentle AI
(`internal/assets/skills/systemic-issue-triage/SKILL.md`, registered in
`internal/catalog/skills.go`). Its central rule is the right one: two or more issues
sharing a root get ONE fix at the root, never N patches. It also already prescribes
where a root's identity lives — bucket B says to *name the canonical tracker*.

What is missing is the link between the two. **Nothing connects an issue to its tracker
in a form a tool can read.** That relationship lives in prose, so it cannot be queried,
filtered, counted, or displayed, and it disappears when the run that produced it ends.

**This repository is the proof, and the numbers are specific.**

#2471 (`meta: the 20 roots behind ~250 open issues`) is this analysis done by hand: 438
open issues read in full on 2026-08-04 against `main` at `9b2cf201`, every root verified
by reading code rather than inferred from threads. It is the highest-quality artifact in
this backlog, and the roots it names are still the right ones.

Measured against the same repository on 2026-08-13, nine days later:

| | 2026-08-04 | 2026-08-13 |
|---|---|---|
| Open issues | 438 | **583** |
| Closed issues | — | 1273 |
| Open issues filed *after* that analysis | — | **268 (46%)** |

**Nearly half the open backlog is now invisible to the analysis that explains it**, and
the only way to recover that coverage is to re-read 583 issues. #2731 (`meta(rc.4): the
four root clusters behind thirteen open blockers`) is the same pattern, now closed and
equally frozen.

The result is that nothing in the tracker answers the three questions a contributor
actually has:

1. Which root does this issue belong to?
2. Is anyone on that root?
3. Is it moving?

Today those answers live in a meta issue that decays, or in Discord, where nothing is
searchable and anyone arriving later cannot recover the context at all.

### 📦 Proposed Solution

Use the primitives already in the repository. **No new file, no new format, no new
state.**

| What it needs to hold | Where it lives today |
|---|---|
| The list of valid roots | the repo's `cluster:*` **labels** — enumerable, each with a description |
| A stable root name | the label itself; renaming it updates every issue carrying it |
| Root state and owner | the **canonical tracker issue** — open/closed and assignee are native |
| Closure evidence | the tracker's closing comment, where the named test already goes |
| Which issues belong to a root | the label on each issue — filterable and linkable |

The label list **is** the registry.

### The one rule that changes in `SKILL.md`

> The skill may assign only `cluster:*` labels that already exist in the repository. A
> root with no existing label is **proposed in the report**, never created by the run.

This sentence is load-bearing. **A model generating cluster names at run time is not
stable across runs** — the same root becomes `review-prepr` today and
`pre-pr-discovery` next month, silently splitting one root in two. That is the precise
failure this skill exists to prevent, and letting the skill invent names would automate
it. Constraining assignment to a human-curated label set removes the failure without
adding anything.

### Field ownership contract

Written into `SKILL.md` alongside it, because it is what keeps the projection safe:

| Field | Owner | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `cluster:*` label on an issue | **machine** | may add, move, remove freely |
| Tracker state / status | **human** | machine never writes it |
| Assignee | **human** | machine never writes it |

A run that would change a human-owned field **reports the discrepancy instead of writing
it**. Plus one escape hatch: a `triage:pinned` label means the machine never touches that
issue's cluster again — one label, no new state.

### The master board

Once issues carry cluster labels, the board everyone has been missing is **pure GitHub
configuration, no code at all.**

One constraint shapes it, and it is worth stating because it is easy to get wrong:
GitHub requires a board layout's column field to be a single select or iteration field,
so **labels cannot be board columns.** The instinct is to add a `Cluster` single-select
field mirroring the label — which would recreate the same truth in a second place.

The better answer comes from asking what the board is for. A board of 583 issue cards is
unreadable and nobody will use it. A board of **one card per root cause** — about 26
today — is a dashboard that fits on a screen.

Since every cluster is already a tracker issue, the master board is a Projects v2 board
whose items are **the trackers**:

| Board element | Source | Custom field needed |
|---|---|---|
| One card = one root cause | the tracker issue | none |
| Columns: pending / in progress / done | native `Status` | none |
| Who is on it | native assignee | none |
| How many issues it explains | the label's issue count | none |

Drilling in is the label: from any cluster card, its `cluster:*` label lists every issue
underneath it. That answers "what is being worked on and what is pending" in one screen,
permanently, instead of in a meta issue that decays.

### Over-engineering self-check

Applying the skill's own rule to this proposal, since not doing so would be
embarrassing: it adds **one sentence of classification behavior and one contract
paragraph**. No new state, no verb, no config flag, no file format, no parallel
representation of existing truth. An earlier draft of this proposal did introduce a YAML
registry, and it failed exactly that test — the tracker issues already were the
registry. It was dropped.

### Scope of this issue

1. Add the assignment rule and the ownership contract to `SKILL.md`.
2. Have the skill apply existing `cluster:*` labels as part of its run, and propose
   missing ones in its report.

Not in this issue, and each only worth proposing once the above proves itself: an Action
classifying on `issues.opened`, batch closure proposals, and a notification bridge. The
master board needs no code and can be configured whenever the labels exist.

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

- **Keep writing manual meta issues** (#2471, #2731). Produces excellent results and
  decays — 46% coverage loss in nine days, with a full re-read as the only refresh path.
- **Let the skill invent cluster names per run.** The one option that cannot work:
  unstable names split roots, and a split root is the failure the skill was written to
  prevent.
- **A `.github/triage-clusters.yml` registry file.** This was the earlier shape of this
  proposal. Dropped: tracker issues already carry cluster identity, state, owner and
  closure evidence, so a file duplicating them is a parallel representation of existing
  truth. One capability is genuinely lost — a YAML `evidence` field could be validated
  before allowing a close, whereas a closing comment cannot — and that cost is accepted
  knowingly, leaving the rule exactly as strong as it is today.
- **Embedding-based clustering instead of the skill's classification.** Groups by textual
  similarity; roots are causal. #2471's roots (a terminal that carries no runnable exit,
  success reported from the attempt rather than a read-back) group issues whose wording
  has almost nothing in common.
- **A separate dashboard or bot.** A second source of truth to keep in sync, for no gain
  over labels the UI already renders.

### 📎 Additional Context

**A candidate taxonomy has already been derived** against this repository on 2026-08-13
to check the shape survives contact with real data: **26 clusters, 15 open and 11
closed.**

It was seeded from #2471's 20 roots rather than re-derived — those were verified by
reading code, which no fresh pass could match — and extended only across the 268 issues
filed after 2026-08-04. The 11 closed entries carry the real test names from #2471's own
progress section (`TestReviewPluginInjectsProviderOwnedLensContext`,
`compact_scoped_walks_test.go`, `TestEveryArtifactMapBuilderSatisfiesTheV1Projection`
and others), so closure evidence is already satisfiable against real history rather than
being aspirational.

Four roots surfaced that #2471 does not contain, all from issues filed after it:

| Proposed label | Issues | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `cluster:delegation-returns-nothing` | ~17 | Delegated agent fails to launch or returns an empty result; caller gets nothing actionable |
| `cluster:sdd-ledger-deadlock` | ~15 | The attempt/remediation ledger refuses its own state — #2834 and #2833 name the shape from inside |
| `cluster:lens-cannot-inspect` | ~14 | Distinct from the closed transport gate: the lens is admitted and *then* cannot read |
| `cluster:engram-persistence` | ~10 | Persistence and sync mutate the wrong scope or fail unrecoverably |

One modelling case worth surfacing, because it tests the design: **#2846 shows a closed
root recurring in a new form** — `review-ledger-contract.md` now deploys, but with an
unbound template placeholder, so the continuation table still reaches nobody. The
candidate taxonomy records this as a *separate* root rather than reopening the closed
one, because the original closure evidence was true: the file did deploy. Reopening
would retroactively falsify a passing test.

Caveat on that derivation: the 268 newer issues were classified from titles, not full
bodies. That is enough to establish a taxonomy, not enough to assign every issue — which
is why per-issue assignment is the skill's job at run time, not a table in this issue.

Happy to open the PR for the two scoped items if this gets `status:approved`.

title: bug(review): start remediation names the base_tree object as --base-ref, silently widening candidate scope
body:
Automated provider-defect report.

## Summary

`gentle-ai review start` invoked without `--contract` exits non-zero and instructs the caller to
rerun with an explicit negotiated form. The `--base-ref` value embedded in that instruction is the
**`base_tree` object hash**, not a commit or a symbolic ref. Following the emitted instruction
verbatim succeeds and creates a lineage whose frozen candidate is scoped against an unrelated base,
roughly 20x larger than the branch's real diff. No error is raised at any point.

This contradicts the documented stop-reason `pre_pr_selector_unrepresentable`, whose continuation
states that `--base-ref` must receive a symbolic ref and never a raw SHA.

## Environment

- gentle-ai 2.3.0 (stable)
- Windows 11, amd64, PowerShell 5.1
- runtime/agent identity: `claude-code`
- repository: private; candidate lives on a linked worktree with a clean working tree

## Operation shape

1. `review status --contract gentle-ai.review-integration/v2 --agent claude-code --next-transition`
   returns `next_transition.kind = collect`, `reason_code = empty_candidate_base_ref_required`,
   with one input `base_ref` / `capture_operation: external.select_base_ref`.
2. `review status` with `--base-ref <symbolic-ref> --committed-only` fails:
   `operation_failed`, `phase: pre_native`, `retry_safe: true`. So the selection cannot be
   satisfied through STATUS.
3. `review start --cwd <repo> --base-ref <symbolic-ref> --committed-only` exits 1 with:

   ```
   review start without --contract cannot produce a completable review because its 4 selected
   lens(es) require repository_context, which only the negotiated contract form publishes;
   rerun with `gentle-ai review start --contract gentle-ai.review-integration/v2
   --agent <your-runtime-identity> --target <target_sha> --projection workspace
   --base-ref <base_tree_sha> --committed-only` instead
   ```

4. The `<base_tree_sha>` in that emitted command is the `base_tree` value later echoed by
   `review.start`. It does not resolve as a commit: `git log -1 <base_tree_sha>` returns nothing.
5. Running the emitted command verbatim returns `action: created`, `state: reviewing`.

## Expected vs actual

**Expected:** either the remediation instruction names a selector the contract accepts (symbolic
ref or commit), or `review start` rejects a tree-object selector with a typed failure instead of
freezing a candidate from it.

**Actual:** the candidate is frozen against an unrelated base and no diagnostic is emitted.

| | files | lines |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| frozen candidate (from the emitted command) | 216 | 13827 |
| branch's real diff vs its merge-base | 9 | 715 |

The frozen candidate's `risk_reasons` cite paths absent from the branch's real diff, including a
workflow file and a docs file, which is how the mis-scope first became visible.

Downstream consequences of the mis-scope:

- `risk_level: high` and a canonical four-lens plan (`risk`, `resilience`, `readability`,
  `reliability`) are selected for a candidate ~20x the intended size.
- `correction_budget` is frozen at 200 from the inflated line count.
- A subsequent negotiated `review status` reports `applicability: unrelated` and routes back to
  `action: start` with the same `empty_candidate_base_ref_required` collect, so the created lineage
  is not reachable from the candidate it was meant to describe.

## Mutation outcome

- Lineage created, `state: reviewing`.
- **No lens executed.** No reviewer result captured, no correction consumed, no receipt produced.
- Consumer state otherwise preserved.

## Minimal reproduction

1. On a linked worktree whose working tree is clean, with committed work ahead of its base.
2. Run negotiated `review status --next-transition`; observe the `base_ref` collect.
3. Run `review start --base-ref <symbolic-ref> --committed-only` without `--contract`.
4. Copy the `--base-ref` value out of the emitted remediation command and compare it against
   `git rev-parse` / `git log -1`: it resolves as a tree, not a commit.
5. Run the emitted command verbatim and compare `changed_files` / `changed_lines` in the
   `review.start` response against the branch's diff versus its merge-base.

## Note

Reported as observed evidence only. No root cause is claimed, and no fix is proposed here.

title: fix(opencode): require confirmation for destructive delegated shell commands
body:
## Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate.
- [x] I understand that PRs will be rejected if the linked issue does not have `status:approved`.

## 📝 Bug Description

Gentle AI-generated OpenCode agents can execute destructive shell commands without a confirmation boundary. A delegated `general` agent intended to remove one disposable test directory, generated malformed PowerShell-to-Cmd quoting, and caused `rmdir` to resolve the current drive root instead of the intended temporary directory.

This issue proposes a proportional Gentle AI-layer fix. It does not require a sandbox, execution broker, token system, or exhaustive command blacklist.

## 🔄 Steps to Reproduce

1. Install or sync Gentle AI support for OpenCode.
2. Delegate a task to the generated `general` agent that creates and later cleans a temporary runtime directory.
3. Let the agent construct a nested PowerShell/Cmd cleanup such as:

```powershell
$runs | ForEach-Object { cmd /c "rmdir /s /q \"$($_.FullName)\"" }
```

4. PowerShell does not treat backslash as a quote escape, so the nested command can receive a root-targeting deletion instead of the intended path.
5. The generated OpenCode permission policy allows the command to execute without human confirmation.

## ✅ Expected Behavior

Gentle AI-generated OpenCode permissions should require explicit confirmation before delegated agents execute narrowly defined high-risk shell shapes, including recursive deletion and nested-shell execution. The exact incident command must resolve to `ask` or `deny`, never `allow`.

Generated agent instructions should also require recursive cleanup to:

- use the active shell directly, without nesting another shell;
- validate a non-empty canonical target;
- prove the target is a strict descendant of the authorized temporary directory;
- reject filesystem roots, home, workspace, `.`, `..`, and ambiguous targets;
- use literal-path semantics where supported;
- stop when validation fails instead of continuing cleanup.

## ❌ Actual Behavior

The delegated agent had unrestricted shell authority. OpenCode executed the malformed command as supplied, and the operating system deterministically traversed the drive root. User configuration directories were deleted before the command timed out.

The model-generated command was the immediate error. The Gentle AI defect is the absence of a proportional confirmation boundary in the OpenCode configuration it generates for delegated agents.

## 🖥️ Environment

### Gentle AI Version

`gentle-ai 2.4.0-rc.7`

### Operating System

Windows

### AI Agent / Client

OpenCode

### 📋 Affected Area

Other, generated agent permissions and instructions

## 💡 Logs / Error Output

```text
Intended effect: remove one disposable runtime directory
Generated shape: nested cmd /c plus recursive rmdir
Observed effect: recursive traversal from the current drive root
Execution: deterministic after command dispatch
```

## Additional Context

### Proposed Minimal Fix

1. Add ordered OpenCode `ask` rules for recursive deletion and nested-shell command shapes used by generated delegated agents. These rules must come after broad allow rules under OpenCode's last-match semantics.
2. Add the short recursive-cleanup contract above to agents that retain shell access.
3. Do not disable all shell access and do not add a runtime service, broker, token, lease, or sandbox in this issue.
4. Do not claim universal protection against arbitrary deletion through Python, Node, Git, or custom binaries. This issue closes the demonstrated cross-shell cleanup class with a proportional boundary.

### Required Regression Proof

- Generated permission ordering makes the exact incident command `ask` or `deny`.
- Normal tests, builds, Git reads, and non-destructive shell commands remain allowed.
- A direct, bounded recursive cleanup remains possible after confirmation.
- A Windows organic OpenCode test proves the incident command does not start the destructive child process before confirmation and leaves an external canary tree unchanged.
- If a bench journey is added, run it in driven mode. `go test ./bench` alone proves only corpus declarations.

This report excludes private paths, project names, usernames, hostnames, credentials, source contents, raw environment values, and internal session identifiers.

bug(review): review start aborts on Windows when Go runtime cannot allocate memory
body:
## Automated provider-defect report

### Environment
- Gentle AI: 2.4.0 release-candidate build
- OS/architecture: Windows amd64
- Client: OpenCode

### Operation shape
Start a medium-risk committed-only review for a frozen base-to-candidate diff containing a small set of executable UI files. Untracked files are explicitly excluded. Candidate consent is granted.

### Observed evidence
- Attempt 1 returned no result. A subsequent read-only status query still reported the exact candidate as fresh and unreviewed.
- Attempt 2 aborted with exit code 2 and `fatal error: runtime: cannot allocate memory`.
- The Go stack identified the failure while the review facade was resolving repository/snapshot Git context.
- No lineage or receipt was created, no review budget was consumed, and repository/consumer state remained preserved.

### Expected behavior
`review start` should either create the review and return its typed start envelope, or return a typed failure envelope without aborting the process.

### Actual behavior
The CLI process aborts with a Go runtime allocation failure before returning a typed result.

### Minimal reproduction
1. On Windows amd64, prepare a repository with a small committed-only diff containing executable files.
2. Request negotiated review status for that frozen base-to-candidate diff, excluding untracked files.
3. Execute the exact provider-returned `review.start` transition with candidate consent granted.
4. Observe the process abort before lineage creation.

### Bounded attempts and outcomes
- Two start attempts were made for the same frozen target.
- First: unknown/no-output outcome, later status definitively showed no committed mutation.
- Second: deterministic process abort with exit code 2.
- No retries were performed after the confirmed runtime abort.

### Preserved-state evidence
The following read-only status still classified the candidate as fresh/unreviewed, and no lineage or receipt existed. Consumer commits, remote state, and publication state were unchanged.

### Safety note
This report intentionally excludes raw argv, absolute paths, repository/project names, usernames, hostnames, credentials, source, diffs, and environment values.

title: fix(persona): make output-style transitions rollback-safe
body:
### Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues and found no separate tracker for this failure mode.
- [x] I understand implementation PRs require `status:approved`.

### Bug Description

Persona output-style transitions are not rollback-safe when removal of the retired style fails. `removeFileAtomic` currently calls `os.Remove` directly after the selected style and settings may already have been written. A removal error can therefore leave a mixed state rather than restoring the pre-transition files and settings.

This failure mode was originally listed in #1810. The declarative resource-plan foundation is being delivered separately by #3161 so the transactional behavior remains a small, independently reviewable work unit.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Start with the Gentleman persona selected, with `gentleman.md` and the corresponding settings value present.
2. Switch to Neutral.
3. Inject a failure while removing the retired `gentleman.md` output-style file.
4. Observe the output-style files and settings after the failed transition.

### Expected Behavior

The transition is target-atomic:

- on success, `neutral.md` exists, `gentleman.md` is absent, and settings select Neutral;
- on failure, the previous Gentleman file and settings are restored, and no partially published Neutral state remains;
- a second successful install or sync is a semantic no-op;
- user-owned files and unrelated settings remain unchanged.

### Actual Behavior

The selected style and settings can be written before `os.Remove` reports failure, leaving a partially applied transition. There is no focused failure-injection regression proving rollback of the complete Persona output-style transition.

### Scope

- Reuse the Persona resource plan introduced by #3161 for the selected and retired extents.
- Integrate removal with the existing install/sync snapshot and rollback boundary where possible.
- Add focused failure injection and end-to-end transition coverage.
- Keep install and sync behavior equivalent.

### Non-goals

- No managed-resource ledger, journal, or global state machine.
- No Claude `@import` work.
- No ownership reconstruction for arbitrary legacy or user-owned files.
- No unrelated lifecycle refactor.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A failed Gentleman-to-Neutral removal restores the previous style file and settings.
- [ ] No partially published Neutral style remains after rollback.
- [ ] A successful transition removes only the retired Gentle-AI-owned output style.
- [ ] Install and sync use the same transition contract.
- [ ] A second successful run is a semantic no-op.
- [ ] Failure-path tests assert externally observable files and settings.

### Environment

- Gentle AI: current `main` plus the #3161 resource-plan foundation.
- Applies across supported operating systems; tests should use synthetic temporary homes and injected filesystem failures.

title: fix(uninstall): rewriteJSONFile mode comment cites a file it never receives
body:
### Pre-flight Checks
- [x] I have searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand this issue needs status:approved before a PR can be opened

### Bug Description

`rewriteJSONFile` preserves the file mode for the wrong stated reason. The comment justifies the behavior with `~/.claude.json`, but no caller of `rewriteJSONFile` can ever reach that file.

`internal/components/uninstall/service.go:1018-1020`:

```go
// Preserve the file's existing mode: ~/.claude.json is injected
// with 0600 because it holds the OAuth session, and an uninstall
// rewrite must not widen it.
```

Inside this package the only operation that rewrites `~/.claude.json` is `rewriteClaudeUserConfig` (`internal/components/uninstall/service.go:1038-1039`), which exists precisely to own that file. The other two non-test callers of `claude.UserConfigPath` (`internal/agents/claude/adapter.go:87-89`) here are `context7Targets` (`service.go:866`) and `engramTargets` (`service.go:911`); both place the path in the pre-uninstall backup-target list that `buildPlan` hands to the snapshotter (`service.go:357-365`, `:417`, `:422`), and neither passes it to an operation.

All 16 call sites of `rewriteJSONFile` pass either `adapter.SettingsPath(homeDir)` or `adapter.MCPConfigPath(homeDir, ...)`:

- `adapter.SettingsPath(homeDir)` — `service.go:647`, `:676`, `:678`, `:680`, `:682`, `:688`, `:881`, `:888`, `:890`, `:939`, `:941`
- `adapter.MCPConfigPath(homeDir, ...)` — `service.go:895`, `:897`, `:899`, `:945`, `:947`

For Claude Code those resolve to `~/.claude/settings.json` (`internal/agents/claude/adapter.go:156-158`) and `~/.claude/mcp/<server>.json` (`:172-174`). Neither is `~/.claude.json`.

`service.go:881` is decisive: it calls `rewriteClaudeUserConfig(homeDir, ...)` and `rewriteJSONFile(adapter.SettingsPath(homeDir), ...)` side by side in the same slice, so the two functions are already understood as covering two different files.

The mode-preserving code itself (`service.go:1021-1024`) is correct and worth keeping — it just protects the agent's own settings and MCP files, not the OAuth session.

### Root Cause

The comment was true when written and became stale in the same squashed commit that landed it. `3603f226` ("fix(mcp): register Claude Code Context7 MCP in ~/.claude.json (#1909)") both added this comment and introduced `rewriteClaudeUserConfig`, moving the `~/.claude.json` handling out of `rewriteJSONFile`. On `main` the comment therefore never described the code beneath it.

### Steps to Reproduce

This is a source-level defect; it is read, not run. Against `08a58756`:

1. Read the comment at `internal/components/uninstall/service.go:1018-1020`.
2. List every caller: `git grep -n 'rewriteJSONFile(' 08a58756 -- '*.go'`.
3. Resolve each path argument through `internal/agents/claude/adapter.go:156-158` and `:172-174`.
4. Observe that no call site passes `claude.UserConfigPath(homeDir)` — the only producer of `~/.claude.json` this package reaches (`internal/agents/claude/adapter.go:87-89`). `internal/components/communitytool` builds the path directly at `codegraph_contract.go:91` and `:110`, but every call site of `rewriteJSONFile` lives in `internal/components/uninstall/service.go`, so none of them is reachable from it either.

### Expected Behavior

The comment states the rationale that actually applies to this function: uninstall must not widen the mode of the agent settings and MCP config files it rewrites.

### Actual Behavior

The comment attributes the behavior to a file this function never receives, and names an OAuth-session threat model that belongs to `rewriteClaudeUserConfig`.

The misdirection is load-bearing in two ways for a future change:

1. **It can license a real regression.** Someone hardening `~/.claude.json` mode handling may read this comment, conclude `rewriteJSONFile` is the guard enforcing 0600, and weaken or drop the equivalent logic in `rewriteClaudeUserConfig` (`service.go:1058-1061`) as redundant. That would actually widen the OAuth session file.
2. **It can trigger a false alarm.** `rewriteJSONFile` deletes its target outright when the cleaned result is an empty object (`service.go:1012-1017`). A reader who believes this function handles `~/.claude.json` will conclude that uninstall can delete the OAuth session file — the exact opposite of the invariant `rewriteClaudeUserConfig` was written to guarantee (`service.go:1034-1037`).

Severity is low: no runtime behavior is wrong today, and no user-visible symptom exists. This is a correctness-of-documentation defect whose cost is paid by the next person to touch mode handling here.

### Proposed Fix

Comment-only, no behavior change. Restate the rationale in terms of the files this function actually receives, for example: preserve the existing mode of the agent's settings/MCP config file so an uninstall rewrite never widens permissions the user or the agent set. Optionally point at `rewriteClaudeUserConfig` as the owner of the `~/.claude.json` 0600 invariant.

### Gentle AI Version

`main` @ `08a58756` (`git describe` reports `v2.4.0-rc.6-168-g08a58756`)

### Operating System

Windows

### AI Agent / Client

Claude Code

### Affected Area

Installation Pipeline

### Additional Context

- The defect is platform-independent; it is a comment in shared uninstall code, not OS-specific. The OS field is filled with the platform the code was read on.
- The "Affected Area" dropdown has no uninstall option; "Installation Pipeline" is the closest fit.
- Not covered by the two related open issues. #1828 concerns `rewriteJSONFile` failing on kimi's TOML settings file; #2232 concerns `rewriteJSONFile` deleting user-owned JSON keys. Neither mentions file mode.
- #2009 ("bug(mcp): the 0600 guarantee on ~/.claude.json does not hold on Windows (chmod sets no DACL)", open, `status:needs-design`) is the change most likely to be misled by this comment: it is exactly the pending `~/.claude.json` mode-hardening work that consequence 1 above describes as hypothetical, and it is still undesigned. Whoever picks it up reads this function first.
- Disclosure: the stale comment was introduced by `3603f226`, the squash that landed PR #1909, which I authored.
- Note for triage: #2232 places `rewriteJSONFile` in `internal/components/uninstall/cleaners.go`. At `08a58756` the function is defined at `internal/components/uninstall/service.go:993` and has never existed in `cleaners.go`; that file holds the key-deletion helpers behind it: `rewriteJSONFile` calls `removeJSONPaths` (`cleaners.go:74`, called from `service.go:1005`), which calls `deleteJSONPath` (`cleaners.go:100`, called from `cleaners.go:82`). That attribution is worth correcting on #2232 independently of this issue.

title: bug(engram): OpenCode sync command-array injection extracts the wrong executable for a two-part wrapper command, corrupting custom MCP wiring on every sync
body:
### Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I searched open and closed issues for `engram command sync overwrite`, `engram mcp command array`, `executableFromCommandValue`, `engram wrapper opencode`, `stableEngramCommandForMergedConfig`, `engram __replace__ command`, `engram ssh wrapper`, `existingMergedEngramCommand`. Found related-but-distinct engram/OpenCode issues (#2762, #125, #512) but no duplicate of this specific defect.
- [x] I understand that PRs require `status:approved` before implementation.

### Bug Description

On Gentle AI 2.3.0, `gentle-ai sync` (component `engram`, OpenCode adapter, `StrategyMergeIntoSettings`) unconditionally corrupts a custom multi-part MCP `command` array for the `engram` server every time sync runs, when that array uses an interpreter+script shape (e.g. `[bash, wrapper-script]`) instead of a single-binary shape (e.g. `[engram]`).

Root cause (read from source, not asserted as the only possible mechanism): `stableEngramCommandForMergedConfig` → `existingMergedEngramCommand` → `executableFromCommandValue` reads only `command[0]` from the existing `mcp.engram` entry to decide what to "preserve." For a two-element command `[interpreter, script]`, this extracts the *interpreter* (e.g. the shell binary) as if it were the engram executable. `engramOverlayJSON` for OpenCode/Kilocode then rebuilds `mcp.engram` via an atomic `__replace__` sentinel as `[extractedValue, "mcp", "--tools=agent"]` — i.e. `[interpreter, "mcp", "--tools=agent"]` — discarding the actual script path entirely. The `__replace__` sentinel in `filemerge.mergeObjects` applies unconditionally (no diff/no-op check), so this happens on every single sync, not intermittently.

This specifically affects setups where `engram mcp` is wrapped by a local script (e.g. to route the MCP stdio session to a remote/shared engram instance via SSH) instead of invoking the `engram` binary directly. The Claude Code adapter path (`StrategySeparateMCPFiles` / `buildSeparateMCPContent`) has an `isEngramCommand(cmd)` guard before preserving an existing command — the OpenCode/Kilocode `StrategyMergeIntoSettings` path has no equivalent guard.

Observed evidence only, no root cause beyond the above is asserted with certainty (I have not traced every caller of `stableEngramCommandForMergedConfig`).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure `opencode.json` so `mcp.engram.command` is a two-element array where element 0 is a shell/interpreter binary and element 1 is a wrapper script path, e.g.:
   ```json
   "engram": { "command": ["<shell-binary>", "<wrapper-script>"], "type": "local" }
   ```
   (The wrapper script's job is irrelevant to the bug — any two-part `[interpreter, script]` shape triggers it.)
2. Run `gentle-ai sync --agent opencode` (any additional flags; reproduced with a bare `-agent opencode` and no other flags).
3. Inspect `opencode.json` → `mcp.engram.command` afterward.

Reproduced 3 times in the same environment, including once as a clean control run immediately after manually restoring the correct two-element array — same result every time.

### Expected Behavior

Either:
- Preserve the full existing `command` array verbatim when it does not match the canonical single-binary shape gentle-ai itself would generate, or
- Detect that `command[0]` is a generic shell/interpreter (not plausibly the engram binary) and skip rewriting, leaving the existing multi-part command untouched (mirroring the `isEngramCommand` guard already used in the Claude Code path).

### Actual Behavior

Before sync (working, hand-verified against the remote MCP server):
```json
"engram": {
  "command": ["<shell-binary-path>", "<wrapper-script-path>"],
  "type": "local"
}
```

After `gentle-ai sync --agent opencode` (broken — element 1, the actual script, is gone; the shell binary is left to receive `"mcp"` and `"--tools=agent"` as if they were script arguments, which is not a runnable command):
```json
"engram": {
  "command": ["<shell-binary-path>", "mcp", "--tools=agent"],
  "type": "local"
}
```

### Environment

- Gentle AI: 2.3.0
- OS / architecture: Windows, x86_64
- Client: OpenCode 1.18.16
- Engram: 1.20.0
- Repository: single global `opencode.json` (not project-scoped), no linked worktrees relevant to this defect

### Preserved-state evidence

No project/repository content was touched by this investigation. The only artifact affected is the global `opencode.json` `mcp.engram.command` field, which was manually restored to its working value after each reproduction. No source checkout of Gentle AI was modified.
