- Issue forms collect symptoms and release context but do not define root-cause investigation readiness.
- `status:approved` currently means only “approved for implementation.”
- `.github/workflows/pr-check.yml` checks linked issue approval but not issue assignment.
- All 23 currently open approved issues have zero assignees; all 23 open PRs would fail an immediate assignment gate.
- GitHub Actions can block merge through a required check, but cannot prevent creating an invalid PR.

## Root cause

Contributor policy, issue intake, approval semantics, and PR enforcement encode different portions of the lifecycle. `status:approved` is therefore weaker than the human process it is expected to represent, and no machine gate establishes implementation ownership.

## Canonical lifecycle

1. Search for a canonical root-cause tracker.
2. Report the observed consequence and release context.
3. Triage and assign an investigator.
4. Reproduce bugs against the exact current remote `main` SHA.
5. Identify the first repository-owned invariant whose violation explains the occurrences.
6. Cluster same-root occurrences under one canonical issue.
7. Propose a proportional design, non-goals, and root-level regression tests.
8. Apply `status:approved` only after maintainer design approval.
9. Implement, open the linked PR, review, and merge.

## Design

### AI-first contribution surfaces

Use stable, explicit headings and machine-readable choices in issue forms and the PR template. Reporters provide symptoms, environment, release version, logs, and impact; they are not required to guess the root cause. Require confirmation that existing issues were searched and direct additional occurrences to the canonical tracker.

### Single approval truth

Reuse `status:approved` as the machine-readable meaning that investigation and design are complete. For bugs, this includes exact-main reproduction and root-cause evidence. Do not add a second design label.

### PR enforcement

Extend the existing required PR check. Every linked issue must:

- have `status:approved`;
- have at least one assignee.

Any issue assignee satisfies ownership; the PR author need not match. Preserve the existing check name and fail closed on API errors.

### Duplicate handling

Use `status:possible-duplicate` while evaluating. Confirm duplicates only when root cause and affected contract match. Move useful occurrence evidence to the canonical tracker, then close with `status:wontfix` and `resolution:duplicate`. Similar symptoms with different roots remain separate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `CONTRIBUTING.md` defines the canonical root-cause-first lifecycle and proportional design rule.
- [ ] Issue forms are AI-first and require an existing-issue search acknowledgement.
- [ ] The PR template states the approved-design and assignee prerequisites.
- [ ] Contributor and triage skills use the same lifecycle and status semantics.
- [ ] The existing PR workflow requires every linked issue to have `status:approved` and at least one assignee.
- [ ] Workflow permissions are explicit and read-only.
- [ ] Deterministic tests cover assigned and unassigned linked issues plus fail-closed API behavior.
- [ ] Existing check names remain stable for branch protection.
- [ ] The 23 current open PRs are reported as migration work; they are not silently grandfathered.
- [ ] Documentation and enforcement ship together in one reviewable change.

## Non-goals

- Fuzzy or AI-generated duplicate detection in CI.
- Parsing prose to decide whether a design is good.
- Automatic assignment.
- Requiring the assignee to equal the PR author.
- Adding a parallel design-approval label.
- Silently exempting existing pull requests.

## Verification plan

- Run focused workflow contract tests.
- Run repository workflow/script tests covering modified policy surfaces.
- Validate YAML and issue-form structure.
- Verify the final diff remains within the 400-line review budget; reduce wording before requesting an exception.

title: feat(sync): harden archive lifecycle retry and cancellation races
body:
### 🔍 Problem Description

The archive lifecycle needs explicit protection around failed fetches and cancellation. A rejected fetch must remain retryable without leaving the lifecycle in a stale state, and cancellation racing with archive completion must not apply an obsolete transition or corrupt session-closure propagation.

### 💡 Proposed Solution

Harden the archive lifecycle state handling so a rejected fetch restores a retryable state, and cancellation and archive-completion paths are serialized or fenced so that only the current operation can finalize lifecycle state. Add focused tests for rejected-fetch retry and archive cancellation race sequences, including the resulting session-closure export behavior.

### 📦 Affected Area

Sync (multi-instance)

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

Handle failures and cancellations only at callers. That duplicates lifecycle ownership and leaves races possible where state is updated after the caller has cancelled or started a retry.

### 📎 Additional Context

Part of umbrella issue #1192. This scope is limited to archive lifecycle hardening for rejected-fetch retry and archive-cancellation races; it does not include the OpenCode archive-to-idle integration tracked separately in #1263.

title: feat(opencode): close matching Engram session when OpenCode archive becomes idle
body:
### 🔍 Problem Description

Archiving an OpenCode session should promptly transition its matching Engram session to idle. Without a dedicated archive-to-idle closure path, the Engram session can remain active until later synchronization, leaving session lifecycle state stale for users and downstream tooling.

### 💡 Proposed Solution

Add an OpenCode archive-to-idle session-closure feature that identifies the matching Engram session and closes it when the OpenCode session is archived. Keep the required mirrored plugin copies aligned, and cover the behavior with focused tests and documentation. This work may require a maintainer-approved `size:exception` because the mirrored plugin copies, tests, and documentation are all required for a complete change.

### 📦 Affected Area

Other

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

Continue relying on delayed synchronization to close sessions. This leaves lifecycle state stale after an archive and does not provide the expected immediate archive-to-idle behavior.

### 📎 Additional Context

Part of umbrella issue #1192. This is intentionally scoped separately from #1259: it covers the explicit OpenCode archive-to-idle integration, including required mirrored plugin copies, tests, and documentation.

title: feat(sync): propagate delayed session closures
body:
## 🔍 Problem Description

Closing a session locally does not surely propagate the closure to synchronized recas when a sync target is unavailable or its manifest chunk does not exist yet. This can leave a remote session open after the local closure.

## 💡 Proposed Solution

Propagate delayed session-closure mutations idempotently through the existing sync outbox. When a required remote manifest chunk is missing, recover it without duplicating mutations. Addtest coverage for delayed propagation and recovery.

## 📦 Affected Area
Sync (multi-instance)

## 🔄 Alternatives Considered
_No response_

## 📎 Additional Context

Parent umbrella: #1192. This is chain unit 2 of 4; it depends on PR`#1250`, the core closure slice. It excludes openCode archive-to-idle detection and archive lifecycle hardening.

title: refactor(opencode): move archive lifecycle policy out of the adapter
body:
### 🔍 Problem Description

The planned OpenCode archive integration needs a clear ownership boundary: the adapter should translate verified host events and identify the exact registered session, while archive lifecycle decisions belong in the Engram core.

The original wording described policy in an adapter implementation from PR #1226. That PR was closed without merging. On `main` at `a43183c2`, the shipped adapter still has no `time.archived` handling, so this is not an immediately actionable extraction from currently shipped archive behavior.

### 💡 Proposed Solution

Keep this as a deferred follow-up to #1192. Once archive behavior is delivered, inspect the merged implementation and extract only lifecycle policy that actually remains in the adapter into the appropriate application-level coordinator/use case. Keep verified event translation, host-session identity, and transport details in the thin adapter. Do not invent a new coordinator before the preceding feature establishes a concrete need.

Acceptance for the eventual refactor:

- Preserve the delivered archive-to-idle behavior, exact session attribution, busy-session safeguards, idempotence, summary preservation, and documented resume/unarchive policy.
- Keep core policy independently testable and mirrored plugin copies aligned.
- Prefer a smaller total implementation with no public API or behavioral changes. If the preceding feature already establishes the correct ownership boundary, re-evaluate whether this separate refactor is needed rather than adding another layer.

### 📦 Affected Area

OpenCode adapter and Engram session lifecycle core.

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

Establish the correct ownership boundary during #1263/#1264 and avoid a later extraction. This may satisfy the architectural intent; the separate issue should be reassessed against the code that actually lands.

### 📎 Additional Context

#1192 explicitly tracks this as the last delivery slice: #1250 (currently open/unmerged), then #1259, #1263, #1264, and finally #1235. Preserve that sequencing unless the maintainer changes the plan. This issue is not a claim that any archive delivery slice is complete and does not authorize implementation before those prerequisites.

Source and dependency state revalidated on `a43183c2`. No implementation or functional tests were run for this update.

title: feat(opencode): close the matching Engram session when an OpenCode session is archived
body:
### 🔍 Problem Description

Archiving an OpenCode session does not currently close its corresponding Engram session. This leaves the Engram session open after the user has archived the conversation, requiring separate lifecycle management.

In the inspected OpenCode adapter, `plugin/opencode/engram.ts` handles `session.created` and `session.deleted`; deletion only cleans local maps. There is no archive-to-session-close integration. The adapter already registers the native OpenCode session ID unchanged and excludes subagents, so the integration should retain that identity boundary rather than infer a session from a project name or title.

### 💡 Proposed Solution

Handle OpenCode session archival in the thin Engram OpenCode adapter and request closure of the exact, already-registered matching Engram session. Upstream documentation/source indicates archival is represented by `session.updated` with `time.archived`, not a dedicated `session.archived` event. Verify the installed SDK/runtime payload contract during implementation; this issue does not claim that contract has been tested locally.

Acceptance criteria:

- Detect archival through the verified OpenCode event payload. Ignore ordinary session updates and unrelated, subagent, or unregistered sessions. Do not synthesize an Engram session solely to close it.
- Use the existing native OpenCode session identity. Keep event translation in the plugin and closure semantics in the Engram core.
- Make closure idempotent and summary-preserving in the core, including repeated archive events and retries. The current `POST /sessions/{id}/end` path calls `Store.EndSession`; an empty payload can overwrite an existing summary with NULL, repeated calls can rewrite the close timestamp, and an unknown ID currently produces no error. Do not blindly forward an empty close request without addressing those safeguards.
- Establish and test an inactive-state check or an explicit safe policy for archival while a session is busy; an archive update must not silently terminate active work.
- Explicitly define and document unarchive/resume behavior. Re-registering the same ID currently does not clear `ended_at`; do not silently assume that registration reopens a session or introduce reopening as an incidental side effect.
- Preserve observations and prompts. Archival is session closure, not data deletion, and must not fabricate or automatically generate a summary.
- Add focused plugin and core tests for the installed event payload, ordinary updates, identity isolation, excluded sessions, repeated events/retries, summary preservation, unknown IDs, busy-session handling, and the chosen unarchive/resume policy. Update the relevant plugin/lifecycle documentation.

Keep this scoped to the archive integration and the safeguards needed to make it safe, not a broad lifecycle redesign.

### 📦 Affected Area

Other

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

_No response_

### 📎 Additional Context

Related closed reports: #48, #1083 and #1131 concern missing session closure or accumulated open sessions; #972 concerns re-registering an already-ended session. The reviewed bodies do not describe handling OpenCode archival through `session.updated` / `time.archived`. This request specifically tracks that archive-triggered integration and its safety requirements.

Relevant implementation locations from the inspected checkout: `plugin/opencode/engram.ts`, `internal/server/server.go`, and `internal/store/store.go`. Existing sync application preserves a prior `ended_at` when an incoming value is null, which must be considered when defining resume behavior. No implementation is included in this request.

## Delivery slices

- [PR #1250](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/pull/1250) — Core closure semantics (383 changed lines).
- [Issue #1259](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues/1259) — Delayed closure sync.
- [Issue #1263](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues/1263) — OpenCode archive-to-idle feature (may require a maintainer-approved `size:exception`).
- [Issue #1264](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues/1264) — Archive lifecycle hardening.
- [Issue #1235](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues/1235) — Later adapter-to-core refactor.

Sequential main-target PR order: [#1250](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/pull/1250), then a PR for #1259, then a PR for #1263, then a PR for #1264, and then a PR for #1235.

title: feat(sync): cloud inbox routing — two-stage key derivation, unenrolled enqueue to inbox, legacy target cleanup
body:
### 📋 Pre-flight Checks

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand this issue needs `status:approved` before a PR can be opened

### 🔍 Problem Description

Slice 2 of the cloud inbox design (#1013). With the slice 1 foundations merged (#1091 / #1098), the target space is closed but nothing routes yet, so the measured pathology keeps reproducing on released builds (rc.11 confirmation in #1013). Four lane-independent gaps remain:

1. **No routing, only minting.** Every mutation is journaled under the legacy `cloud` target with a project column (`enqueueSyncMutationWithSourceTx`, internal/store/store.go ~L8240-8257), and that same writer unconditionally mints a `cloud:<derived>` `sync_state` row for any non-empty project (~L8268-8285); `refreshProjectSyncStateTx` (~L7909) and the read path (`GetSyncState` → `ensureSyncState`) mint on touch. Unenrolled keys therefore keep producing exactly the foreign targets the slice 1 doctor invariant flags. Delivery filters by enrollment, so those rows also stay pending forever.
2. **The basename fallback is still the derivator for non-repo cwds** (`fallbackProjectName`, internal/project/detect.go ~L410; Case 5 ~L166-172; CLI-compat branch ~L389-401; synthetic `dir_basename` result in internal/mcp/mcp.go ~L2185). The design rejects it (#1013 §4): the measured backlog is its output — up to 3 keys per folder, the user home resolving to 538 sessions, UUID-named dirs.
3. **No alias map exists.** Nothing translates key→project (renames) or cwd→project (non-repo working dirs); the schema has no alias table and `MergeProjects` only consolidates after the fact. The design's Stage B lookup has no storage today.
4. **Unenrolled telemetry keeps churning, and legacy drift has no exit.** Sessions/prompts are journaled unconditionally at store level (L2545+, L3366/L3430, backfills ~L7859-8208): 880 of the 892 measured stuck rows were telemetry. Meanwhile, on real unenrolled stores the closed-space check grades legacy `cloud:<derived>` rows as permanent errors with no repair (#1158), and its own guidance text promises "a later cloud-inbox slice removes these legacy rows automatically" (internal/diagnostic/checks.go ~L353).

### 💡 Proposed Solution

Land the lane-independent routing half of #1013 (the delivery-lane decision stays in slice 3):

1. **Two-stage derivation at enqueue time** (#1013 §4). Stage A, a single early return: session designation → slug(git root) → no candidate. The basename fallback never produces a sync key. Stage B: alias map (by key and by cwd) → match with enrolled → else `cloud:inbox` with `project` = the candidate key (an unresolvable designation is filed under its designated name; no candidate → `unsorted`). The payload keeps the raw original for forensics.
2. **Alias map storage.** New table with the two entry types (key→project for renames, cwd→project for non-repo working dirs — the #104 lineage never landed). The map governs future derivation only; existing history is not rewritten.
3. **Inbox enqueue routing.** In `enqueueSyncMutationWithSourceTx`, mutations for unenrolled keys journal to `cloud:inbox` (project column = resolved key) and never mint `cloud:<key>` state rows; the read/refresh paths stop creating foreign targets for unenrolled keys. Enrolled keys keep today's enqueue behavior untouched until the lane slice.
4. **Unenrolled telemetry exclusion** per the protocol finding: session/prompt mutations for unenrolled keys are not journaled (the measured churn). Enrolled telemetry keeps syncing unchanged — sessions are load-bearing in the current protocol (server-side chunk validation, client-side FKs), so its exclusion stays a separate protocol decision.
5. **Legacy foreign-target cleanup** (deferred from #1158). One migration pass over foreign `cloud:<derived>` rows: unacked mutations are re-filed into the inbox under their key (precedents: `SkipAckNonEnrolledMutations` ack-without-delivery, `QuarantineIrreparableSyncMutations` disposition), inert state rows are deleted (first production `DELETE FROM sync_state` — the cleanup must not re-mint rows via `GetSyncState`), and any residual inert drift grades as warning-tier, consistent with the finding's own "no action required" text.

Out of scope: the delivery-lane change and relations forwarding contract (slice 3, gated on the lane decision); `inbox list/claim/drop` CLI, enroll notification, `inbox_depth` and save-time warnings (slice 4); the enrolled-telemetry protocol decision.

### 📦 Affected Area

Sync (multi-instance)

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

- Keep the basename fallback and slugify harder: rejected in #1013 §4 — slugify renames the collisions instead of removing them (one non-repo dir produced two different keys months apart via context-dependent resolution).
- Extend rc.6's blocking unenrolled-mutations check instead of routing: rejected — a tripwire after the fact that halts on noise and offers no destination.
- Wait for the lane decision before routing anything: unnecessary — unenrolled→inbox routing is lane-independent by construction; enrolled behavior is untouched.

### 📎 Additional Context

Part of #1013 (slice 2 of 4, per the slicing agreed in that thread). Slice 1: #1091, merged via #1098. Legacy cleanup deferred from #1158. Released-binary confirmation of the umbrella's problems on v2.0.0-rc.11: https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues/1013#issuecomment-5669973065. Telemetry boundary decision: https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues/1013#issuecomment-5594050631. All counts cited are from the #1013 design body, measured on a real single-machine deployment.

title: perf(sync): share decoded chunks in local import classification and apply
body:
## Problem

Local import still reads and decodes pending chunks more than once. On `main` at `a43183c2`, `sessionIDsAvailableInChunks` in `internal/sync/sync.go:1467` reads manifest entries to collect available session IDs, then `importEntriesDependencySafeWithProgress` (around lines 955–1024) reads pending chunks again for apply. Current-version local imports do not share those decoded values.

The original cloud report is no longer current. The cloud dependency oracle already has an import-scoped `chunkCache` and the apply loop consults it. Do not generalize this proposal across both transports or reimplement the existing cloud cache.

## Evidence

- Current source confirms separate local classification and apply reads with `ReadChunk` and `json.Unmarshal`.
- The contributor's September 21 evidence on `main@7087098` used the real `Import()` flow with a read-counting wrapper around `FileTransport`: six pending version-2 chunks produced 12 reads and a 2.00x decoded-byte factor. See the existing comment for the fixture and benchmarks.
- That measurement is historical, not a benchmark rerun on `a43183c2`. Refresh the count-based proof against the implementation candidate before claiming an improvement.

## Proposed direction

Share decoded chunks between local session dependency classification and apply using an import-scoped cache or a smaller equivalent structure. Keep the existing cloud cache intact and preserve ownership validation, missing/corrupt known-chunk handling, recovery, classification, retry/apply ordering, and warning semantics. Retain any evidence obtained from already-known manifest entries; do not narrow the classification scan to pending chunks without proving equivalent behavior.

## Acceptance

- A read/decode-count regression through the real local `Import()` path shows reuse for each pending current-version chunk instead of classification-plus-apply rereads.
- Cover retries, already-known entries, legacy ownership preflight, and missing/corrupt chunks without changing observable import behavior.
- Keep any benchmark claims tied to their exact candidate and fixture. Prefer net simpler code over an additional general caching framework.

## Scope and coordination

Local-import performance only. No public API, classification, ordering, ownership, or warning behavior changes. The existing contributor lane in this thread remains active; coordinate with @danielgap rather than creating a competing implementation. This body incorporates the maintainer's September 20 local-only scope correction.

Source revalidation only on `a43183c2`; no implementation or functional test/benchmark rerun was performed for this update.

title: feat(store): carry `org` through the passive-capture write path
body:
Follow-up to #1151, split out to keep that PR reviewable.

The passive-capture write path does not carry `org`: `PassiveCaptureParams` has no `Org` field, and its dedup lookup matches on `normalized_hash + project` only. Observations captured passively in an org-scoped repo therefore land without an org tag and do not surface in org-filtered searches or project listings.

Bringing it in line would mean threading `org` through `PassiveCaptureParams` (with the same `.engram/config.json` inheritance `mem_save` and `mem_session_summary` use) and adding it to the passive dedup identity, mirroring what #1151 does for `AddObservation`.

Related, lower priority: the memory-conflict-surfacing subsystem (`internal/store/relations.go`) also matches candidates by `project + scope` without `org`, so same-project observations from different orgs can still be flagged against each other. Pre-existing behavior, untouched by #1151.

title: feat(server): add authenticated HTTP parity for project merge
body:
### 📋 Pre-flight Checks

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand this issue needs `status:approved` before a PR can be opened

### 🔍 Problem Description

Local clients that integrate directly with `engram serve` cannot invoke the existing project-merge capability without also starting MCP or using the interactive CLI consolidation flow.

The capability already exists through:

- MCP: `mem_merge_projects`
- CLI: `engram projects consolidate`
- Store: `Store.MergeProjects`

There is no equivalent HTTP endpoint. The existing `POST /projects/migrate` route is not an alternative project-merge API: it is a deprecated compatibility alias for the ownership-rescue handler.

This is an administrative transport-parity gap, not a request for new merge semantics.

`mem_merge_projects` is intentionally restricted to the MCP admin profile and is annotated as destructive, idempotent, non-read-only, and closed-world. `Store.MergeProjects` already provides the authoritative safety behavior:

- every source must normalize to the canonical project;
- all sources are validated before mutation;
- observations, sessions, prompts, pending sync mutations, and sync enrollment are handled in one transaction;
- unsafe mixed-source requests fail without partial mutation;
- repeated valid requests are idempotent.

HTTP clients should be able to use that existing behavior without reimplementing it or mounting MCP solely for this administrative operation.

### 💡 Proposed Solution

Expose a narrowly scoped, authenticated JSON endpoint from `engram serve` that delegates directly to `Store.MergeProjects`.

One possible HTTP shape is:

```http
POST /projects/merge
Authorization: Bearer <ENGRAM_HTTP_TOKEN>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "from": ["Engram", "ENGRAM"],
  "to": "engram",
  "confirmed": true
}
```

A successful response could use the existing `store.MergeResult` JSON shape:

```json
{
  "canonical": "engram",
  "sources_merged": ["Engram", "ENGRAM"],
  "observations_updated": 12,
  "sessions_updated": 2,
  "prompts_updated": 4
}
```

The route and property names above are illustrative rather than a closed design decision. The final contract should follow maintainer preference and existing HTTP conventions.

Whichever contract is selected, the implementation should:

- protect the endpoint with `requireConfiguredAuth`, not optional `requireAuth`;
- return `503` when `ENGRAM_HTTP_TOKEN` is not configured;
- return `401` for missing or invalid bearer credentials;
- cap the request body at 8 KiB, matching the existing ownership-rescue admin endpoint;
- require an explicit `confirmed: true`;
- require at least one non-blank source and a non-blank canonical target;
- call `Store.MergeProjects` directly;
- keep normalization, source eligibility, atomicity, sync migration, and idempotency authoritative in the store;
- avoid raw SQL or duplicated merge rules in the HTTP handler;
- map store validation failures to `400` without relying on error-string matching or reimplementing those validations;
- return `200` for successful merges, including valid idempotent no-ops;
- return a generic `500` for unexpected store/infrastructure failures;
- call `notifyWrite()` after a successful merge so autosync can observe any record, journal, or enrollment changes;
- not gate `notifyWrite()` solely on observation/session/prompt counters, because sync identity or enrollment may change independently;
- preserve all existing MCP, CLI, sync, and HTTP behavior;
- document the final contract in `DOCS.md`.

Suggested acceptance criteria:

- A valid authenticated and confirmed request merges observations, sessions, and prompts and returns the existing merge result fields.
- Pending sync mutations and enrollment continue to follow the canonical project through `Store.MergeProjects`.
- Autosync is notified after a successful merge.
- A repeated valid request succeeds idempotently with no additional records moved.
- An unset server token returns `503` without mutation or autosync notification.
- Missing or invalid credentials return `401` without mutation or autosync notification.
- Missing/false confirmation returns `400` without invoking the merge.
- Invalid JSON, oversized payloads, missing targets, and empty source lists return `400`.
- A source that does not normalize to the canonical project returns `400`.
- A mixed valid/invalid source list fails closed with no partial mutation.
- Unexpected store errors return `500` without exposing infrastructure details.
- Existing MCP and CLI merge tests continue to pass unchanged.

### 📦 Affected Area

Other — HTTP API (`engram serve`)

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

- **Require HTTP clients to start MCP:** this adds a second transport solely to access behavior already available in the same Engram process and store.
- **Require the interactive CLI consolidation flow:** this does not serve applications integrating programmatically with `engram serve`.
- **Reimplement merge behavior in HTTP clients:** rejected because validation, atomicity, and sync behavior would drift from Engram.
- **Implement merge logic in the HTTP handler:** rejected because `Store.MergeProjects` is already the authoritative domain/store operation.
- **Reuse `POST /projects/migrate`:** rejected because that route is now a deprecated alias for ownership rescue and has different semantics.
- **Include this in #1105:** rejected because project merge is an administrative/destructive operation with stricter authentication, confirmation, payload, and sync requirements.

### 📎 Additional Context

Verified against current `main` at commit `9632b56f21e37b41fc40bdb9c8a23bc1d6e5ecf6`.

Relevant implementation:

- `internal/mcp/mcp.go`
  - `ProfileAdmin`
  - `mem_merge_projects` registration and annotations
  - `handleMergeProjects`
  - `queuedWriteHandler`
- `internal/store/store.go`
  - `MergeResult`
  - `Store.MergeProjects`
  - `projectMergeSourceVariants`
  - `migrateProjectSyncIdentityTx`
  - `backfillProjectSyncMutationsTx`
- `internal/server/server.go`
  - `Server.routes`
  - `requireConfiguredAuth`
  - `handleRescueProjectOwnership`
  - `notifyWrite`
- `cmd/engram/main.go`
  - `cmdProjectsConsolidate`

Related work:

- #1105 / PR #1109 explicitly leave `mem_merge_projects` for a separate administrative issue.
- #200 / PR #429 established bearer-token protection for sensitive HTTP operations.
- #578 / PR #810 hardened project consolidation and its sync behavior.
- #595 documented sync divergence after project merge/rename.
- #749 and #911 covered historical case-only merge failures.
- #1007 / PR #1063 established fail-closed confirmation behavior for CLI consolidation.

No existing issue or PR was found for authenticated HTTP exposure of `Store.MergeProjects`.

title: feat(ci): token budget ratchet — first slice over agent eager schemas and server instructions
body:
### 📋 Pre-flight Checks

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand this issue needs `status:approved` before a PR can be opened

> **Revised 2026-09-24** per [maintainer feedback](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues/1078#issuecomment-5800002092): narrowed to a first slice over two stable, high-cost surfaces. Responses, hook prose, and plugin payloads become candidates for later measured additions, each landing as its own follow-up once the harness exists.

### 🔍 Problem Description

Engram's context cost is invisible and unmeasured. Two surfaces dominate the per-session bill and have no ratchet today:

1. **Eager tool schemas (agent profile)** — every agent session receives the full `tools/list` payload for `ProfileAgent` at handshake, before any call happens. Today a field added to a response schema, a paragraph added to a tool description, or a tool moved into the agent profile costs a few hundred runes permanently, per session, with no CI signal.
2. **Server instructions (agent profile)** — a `serverInstructions` constant with a documented failure class: Claude Code truncates the handshake `instructions` field at 2048 runes and `mem_*` tools stopped responding shortly after connect in the field reports (`serverinstructions_length_test.go` documents the empirical `2539 → 2048` truncation). Today only a ceiling test exists; it can never shrink, so any growth up to the cliff is free.

Both surfaces are pure functions of the code (no DB fixture, no runtime state), which is what makes them the right first slice: deterministic to regenerate, immune to fixture churn.

### 💡 Proposed Solution (first slice: agent eager schemas + server instructions)

**Budget file** — `internal/mcp/testdata/token_budgets.json`, rune counts (the client's currency, same rule as the existing truncation test):

```json
{
  "eager_schemas.agent": <measured at first pin>,
  "server_instructions.agent": <measured at first pin>
}
```

**Test** — `token_budget_test.go` in `internal/mcp`, next to the surfaces it measures:

- `eager_schemas.agent`: build the server via `NewServerWithConfig` with the agent allowlist, invoke the `tools/list` result the SDK produces, marshal once, count runes. The first `go test -run TestTokenBudget -update` run pins the baseline; from then on CI asserts `measured <= budget`.
- `server_instructions.agent`: same measurement for the instructions constant, consolidating the existing 2048-rune ceiling test into the same file. The ratchet baseline replaces the "free growth up to the cliff" behavior; the ceiling stays as a hard backstop above the budget.

**Reproducible baseline** — the test is the reproduction: `-update` regenerates from code alone (no LLM, no tokenizer, no manual audit, no network). The manual-audit figures quoted in perf backlog items (#1040, #1041) get replaced by this pinned number at first landing.

**User-facing regressions this catches:**

- A tool added to `ProfileAgent`, a schema field, or a description paragraph inflating every agent session's handshake cost (the #163 class, found manually last time).
- Instructions growth heading back toward the documented 2048-rune truncation cliff where `mem_*` tools stopped responding.

**When a budget increase is legitimate:**

- Decreases are always free.
- An increase is legitimate only when the PR body names the capability that grew (new agent tool, new required field), states the per-session rune delta, and the maintainer acks it explicitly. Rewording, extra examples, or restating the same capability do not qualify; those land as decreases or no-change.
- SDK bumps (`mark3labs/mcp-go` in go.mod) that change serialization show up as a single reviewable budget diff — that is signal, not noise: the client really pays the new size.

**Avoiding false positives on harmless changes:**

- Only code-pure surfaces are measured in this slice: no fixture DB, no golden query data, no timestamps or IDs inside the payloads. Fixture churn is structurally impossible here; it is the reason responses/hooks/plugins are not in slice one.
- Rune counting matches the client decode rule already established by the truncation test, so byte/rune drift never trips the gate.
- A companion assertion fails when a tool is registered in the agent profile without a budget entry, so nothing silently opts out of the ratchet.

**Later additions (candidates, not requirements):** `response.mem_search.*` golden queries, the ToolSearch hook prose from #1077, and plugin static payloads (pi, opencode, claude-code), each as its own measured budget line once slice one's harness lands.

**Update flow** — `-update` rewrites the JSON; increases gated by the rule above. Perf PRs demonstrate wins as budget-file diffs (e.g. `11700 → 11060`) instead of hand-computed estimates, and the `perf-check` make target family gains a `token-budget-check` sibling.

### 📦 Affected Area

MCP Server (tools, transport) — `internal/mcp` tests + `testdata` only for this slice.

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

- Full-suite ratchet from day one: rejected per maintainer feedback; cross-package fixture and maintenance contract before the first value lands.
- Keep only the ceiling test: covers instructions alone and never shrinks; schemas (the larger surface) stays invisible.
- Manual audits (status quo): unverifiable, stale immediately, what produced #163's late discovery.
- Real tokenizer in CI: heavyweight dependency for precision a ratchet does not need; rune counts rank and regress-detect identically for gating purposes.

### 📎 Additional Context

Completes the cost-coverage matrix direction started by #897 (latency) and #974 (dead code) with the first context-cost gate: latency, dead code, context. Aligns with the executable-invariants direction of #872.

title: feat(sync): explicit inbox for mutations from unenrolled projects
body:
## Summary Forward-looking design for what happens to sync mutations whose project is **not enrolled**. Today the target space is open: every cwd-derived key creates its own `sync_state` row, and mutations from unenrolled keys accumulate silently in the legacy `cloud` target. This proposal replaces that with a **closed target space**, a single reserved `cloud:inbox`, explicit human operations (list/claim/drop), and warnings that surface **at save time**. The design was developed and reviewed against a real machine (Linux, engram 1.20.0, self-hosted cloud). All counts below were measured on that machine on 2026-09-05; project names and paths are anonymized. ## Problem (measured) 1. A mutation whose derived key is not enrolled lands in the legacy `cloud` target with `project` = derived key. The worker only delivers enrolled projects → the row stays unacked **forever**. 2. The sync layer creates an empty `sync_state` row per derived key (`cloud:`): lifecycle `pending`, no failures, no error of any kind — invisible by construction. *(Measured on 1.20.0 — on 2.0.0-rc.6 the invisibility is gone: a new blocking doctor check fires on exactly this pathology. What it does and does not do: rc.6 note below the list.)* 3. Measured result: **892 rows stuck + 35 phantom targets accumulating for ~3 months with zero alarms**, because nothing failed — nothing was broken, nobody was looking. 4. Key derivation fragments. On one machine, within one backlog: one folder produced up to 3 keys (casing/separator variants); one non-repo working dir produced **two different keys at different times** (24 sessions under key A from July, 1 under key B in August — context-dependent resolution, not a typo variant); the basename fallback for non-repo cwds is exactly what generated the noise keys (`/` → `/`, scratch dirs → their basenames, a UUID-named project dir, the user home dir → 538 sessions under its basename). 5. 880 of the 892 rows were session/prompt **telemetry** that does not go to cloud by policy — pure churn that should never have been enqueued. 6. **And the per-project lane never delivers.** Measured: the only lane the worker has ever delivered observations from is the legacy `cloud` target, grouped by the `project` column (a fresh observation for an enrolled project enqueued there was delivered in <60 s). The per-project `cloud:` targets hold 135 rows in their entire history — **not one of them has ever been delivered**. The lane this design uses as its central target model has a measured delivery record of zero. ## Problem — rc.6 status of Problem 2 (measured 2026-09-06, same machine, 2.0.0-rc.6) The 2.0.0-rc.6 doctor ships 7 checks (1.20 had 4). One of the new ones is **blocking**, and it fired live here: ``` [blocked] sync_mutation_required_fields non_enrolled_pending_mutations: Pending cloud sync mutations for project "scratchpad" are blocked because it is not enrolled. evidence: {"pending_mutations":2,"project":"scratchpad"} ``` The reproduction was accidental: a few commands run from a temp dir minted a phantom project key from the cwd — exactly this issue's pathology, reproduced without anyone trying to. Honest status, without inflating or deflating: - **What rc.6 fixed: the invisibility.** There is now a signal, and it is blocking — a phantom key can no longer accumulate for three months without a tripwire. - **What rc.6 does not do: route.** The blocked mutations have no destination — no `cloud:inbox` (confirmed absent from `sync_state`), no claim/drop, no save-time warning. The detection has no exit. - **The check blocks on pure telemetry.** The two live rows were one session and one prompt — zero observations. Per §1 that traffic does not go to cloud at all and should never be enqueued; rc.6 enqueues it and then raises a blocking verdict over it. (Both rows were later auto-acked locally without any push — the block bought nothing but an intervention.) A blocking doctor verdict over two rows of `cd` noise is a worse remedy than the silence it replaces: 1.20 hid the problem, rc.6 halts on it. The design's core — a destination, human operations, and the save-time warning — is what closes the gap; the rc.6 check is a tripwire on the problem, not the routing this proposal asks for. I am reporting against the version currently under validation (2.0 RC), not the one already left behind. ## Design ### Central invariant The target space is **closed**. Only these targets may exist: - `cloud:` for enrolled projects, - `cloud:inbox` (reserved constant), - `cloud` (legacy: transport lane for relations only, see §1). A derived key never creates state of its own. The doctor enforces the invariant: any `sync_state.target_key` outside that set is an immediate finding. **Lane choice — explicit.** This design proposes the **per-project target as the delivery lane** for observations: the worker reads `cloud:` and delivers from it; legacy stays frozen for new writes (the sole exception is the relations forwarding contract, §1). This is a change from the measured status quo (Problem 6: today only legacy delivers), and it is what makes item 1 real — routing enrolled mutations to a target nobody delivers from would be inventing a new way to strand rows. The controlled test (item 7) confirms that once a lane delivers, identical-content re-delivery works — so the lane change alone unblocks project moves; there is no dedup key to change. ### 1. Inbox mechanism When an observation or relation mutation arrives whose key (resolved by the §4 pipeline) is not enrolled: - `target_key = cloud:inbox` (constant, never derived). - Column `project` = resolved key: slugged repo name, an unresolvable session designation (filed under the designated name, pipeline B.3), or `unsorted`. - The payload's `project` field keeps the raw original (forensic, lossless). - **Telemetry (session, prompt) is not enqueued for cloud at all** (local only). Codified policy: it does not go to the cloud. This eliminates the largest backlog source (880/892 of the stuck rows were telemetry). Measured (2026-09-05): per-project targets `cloud:` contain **only observations** (135 rows in the whole history); all 4,799 sessions and 1,188 prompts live in legacy. So "telemetry does not enter per-project targets" **is already de-facto behavior** for enrolled projects; this design codifies and extends it (telemetry is not enqueued anywhere — today it goes to legacy and the worker auto-acks it: pure churn). Note the consequence for item 1: it is a real behavior change, not a formal one — today enrolled observations are enqueued to and delivered from legacy `cloud` (Problem 6); under this design, both enqueue and delivery move to `cloud:`. The failure mode is bounded: rows sitting undelivered in per-project targets — exactly the Problem 6 pathology, which the doctor's closed-target invariant surfaces instead of hides; and item 7's control shows that once the lane is live, identical-content re-delivery works, so no follow-up mechanism is needed. How the inbox is kept distinct from real targets: - The name `inbox` is a reserved constant: `engram cloud enroll inbox` is rejected; no project may be named `inbox`. - The inbox `sync_state` row has its own lifecycle (`inbox`), not `pending`: no delivery cursor; the worker never "syncs" it; only tools list and count it. - The doctor invariant protects it: any new non-enrolled target is a finding. Legacy `cloud` is **frozen for new writes**, except relations forwarding. It changes from backlog dump to transport lane. Relations — observed behavior (measured 2026-09-05, marked observed, not contract): the daemon re-enqueues only enrolled projects' relations toward the legacy target, and the worker delivers them there (167/167 historical relation acks live in legacy; 9 re-enqueued relations delivered in 12 s). The design **formalizes that forwarding as contract** (upstream item 6), it does not reimplement it. ### 2. Warnings Design rule: **a warning that depends on someone opening a log does not exist**. This backlog lived for 3 months because nothing shouted. Surfaces (a and b mandatory in v1): **a. At save time (primary, synchronous).** The save response says it all (MCP: structured field `routed_to: "inbox"` + `project_key`; CLI: stderr line): warning: saved to inbox: "" (cwd ) is not enrolled — will not sync to cloud. To enroll it: engram cloud enroll The only surface that cannot be ignored: it appears in the conversation where the memory was saved, at the moment the user decides whether that project deserves the cloud. **b. Doctor (audit, per-key tripwire with `unsorted` excluded).** New `inbox_depth` check (warning), **per key**: - For each distinct key other than `unsorted`: oldest row > 7 days → warning. A key waiting 7 days is a pending decision (enroll, claim, or drop). - `unsorted` is **excluded from the age tripwire**: it receives noise by design forever, and an age warning would be permanent — alarm fatigue, reinventing the log nobody opens. Instead, a **growth** threshold: `unsorted` delta > 100 rows in 7 days → warning (tunable). Sustained noise does not alarm; a burst does. **c. Status (overview).** `engram cloud status` always prints a line when the inbox is non-empty: inbox: 214 memories in 9 unenrolled keys (oldest non-unsorted: 81 days) (d. Optional, out of v1: session-start context line when the inbox grew since the last session.) ### 3. Lifecycle The inbox **does not drain itself, does not expire, has no TTL**. Decisions about data are human. Operations: - `engram cloud inbox list` — counts + ages per key (read-only). For `unsorted` it **breaks down by cwd** (the payload keeps the raw cwd): the summary shows which directories compose the key. - `engram cloud inbox claim --project [--as ] [--cwd ]` — moves those rows to the enrolled target (new INSERT + **ack** of the original; never delete — the mutation log is append-only forensics). `--cwd` is a selector **inside `unsorted`**: acts only on rows whose raw payload cwd is that path — without it, claiming `unsorted` would be all-or-nothing over unrelated directories. If `--as` names an enrolled project, the mapping is registered in the alias map (§4) and, for relations, the daemon forwarding does the rest (contract §1). - `engram cloud inbox drop --project [--noise] [--cwd ]` — acks as discarded, no delivery. `--noise` applies the noise pattern; `--cwd` restricts the operation to one cwd inside `unsorted`. How the human finds out: - The save-time warning (§2a) is the primary channel: every save routed to the inbox announces itself in its own conversation. - The doctor per-key tripwire (§2b) is the backstop: if the warning escaped (another agent, batch flow), at 7 days the doctor shouts — for every real key, never for `unsorted`. - The status line (§2c) gives the permanent overview. - **Enroll closes the loop**: `engram cloud enroll ` inspects the inbox after enrolling; if rows exist for that key (or an alias of it), it prints the count and suggests the claim: $ engram cloud enroll ok: "" enrolled. -> 16 memories of "" waiting in the inbox. Claim: engram cloud inbox claim --project --as Without this, enrolling `` tomorrow would leave 16 rows waiting in silence — the same design failure, at a smaller scale. The only automation: post-enrollment relations forwarding (daemon, observed) and telemetry exclusion (never enters the queue). For observations and relations from unenrolled projects: **zero automation**. ### 4. Key derivation (two stages) A v1 draft proposed `key = slug(basename(cwd))` as the derivation rule, and review showed it was wrong. What the data shows (sessions table, 2026-09-05): - Current derivation is **not basename**: a git repo cwd resolves via **git root** (`project_source: git_root`). Basename is the **fallback** when git resolution fails. - The backlog noise is **exactly the fallback's output** for non-repo directories: a non-repo model-staging dir, a non-repo scratch dir (`prueba`-like keys in saves while the session says another project), the user home (538 sessions), `/`, and a UUID-named app project dir. - The same directory produces **different keys at different times** — a collision slugify cannot touch because it is not a typo variant, it is context-dependent resolution: one non-repo working dir mapped to key A in 24 sessions (July) and key B in 1 session (August). - And there is a dominant path the v1 draft ignored: **explicit project designation on the session**. A non-repo agent workspace dir was designated as one enrolled project in **348 sessions**. A pipeline starting at git root would send those 348 to `unsorted` and lose the attribution the agent gave. Conclusion: promoting the fallback to the v1 rule **institutionalizes the bug** (the backlog is its output), and slugifying basenames would only rename the collisions. Slugify stays, but **as a normalizer of the repo name, not as a derivator**. **Derivation pipeline v1 (at enqueue time), in TWO stages:** The split is structural, not cosmetic: Stage A produces a **candidate key**; Stage B decides the **target**. Written as five sequential steps, an implementer codes five `if ... return`s — and then git root returns before the alias map is ever consulted, making key→project entries (renames) unreachable, which are exactly the repo case. **Stage A — resolve the candidate key** (a single early return): - **Session designation present** → candidate = the designated name; Stage A ends. **No enrollment guard**: if the designated project is neither enrolled nor in the alias map, the designation is kept anyway — Stage B resolves it (and if unresolvable, the inbox files it under that name, Stage B.3). Losing it here would betray the point of the step: it is the ideal inbox case — someone explicitly said which project this belongs to, it just needs enrolling. (The 348-session workspace case.) - Else, **git root**: cwd inside a repo → candidate = slug(repo name). Slugify normalizes the repo name (lowercase, spaces/underscores → hyphen): a repo named `LM_Studio_Model` would yield `lm-studio-model`. - Else, **no candidate** (no designation, no repo). **Never basename**: a cwd without a repo never creates its own key. **Stage B — resolve the target with the candidate:** 1. **Alias map**, queried by **candidate key and by cwd** — two entry types: - key → project (renames): ` → `. Reachable: git root no longer returns early, it only leaves a candidate. - cwd → project (non-repo working dirs): ` → ` — the direct fix for the measured collision. Hit → `cloud:`. 2. **Match with enrolled**: candidate == enrolled project → `cloud:`. 3. **Inbox**: `cloud:inbox` with key = the candidate — an unenrolled repo keeps its identity (repo `` → inbox key ``), and an unresolvable designation is filed under the designated name — or `unsorted` if Stage A produced no candidate. `unsorted` is the only key that can grow sustainably by design (hence its own growth tripwire in §2b, not age). ## Out of scope (explicit) - **The cloud allowlist**: untouched. Enrolling a new project still requires server-side authorization (self-hosted). The inbox does not bypass or extend it. - **What is worth syncing**: claim/drop is human. No auto-enrollment, auto-drop, or memory expiry. - **The noise source**: does not prevent agents from saving memories from scratch cwds (tmp, `/`, test dirs, home); it contains the damage (`unsorted` key, visible, growth tripwire) but not the saves. "Don't save from scratch" is a separate client-side policy. - **Historical designations are not rewritten**: sessions already filed under a different key stay that way in the history; the alias/cwd map governs **future** derivation only. - **The relations delivery architecture**: the design consumes it (legacy + forwarding) and asks for it to be formalized as contract upstream (item 6); it does not reimplement it. - **Semantic re-filing**: the inbox key is the repo/cwd, not the topic. Re-filing by topic is a separate (semantic) problem, out of scope. - **Stage A without a tiebreaker relies on a data property, not a design guarantee**: measured 2026-09-05, **0 sessions** with more than one directory over their lifetime (`group by id having count(distinct directory) > 1` = 0). The classic failure mode of session designation (designate a project, move to another repo, memories keep filing under the first) does not exist in this data. If long sessions crossing repos appear, the designation needs a tiebreaker: **it wins while the cwd stays inside the designated project's root**. - **Multi-node**: assumes a single machine / single engram DB. ## Upstream work items 1. **Enqueue routing + delivery lane**: enrolled → `cloud:

` (both enqueue **and** delivery — see the lane choice in the invariant and Problem 6); unenrolled → `cloud:inbox` (pipeline §4); telemetry → not enqueued. 2. **`cloud:inbox` constant** + its own lifecycle + rejection of `enroll inbox`. 3. **Doctor**: closed-target invariant + `inbox_depth` check per key (7-day age tripwire; `unsorted` on a growth threshold, age-exempt). 4. **CLI**: `inbox list | claim | drop` + **enroll notification** (pending-rows count for the key or its aliases + claim suggestion). 5. **Two-stage derivation pipeline** (§4): Stage A = session designation (single early return, no guards) → slugged git root → no candidate; Stage B = alias map (by key and cwd) → match with enrolled → inbox (unresolvable designation under the designated name; `unsorted` without candidate). **Remove the basename fallback.** 6. **Relations forwarding contract** (formalize the observed daemon behavior). 7. **Correction to the export mechanism — controlled test (2026-09-06).** The first draft of this item claimed the worker skips memories whose content matches an already-ACKED upsert (a "content-identity dedup"). A controlled test refutes that: a byte-identical re-enqueue of an already-ACKED observation (same target, entity, op, payload, and project column; only seq and timestamp differ) was **delivered by the worker within one cycle** on the legacy `cloud` lane. A content revision of an observation with ACK history was likewise delivered. Read with the 67-move and 135-straggler cases, the pattern is single-factor: **every observed non-delivery sat on the per-project lane, which has never delivered (Problem 6); every delivery sat on the legacy lane.** The worker reads only the legacy `cloud` target (grouped by the `project` column). There is no dedup key in the evidence; the earlier 7-case table (which confounded lane and change type in the move rows) is withdrawn as dedup evidence and stands only as evidence for Problem 6. Consequence for the design: project moves need no dedup-key fix. They fail solely because the per-project lane is dead. The fix is the lane itself (item 1 + the invariant), and the control shows that once a lane delivers, identical-content re-delivery works — so moves will flow once per-project targets become the delivery lane. ## Local work (not upstream) Executed or executable on the affected machine; separate from the upstream items above. - **One-time cleanup (done-ready, under backup)**: delete the **35 phantom `sync_state` rows** (0 unacked, target ∉ {enrolled, inbox, legacy}) + one long-dead 403 phantom row. Empty state rows, not the log: the mutation log (`sync_mutations`) is untouched — it is append-only forensics, rows are retired via ack, never deleted or rewritten. Nothing else: the data debt is already drained (880 telemetry rows acked, 9 relations delivered) and 20 permanent seq gaps remain by append-only design. - **Stopgap canary (optional, reversible)**: a local job that compares `sync_state.target_key` against {enrolled, inbox, legacy} and warns on new targets — real-time drift detection, no code change. Stays in place until the doctor invariant (item 3) lands upstream. ## Related - #1007 — `projects consolidate` ignores piped stdin and proceeds with the full candidate set (the consolidation flow that item 1 (the lane) makes actually deliverable) - #699 — unenrolled machines accumulate sync_mutations and the doctor's prescribed repair was circular (closed; this design is the forward-looking fix for cloud-configured machines) - #578 — consolidate over-merges; cwd-based detection creates duplicate projects - #570 — named remotes with per-project sync routing - #104 — project aliasing system - #136 — normalize project names to lowercase ## What this issue is asking for This is a design proposal from a long-running single-machine deployment (10 enrolled projects, ~7.6k mutation rows, self-hosted cloud) — every number in it was measured, not estimated. I am not asking for a PR; I am asking for a decision: 1. **Confirm the measured lane behavior** the design is built on: the worker reads only the legacy `cloud` lane (Problem 6), verified by the controlled test in item 7 (identical-content re-enqueue delivered on the legacy lane; every observed skip sat on the dead per-project lane). If that model is wrong, tell me where — the rest of the design holds or falls with it. 2. **Decide the lane question** in the invariant: per-project targets as the delivery lane (this design's proposal), or keep legacy as the one observations lane and document it. 3. If the direction is approved, I'd suggest **item 1 (the lane) as the first slice**, with the doctor invariant (item 3) as the guardrail, and the rest following in order. I'm not going to open a PR before the direction is settled, but I can do something rarer than code review: **validate any implementation against a real, messy, single-user deployment with a full history** — the machine where this whole issue came from. Happy to run betas, hit the edge cases, and report back with data. If the first slice is approved, I can also prepare a PR implementing item 1 (the lane), with item 3 (doctor invariant) as the guardrail — say the word. ## Risk / rollback The routing change is client-side: if a version routes wrongly, the doctor detects it in the first cycle (closed-target invariant). The bounded regression is unenrolled mutations sitting in the inbox (ack-based, no deletes from the log) — not lost data. For the lane change (item 1), rollback is the inverse change.

title: Harden performance-ratchet local validation and mode coverage
body:
### 📋 Pre-flight Checks

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand this issue needs `status:approved` before a PR can be opened

### 🔍 Problem Description

The performance ratchet introduced by #1002 has two follow-up reliability gaps.

First, the default `make perf-check` compares fresh results with the committed `.perf-baseline.txt`. The ratchet correctly rejects different OS, architecture, CPU, or other benchmark headers, and the documentation says the local host must match. In practice, the default target therefore stops before measuring performance for contributors whose host differs from the baseline-producing machine.

Second, the automated shell tests exercise only `--compare`. The operational `--against` path used by CI, its strict-subset bootstrap fallback, standalone `--bootstrap`, and `--update` are not covered by deterministic tests. These modes were manually validated for #1002, but later changes could regress them without a focused test failure.

### 💡 Proposed Solution

Make the local validation modes explicit without weakening the ratchet:

1. Preserve `--against <git-ref>` as the same-runner timing comparison used by CI and support it as the recommended local performance check.
2. Avoid presenting cross-host bootstrap validation as a latency comparison. Either require an explicit matching-host baseline mode or split suite-shape bootstrap validation into a clearly named target.
3. Add deterministic tests for `--against`, strict-subset bootstrap fallback, standalone `--bootstrap`, and `--update` using fixture benchmark output and a temporary Git worktree.
4. Cover successful comparisons, allowed strict-subset bootstrap, rejected benchmark/configuration mismatches, bootstrap validation failures, and deliberate baseline updates.

### 📦 Affected Area

Other

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

- Keep the current documented matching-host requirement. This preserves semantics but leaves the default target unusable on most contributor machines.
- Make the default target run only `--bootstrap`. This is portable, but it validates benchmark-suite shape rather than performance and could give a misleading sense that latency was checked.
- Rely on the manual verification performed for #1002. This does not protect the CI and maintenance paths from future regressions.

### 📎 Additional Context

Follow-up to #897 and #1002.

CodeRabbit surfaced the local-baseline concern and missing mode coverage during the final review of #1002:

- https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/pull/1002#discussion_r3938928938
- https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/pull/1002#discussion_r3938928946

A separate CodeRabbit claim about duplicate `TestMain` definitions was checked and is not part of this issue: the package contains only one `TestMain`, and the store test binary compiled and passed.

title: Remove dead code proven unreachable even from tests
body:
### 📋 Pre-flight Checks

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand this issue needs `status:approved` before a PR can be opened

### 📦 Affected Area

Mechanical dead-code cleanup across CLI, cloud dashboard/server, store, TUI, and orphan test helpers.

### 🔍 Problem Description

The proposed cleanup remains relevant, but the original symbol counts and deletion list were measured on an older revision. Current source and static analysis on `main` at `a43183c2` report **17 unreachable functions** with tests included as analysis roots and **19 U1000 findings**. These are overlapping sets, not 36 distinct deletion candidates.

Current candidate groups:

| Cluster | Candidates to revalidate before deletion |
|---|---|
| `internal/cloud/dashboard` | `Handler`, `staticSyncStatusProvider` and its `Status` method, `totalStatObservations`, `totalStatPrompts`, `totalStatSessions`, `paginationURL`, `parsePagination` |
| `internal/cloud/cloudserver` | `withAuthHandler`, `validateLegacyPayload`, `validateMutationEntry` |
| `cmd/engram/main.go` | `stdinScanner`, `userHomeDir` globals |
| `internal/tui/styles.go` | `colorSurface`, `searchHighlightStyle`. **Keep `colorBase`: it is referenced by a live style.** |
| `internal/store` | `pairResult`, unused `fakeSemanticRunner` / `routingRunner` test scaffolding, and the unused `sessionID` field in migration test scaffolding |
| Orphan test helpers | `httpPushMutations`, `countElementsWithClass`, `assertClaudeCodeWritesUnderRoot`, `runHookInDir`, `writeMigratingEngramStub` |

`Handler`, `staticSyncStatusProvider`, and `Status` remain a single reachability/deletion unit. Review references within each package rather than treating every reported name as an independent unused symbol.

### 💡 Proposed Solution

Prepare a focused `type:refactor` cleanup of candidates proven dead on the implementation base. Delete rather than introduce replacement abstractions. Refresh the existing dead-code baseline in the same change when debt is removed.

Acceptance:

- Revalidate the candidate set on the exact implementation revision and exclude any symbol that is now live, including `colorBase`.
- Check Linux, Windows, and Darwin, tagged tests, documentation references, and current open PR diffs before deletion. The present revalidation is Windows-only; older cross-platform/open-PR checks do not establish today's coverage.
- Preserve behavior and run the affected tests and repository ratchets. Use the repository-pinned deadcode tool for baseline refresh; do not change the tool version or relax the ratchet as part of cleanup.
- Keep tests and the reviewed baseline tightening with the deletion work, splitting into coherent cleanup units if needed.

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

Leave the existing debt in place, with the current ratchets preventing new debt. Cleanup still reduces misleading reading surface, but does not require a new CI policy or framework.

### 📎 Additional Context

The deadcode CI ratchet is already implemented. `CONTRIBUTING.md` documents `make deadcode-check`, `make deadcode-baseline`, and the pinned `golang.org/x/tools/cmd/deadcode@v0.30.0` comparison against `.deadcode-baseline.txt`. The original claim that CI has no guard is no longer current.

Current analysis was executed on Windows/amd64 with Go 1.26.4 against an isolated archive of `a43183c2`:

```bash
go run golang.org/x/tools/cmd/deadcode@v0.50.0 -test ./...          # 17 unreachable functions
go run honnef.co/go/tools/cmd/staticcheck@v0.8.1 -checks=U1000 ./... # 19 findings
```

Staticcheck exited nonzero because it reported the listed unused-code findings. These exploratory tool versions are recorded for reproducibility, not proposed replacements for repository-pinned CI tools. No deletions or functional tests were performed for this update, and no refreshed Linux/Darwin, tagged-test, or open-PR reachability proof is claimed.

title: feat(store): extend review_after decay beyond decision/policy/preference and start using expires_at
body:
### 📋 Pre-flight Checks

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand this issue needs `status:approved` before a PR can be opened

> **Revised 2026-09-24** per [maintainer feedback](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues/957#issuecomment-5800001793): narrowed to one first slice with measured, per-type `review_after` defaults only. Hard expiry (`expires_at`) is deferred until an explicit read/sync/recovery contract for expired memories exists.

### 🔍 Problem Description

Memory decay currently only fires for three observation types: `decision` (6 months), `policy` (12), and `preference` (3) via `decayReviewAfterMonths` (`internal/store/store.go:371`). Every other knowledge type, `bugfix`, `discovery`, `pattern`, `config`, `architecture`, gets `review_after = NULL` forever (documented as Phase 1 behavior).

The practical consequence: most knowledge ages silently. A stale `bugfix` note about code that no longer exists, an outdated `config` observation after an environment change, or a superseded `pattern` never surfaces for review, so dead facts keep flowing into search and context indefinitely. Nothing ever asks "is this still true?" for the majority of what agents save.

### 💡 Proposed Solution (first slice: `review_after` defaults only)

**Slot the five missing knowledge types onto the already-shipped offsets.** The shipped ladder is the calibration baseline: `preference` 3 / `decision` 6 / `policy` 12. This slice introduces **zero new offsets**, every new default reuses a shipped one, so queue behavior stays comparable with what already ships:

| type | months | anchored to | drift rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| `config` | 3 | `preference` | environment-tied, fastest-drifting knowledge type |
| `discovery` | 6 | `decision` | facts about code, true until the code moves |
| `pattern` | 6 | `decision` | conventions and practices, medium-stable |
| `architecture` | 12 | `policy` | structural facts, slow-drifting, costly when wrong |
| `bugfix` | 12 | `policy` | failure-mode knowledge outlives the code it describes |

Types absent from the map keep `review_after = NULL`, identical to today: `learning`, `manual`, `tool_use`, `file_change`, `file_read`, `command`, `search`, `session_summary`, and everything else operational/high-volume. Purely additive write-side change; `review_after` already syncs (it is in `observationSelectColumns` and the sync payload), so no sync change is needed.

**How the defaults surface in the existing review queue** (no new tooling):

- Save a `config` observation on 2026-09-24 → `review_after = 2026-12-24`. Until then `mem_search` returns it exactly as today with `state: "active"`.
- On 2026-12-25 the observation is fully returned by every search, but now carries `state: "needs_review"` (`Observation.State()` derives it virtually from `review_after`; search/FTS never consults `review_after`, so ranking, visibility, and content are untouched).
- `mem_review action=list` includes it; `action=mark_reviewed` resets `review_after = now + 3 months` per the type's map entry. `mem_update` / `mem_delete` remain the act-on-it paths.

**Acceptance criteria (tests the PR carries):**

1. Per-type write test (RED→GREEN): saving each of the five types sets `review_after = save-time + offset` (table test over `decayReviewAfterMonths`).
2. Phase-1 regression guard: every unmapped type still gets `review_after = NULL`.
3. Overdue-visibility test: an observation with a past `review_after` remains returned by search (FTS and fallback paths) with `state: "needs_review"`, asserting no filter or silent hiding; `mem_review action=list` surfaces it while active observations are excluded.
4. `mark_reviewed` resets using the new map entries.

### 📦 Affected Area

Store (database, queries) — write-side decay map plus tests only.

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

- Status quo: only decisions/policies/preferences decay, leaving knowledge types permanently unaudited.
- New offsets per type (e.g. `bugfix` 9): rejected for slice one; reusing the shipped 3/6/12 ladder keeps the queue comparable and avoids inventing unmeasured numbers.
- Also mapping `learning`/operational types: rejected; volume would flood the review queue without a curation story.
- `expires_at` population: **deferred** until an explicit read/sync/recovery contract for expired memories exists (maintainer feedback above); a review-prompting default must never make useful history disappear without a user decision.

### 📎 Additional Context

Substrate already shipped: `review_after` column applied idempotently, `Observation.State()` derives `needs_review`, `mem_review` list/mark_reviewed tooling landed with #437. This slice only widens the write-side map.

title: Define a canonical PostgreSQL configuration path for Compose and cloud startup
body:
### 📋 Pre-flight Checks
- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand this issue needs `status:approved` before a PR can be opened

### 🔍 Problem Description
The published GHCR reference Compose configuration initializes PostgreSQL with `POSTGRES_USER`, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, and `POSTGRES_DB`, while the cloud service independently connects through `ENGRAM_DATABASE_URL`. `cloudstore.New` performs the actual `PingContext`.

The documented `.env` therefore duplicates database identity and credential information in `POSTGRES_*` values and in the DSN, without one canonical user-facing configuration path. This creates an observable contradiction when the two representations do not agree, particularly for URI-sensitive password values.

### 💡 Proposed Solution
Define one canonical, safely validated PostgreSQL configuration path for Compose initialization and the cloud service’s runtime connection.

The intended behavior should:
- make the relationship between PostgreSQL initialization values and `ENGRAM_DATABASE_URL` explicit and safely validated;
- handle URI-sensitive credential values correctly when constructing or accepting a DSN;
- ensure readiness checks are not treated as proof that the runtime credentials and database target are usable;
- add a behavior-level fresh-volume startup test proving initialization and the cloud store’s actual connection path succeed together.

### 📦 Affected Area
Store (database, queries)

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered
Continue documenting `POSTGRES_*` and `ENGRAM_DATABASE_URL` as independently supplied values. This leaves database identity and credentials duplicated and does not provide a canonical or validated relationship between them.

### 📎 Additional Context
PR #691’s `pg_isready` healthcheck change was closed as not root-causal. `pg_isready` can report readiness without correct user or database values, whereas the actual cloud connection is established by `cloudstore.New` through `PingContext`.

This report does not claim a production incident, a local Docker reproduction, or data loss. Docker and `pg_isready` were unavailable locally.

title: feat(cloud): define byte-exact session identity across sync boundaries
body:
### 📋 Pre-flight Checks

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand this issue needs `status:approved` before a PR can be opened

### 🔍 Problem Description

Session identities can cross local chunks, mutation payloads, cloud materialization, migration backfill, signatures, server validation, and dashboard read models. Those paths do not currently share one explicit rule for whether a nonblank session ID is byte-exact or canonicalized.

A partial fix is unsafe: preserving bytes in the codec while trimming during backfill or dashboard indexing can split one logical session, orphan observation or prompt references, or make historical replay disagree with live sync. PR #780 contained a prototype for byte-exact handling, but migration and projection paths still need a system-wide contract.

### 💡 Proposed Solution

Choose and document one end-to-end session identity contract:

- either preserve accepted nonblank IDs byte-for-byte, or reject noncanonical IDs at one explicit ingress boundary;
- assign one validator as the executable owner of the invariant;
- apply the same rule in chunk encoding, mutation normalization, cloud materialization, signatures, migration/backfill, server validation, and dashboard indexing;
- define compatibility behavior for already-persisted identities;
- prohibit silent remapping between a session and its observation or prompt references;
- add cross-layer conformance tests for push, pull, bootstrap, migration, replay, and dashboard projection.

Implementation should begin only after the compatibility and migration policy is approved.

### 📦 Affected Area

Sync (multi-instance)

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

Trimming IDs independently in every layer hides contract drift and can merge byte-distinct identities. Preserving bytes only in new transport paths leaves older migration and projection paths inconsistent. Porting the final PR #780 commit directly would therefore be incomplete.

### 📎 Additional Context

PR #780 was preserved as historical reference after closure. Issue #872 is a broader invariant-ownership proposal, while #631 concerns diagnosis of dangling session references; neither defines this specific end-to-end identity and migration contract.

title: feat(sync): define recovery semantics for incomplete chunk history
body:
### 📋 Pre-flight Checks

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand this issue needs `status:approved` before a PR can be opened

### 🔍 Problem Description

Local chunk sync has no single recovery contract for incomplete history. A manifest can reference chunks that are unavailable on the current machine, while existing chunks can contain partial session, prompt, observation, relation, or tombstone history.

The current behavior mixes several decisions: when missing history should be treated as unknown, when local SQLite should re-export idempotently, when import should defer a dependency, when corruption must fail loudly, and how long histories should be scanned without unbounded work. PR #780 experimented with several of these policies while solving #615, but #894 delivered only the scoped observation-watermark fix. The remaining lifecycle policy needs its own design before implementation.

### 💡 Proposed Solution

Define one explicit recovery contract for local and cloud sync:

- distinguish unavailable history from corrupt readable history;
- keep local SQLite as the source of truth and never silently drop data;
- specify when to re-export idempotently, rebuild derived history, defer dependencies, or stop;
- align dependency ordering and terminal lifecycle states across local and cloud import;
- define bounded behavior for full-history scans;
- cover missing, corrupt, partial, tombstoned, and dependency-stalled histories with deterministic push and pull tests.

Implementation should be split into focused work units only after the contract is approved.

### 📦 Affected Area

Sync (multi-instance)

### 🔄 Alternatives Considered

Continuing the global timestamp-only watermark can silently miss identities. Porting the accumulated PR #780 logic would mix multiple roots and unresolved policies. A destructive full reset would discard useful delivery state and violate local-first expectations.

### 📎 Additional Context

PR #780 was closed after PR #894 resolved issue #615. Related but non-equivalent issues include #595 (explicit full re-sync after project migration), #649 (orphan relation import stalls), and #849 (dead-row retention). This tracker owns only the incomplete-history recovery contract.

title: feat(mcp): batch semantic judgments and finalize sessions atomically
body:
### 📋 Pre-flight Checks

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand this issue needs `status:approved` before a PR can be opened

### 🔍 Problem Description

Engram's current MCP lifecycle requires LLM clients to cross several dependent tool boundaries during session closure:

```text
mem_save
  → model continuation to classify returned judgment IDs
  → one or more mem_judge calls
  → model continuation
  → mem_session_summary
  → model continuation
  → mem_session_end
  → model continuation
  → final response
```

The Engram operations themselves are not the bottleneck. In one measured OpenCode occurrence, `mem_save`, three `mem_judge` calls, `mem_session_summary`, and `mem_session_end` consumed 901 ms in aggregate. However, every dependent result forced the client to re-enter a large parent-model context, amplifying unrelated provider latency by several minutes.

The API currently offers no batch operation for semantic judgments and no ordered operation that persists caller-authored summary content and ends the session together. Clients must either accept repeated model continuations, attempt unsafe parallel ordering, or weaken the memory-governance lifecycle.

### 💡 Proposed Solution

Add an MCP contract for batched relation judgment and ordered session finalization.

1. Provide a batch judgment operation, such as `mem_judge_many`, that:
