title: bug(review): in-process lens completion never sends the provider session header, so no opencode-go model can serve any reviewer role
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this bug.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

Since gentle-ai #4784 made Pi reviewer roles **host-mediated in-process completions**, no lens can run against a provider that requires per-session request headers. Every lens capture against `opencode-go` fails typed:

```
{"tool":"gentle_review_capture","status":"blocked",
 "outcome":"pi-host-relay-transport-failure",
 "failure":{"kind":"pi-failed","stage":"pi","exit_code":null,"timed_out":false,
            "elapsed_ms":322,"timeout_ms":908996},
 "reason":"Reviewer completion failed for review-reliability: 400:
   {\"type\":\"MissingSessionID\",\"message\":\"Error from provider (Console Go):
   Request is missing x-opencode-session and cannot be routed efficiently.\"}",
 "mutation_performed":false,"mutation_outcome":"none"}
```

`opencode-go` began enforcing `x-opencode-session`. Pi's normal request path supplies it via `mergeProviderAttributionHeaders(model, settingsManager, sessionId, ...)` (`pi-coding-agent dist/core/sdk.js:201`). The in-process reviewer bypasses that path entirely, so the header is never sent.

`docs/review-integration.md` documents the omission as intentional design: the completion has *"no systemPrompt, no tools, no session, no extension hooks, no child process."* That is exactly what makes this a structural incompatibility rather than a slip — the design says "no session", the provider requires a session. Neither the extension-hook workaround nor the child-process path is available by construction.

### Root cause chain (verified on gentle-pi 3.3.0)

1. `lib/review-host-relay.ts:36` imports the completion from the bare SDK package, not from Pi's own streaming surface:
   ```ts
   import { completeSimple } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/compat";
   ```
2. `lib/review-host-relay.ts:736` passes it straight through as the completion dependency:
   ```ts
   { registry: preparedRequest.reviewerRegistry!, complete: completeSimple },
   ```
3. `lib/inprocess-reviewer.ts:187-194` builds options that carry auth only — there is no session identifier to forward, because the type has no such field:
   ```ts
   const options: SimpleStreamOptions = {
     signal: combinedSignal,
     timeoutMs: request.timeoutMs,
     ...(auth.apiKey === undefined ? {} : { apiKey: auth.apiKey }),
     ...(auth.headers === undefined ? {} : { headers: auth.headers }),
     ...(reasoning.reasoning === undefined ? {} : { reasoning: reasoning.reasoning }),
   };
   ```
4. `pi-ai/dist/types.d.ts:219` — `SimpleStreamOptions extends StreamOptions` has **no `sessionId`** member.
5. `pi-coding-agent dist/core/model-registry.js:30` — `getApiKeyAndHeaders` returns `resolution.auth.headers` only; the session header is added later by the SDK, never by the registry.
6. `pi-coding-agent dist/core/provider-attribution.js:49-58` — `getSessionHeaders` gates on `provider === "opencode" || provider === "opencode-go" || hostname === "opencode.ai"`, so this affects every `opencode`/`opencode-go` model.

`grep` over the installed package finds no reference to `mergeProviderAttributionHeaders`, `x-opencode-session`, or `sessionId` anywhere in `lib/review-host-relay.ts` or `lib/inprocess-reviewer.ts`.

### Minimal repro

1. Configure any `opencode-go` model for a lens in `~/.pi/gentle-ai/models.json`:
   ```json
   { "review-reliability": { "model": "opencode-go/glm-5.3-flash", "thinking": "high" } }
   ```
2. Start any ordinary review and reach the lens capture slot.
3. The capture fails `pi-host-relay-transport-failure` with `400 MissingSessionID`. No mutation occurs and no verdict is produced.

### Evidence that the config side is correct

The failure is not a routing-config problem. With a model configured, the relay **resolves the selection and reaches the provider** (`elapsed_ms: 322`, a real HTTP 400 from the provider). Pointing the same lens at a provider that does not gate on this header reaches the model itself and fails only on that provider's own quota:

```
"reason":"Reviewer completion failed for review-reliability:
          Codex error: The usage limit has been reached"
"elapsed_ms":1861
```

So the completion launches correctly and authenticates; only the `opencode-go` session header is missing.

### Provider matrix (from the local catalog's `baseUrl`)

| Provider | Models | Host | Needs `x-opencode-session` | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `opencode-go` | 27 | `opencode.ai` | all | all blocked |
| `openai-codex` | 6 | `chatgpt.com` | none | works |

This means the whole `opencode-go` catalog — the default provider in many setups, including this one — cannot serve any reviewer role.

### Suggested direction

The session header is an attribution/routing hint, not review authority, so supplying it does not widen what the reviewer is allowed to do. Options a maintainer may prefer:

- Thread an opaque per-completion session id into the completion and merge it through the same `getSessionHeaders` logic the SDK uses, keeping the "no ambient session, no extension hooks" guarantee intact.
- Or have the coordinator pass `auth.headers` that already include a synthesized per-completion session id, so the header travels with the credentials the registry already returns.

I deliberately did **not** apply the obvious user-side workaround of adding a static `x-opencode-session` via `~/.pi/agent/models.json` provider `headers`. It is mechanically effective (`model-runtime.js:345` merges configured headers into `auth.headers`) but unsafe: `mergeProviderAttributionHeaders` applies `getSessionHeaders` **first** and then `Object.assign(merged, headers)` over it, so a static configured header would override the real session id on the user's primary session, degrading routing and prompt caching. Worth guarding against if this is ever suggested as a fix.

### Environment

- gentle-pi `3.3.0` (npm `latest`, verified current)
- gentle-ai `3.4.0`
- Pi host relay on macOS, Pi `defaultProvider: opencode-go`
- Provider contract `1.2.0`; status schema `gentle-ai.review-integration.status/v9`
- Two lineages remain in state `reviewing` with no verdict and no mutation: `review-594082f6db48d94d`, `review-bdd47350c410239c`

title: fix(todo): validate persisted Gentle snapshots before replay
body:
## Problem

Gentle Todo restores its state from persisted tool-result snapshots through `replayTodo()`.

For native Gentle snapshots, the replay boundary currently performs only a minimal structural check:

    const ours = details[TODO_DETAILS_KEY] as TodoState | undefined;

    if (ours && Array.isArray(ours.tasks)) {
        state = {
            tasks: ours.tasks,
            nextId: ours.nextId,
            updatedTurn: ours.updatedTurn ?? null,
        };
    }

The `as TodoState` assertion does not provide runtime validation.

As a result, a malformed or inconsistent persisted snapshot can be restored as live `TodoState` and later passed to `applyTodo()`, rendering, prompt generation, and other Todo operations.

## Reproduction

Consider a persisted Gentle snapshot containing one existing task but an inconsistent `nextId`:

    const branch = [{
        type: "message",
        message: {
            role: "toolResult",
            toolName: "todo",
            isError: false,
            details: {
                gentleTodo: {
                    tasks: [
                        {
                            id: 1,
                            title: "Existing task",
                            status: "pending",
                        },
                    ],
                    nextId: 1,
                    updatedTurn: 3,
                },
            },
        },
    }];

    const restored = replayTodo(branch);

The restored state is effectively:

    #1 Existing task
    nextId = 1

This violates the state invariant that the next generated ID must not collide with an existing task.

A subsequent valid operation:

    const result = applyTodo(
        restored,
        { action: "add", title: "New task" },
        4,
    );

can then produce:

    #1 Existing task
    #1 New task
    nextId = 2

The live Todo state now contains two tasks with the same identity.

## Observable consequence

Duplicate IDs make later operations ambiguous.

`update()` locates a task by ID and subsequently maps replacements using that ID. Once two tasks share the same ID, an update intended for one task can affect multiple entries.

The failure chain is therefore:

    inconsistent persisted snapshot
            |
            v
        replayTodo()
            |
            | snapshot accepted
            v
    #1 Existing task
    nextId = 1
            |
            v
          add()
            |
            v
    #1 Existing task
    #1 New task
            |
            v
      update(id: 1)
            |
            v
    ambiguous task identity

This is not only a malformed-display problem: persisted state can violate assumptions required by subsequent Todo mutations.

## Validation gap

The native Gentle replay path trusts persisted data considerably more than the legacy `rpiv-todo` migration path.

Legacy snapshots pass their tasks back through `buildTask()` before entering the live state.

Native Gentle snapshots are effectively cast directly from persisted `unknown` data to `TodoState`.

The replay boundary should validate the persisted representation before allowing it to become authoritative live Todo state.

## Expected behavior

`replayTodo()` should only restore a native Gentle snapshot when it satisfies the Todo state invariants.

At minimum, validation should cover:

- `tasks` is an array;
- every task ID is a positive integer;
- task IDs are unique;
- every title is a valid non-empty string;
- every status is a supported Todo status;
- optional task fields have valid types;
- `nextId` is a positive integer;
- `nextId` is greater than the highest existing task ID;
- `updatedTurn` is either `null` or a valid non-negative integer.

Invalid persisted data must not enter the live reducer as a trusted `TodoState`.

## Failure behavior

Replay should fail closed for an invalid native snapshot.

Because `replayTodo()` walks the branch chronologically, a malformed later snapshot should not need to destroy an earlier valid state.

Conceptually:

    valid snapshot
         |
         v
    current replay state
         |
    malformed snapshot
         |
         +--> ignore
         |
         v
    previous valid state remains authoritative

The exact failure policy can remain an implementation decision, provided malformed state cannot become live `TodoState`.

## Scope

A focused implementation should remain around the Todo replay boundary:

    unknown persisted details
            |
            v
    parse/validate Gentle snapshot
            |
            +-- valid --> TodoState
            |
            +-- invalid --> ignore/fail closed

This should not require changes to Pi session internals or other Gentle subsystems.

Expected primary files:

    lib/shell-todo.ts
    tests/shell-todo.test.ts

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Native Gentle Todo snapshots are runtime-validated before replay.
- [ ] A snapshot whose `nextId` can collide with an existing task is not restored as live invalid state.
- [ ] Duplicate persisted task IDs are rejected.
- [ ] Invalid task IDs are rejected.
- [ ] Invalid task statuses are rejected.
- [ ] Invalid or empty task titles are rejected.
- [ ] Invalid `nextId` values are rejected.
- [ ] Invalid `updatedTurn` values are rejected.
- [ ] A malformed later snapshot cannot corrupt a previously valid replay state.
- [ ] Valid Gentle snapshots continue to replay unchanged.
- [ ] Legacy `rpiv-todo` replay/migration remains compatible.
- [ ] Error tool results continue to be ignored.
- [ ] Focused regression tests reproduce the `nextId` collision before the fix.

## Non-goals

- Changing normal Todo ID allocation semantics.
- Redesigning `write`.
- Fixing general Todo staleness behavior.
- Synchronizing Todo with SDD or ODD state.
- Changing the Todo UI.
- Changing Pi session persistence.
- Repairing arbitrary malformed snapshots by inventing replacement task identities.
- Introducing another Todo state authority.

## Relationship to #737

This is separate from #737.

#737 concerns identity behavior during `write()` starting from live Todo state.

This issue concerns the persistence boundary before normal Todo mutations begin:

    #737:

    valid TodoState
        -> write()
        -> incorrect identity behavior


    this issue:

    persisted snapshot
        -> replayTodo()
        -> invalid TodoState enters the live reducer

Fixing `write()` does not prevent `replayTodo()` from restoring an inconsistent `nextId`, duplicate IDs, invalid statuses, or otherwise malformed native snapshots.

## Duplicate analysis

Existing Todo issues cover the original Gentle Todo implementation, migration/package conflicts, Todo/SDD reconciliation, stale-list behavior, and `write()` identity behavior.

No dedicated issue or PR was found for runtime validation of native persisted `gentleTodo` snapshots at the `replayTodo()` boundary.

## Suggested regression test

The minimal regression should demonstrate the observable identity failure rather than only testing type validation:

    persisted:
        #1 Existing
        nextId = 1

    replay
        -> malformed snapshot must not become live state

    without validation:
        add "New"
        -> #1 Existing
        -> #1 New

Additional focused tests should cover duplicate IDs, invalid statuses, invalid titles, invalid counters, preservation of the last valid snapshot, and continued legacy replay compatibility.

title: bug(profiles): /gentle:profiles never shows agent models on terminals narrower than 60 columns (portrait mobile)
body:
### Before submitting
- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem
On a portrait phone terminal (about 40-55 columns), `/gentle:profiles` renders only the profile-name list. The detail pane that shows each agent's model routing (the "Profile routing" / "Current routing" tables) is never drawn, and no key reveals it. Rotating the phone to landscape (80+ columns) makes the pane appear beside the list.

Root cause from source (`extensions/gentle-ai.ts`, `lib/agents-view-layout.ts`): the shared overlay layout enters panes mode only at 60 or more columns (22 + 32 + 6). `ProfilesPanel` renders detail lines only when the mode is `panes`; in `narrow` mode it draws the list column only. Unlike the Agents view (`lib/agents-view.ts`), which has narrow List/Details navigation via the `tab` key (#755), the profiles panel has no narrow toggle, so the routing is unreachable in portrait.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Open a terminal narrower than 60 columns (a phone in portrait over SSH, or any terminal resized to 46 columns).
2. Run `/gentle:profiles`.
3. Observe: only the profile list renders; the agent-to-model routing tables are absent.
4. Rotate to landscape or widen the terminal to 60+ columns and reopen `/gentle:profiles`: the routing tables appear beside the list.

### Expected and actual behavior
Expected: the per-agent model routing stays reachable on narrow terminals, for example a `tab` toggle between the profile list and the detail pane, as the Agents view already does in narrow mode.
Actual: in narrow mode the detail pane is never rendered and cannot be shown; the routing is only visible after widening the terminal to 60+ columns.

3.2.1 (from source, commit 32e2416d on main)

0.85.1

Linux

title: feat(runtime): support bounded parent-input round trips for managed Pi tasks
body:
## Problem

The managed Pi runtime has a lifecycle state for tasks that are waiting for input, but the planned foreground `AgentSession` executor does not currently define a way for a running managed child to request information from its parent and continue after receiving the response.

The authoritative task registry in #440 already defines:

    running
      -> waiting-for-input
      -> running

However, #446 intentionally owns only a bounded foreground execution:

    prepare session
      -> create task
      -> running
      -> subscribe
      -> prompt once
      -> cleanup
      -> settle

Its contract explicitly excludes queueing, steering, follow-ups, cancellation, and other interactive behavior during the prompt.

This leaves a capability gap for managed tasks that cannot complete safely without asking their owning parent for bounded input.

## Existing behavior

The current subagent runtime already supports parent/child interaction through `subagent_parent_message`.

A child can send a correlated query to its parent and continue after receiving the response.

That capability currently belongs to the existing child-process/IPC execution path.

As managed execution moves toward process-local Pi `AgentSession`, the equivalent capability should not require introducing another lifecycle authority or treating an owned child as an authenticated peer session.

## Goal

Add one bounded parent-input interaction for an already-running managed Pi task.

Conceptually:

    child AgentSession
           |
           | request parent input
           v
    managed interaction boundary
           |
           | registry transition
           v
    waiting-for-input
           |
           v
    parent
           |
           | correlated response
           v
    managed interaction boundary
           |
           | registry transition
           v
    running
           |
           | Pi-supported live input
           v
    child AgentSession continues

The task registry remains the sole lifecycle authority and Pi remains the sole conversation/session authority.

## Authority boundaries

This capability must not introduce another task or lifecycle store.

- #440/#448 remain the sole task identity, lifecycle, terminal-state, and final-result authority.
- #445 remains the `AgentSession` preparation boundary.
- #446 remains the foundational foreground execution transaction.
- Pi `AgentSession` remains the live model/session authority.
- This child owns only the bounded correlation and delivery of parent-input interaction for an existing managed task.

A task waiting for parent input must be represented through the existing authoritative registry transition:

    running -> waiting-for-input

and successful response delivery returns it through:

    waiting-for-input -> running

No local boolean, mirrored task state, inferred state, timer, prompt text, or message content may become a second lifecycle authority.

## Pi integration

Delivery back into the running child must use a supported public Pi `AgentSession` interaction primitive appropriate for an active run.

The implementation must not mutate `agent.state.messages` or otherwise edit Pi conversation state directly.

The exact Pi primitive must be selected against the repository-pinned Pi API at implementation time rather than assuming behavior from a newer global Pi release.

## Correlation

Each parent-input request must have one bounded correlation identity.

A response may satisfy only the matching live request.

The interaction must deterministically reject or ignore:

- unknown correlation IDs;
- duplicate responses;
- responses for an earlier request;
- responses after terminal settlement;
- responses after cancellation/shutdown invalidates the request;
- responses belonging to another task.

A late response must never reactivate a terminal task.

No durable request/reply history or replay mechanism is introduced.

## Lifecycle behavior

A valid interaction follows this logical sequence:

    task is running
      -> child requests parent input
      -> registry: running -> waiting-for-input
      -> parent receives bounded request
      -> matching response is accepted
      -> registry: waiting-for-input -> running
      -> response is delivered through Pi
      -> child continues execution

Failure to establish or deliver the interaction must fail closed according to the managed runtime's authoritative lifecycle/settlement contract.

This issue must not invent a second terminal-result format or bypass #448 settlement.

## Privacy boundary

The managed-task registry must not store:

- request text;
- response text;
- prompts;
- model output;
- reasoning;
- tool arguments/results;
- credentials;
- provider/model details;
- session internals.

Interaction payloads exist only for the lifetime required to complete the bounded round trip.

Lifecycle projections continue to expose lifecycle metadata only.

## Relationship to peer messaging

This is not peer messaging and does not extend #442.

#442 owns communication between separately addressable Gentle Pi peer sessions, including trust, authentication, peer discovery, project inspection, and peer delivery.

This issue is limited to an already-owned parent/child relationship inside one managed execution tree:

    #442:

    session A --------> session B
            trusted peer


    this issue:

    parent task ------> owned child task
            managed execution tree

No peer directory, bilateral trust, authentication protocol, network transport, project discovery, or generic session-to-session messaging is introduced here.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An already-running managed Pi task can issue one bounded request for parent input.
- [ ] Entering the wait uses the authoritative `running -> waiting-for-input` registry transition.
- [ ] A matching accepted response uses the authoritative `waiting-for-input -> running` transition.
- [ ] The response is delivered through a supported public Pi `AgentSession` interaction primitive; Pi message state is never mutated directly.
- [ ] Requests and responses have deterministic correlation.
- [ ] Unknown, duplicate, stale, cross-task, and post-settlement responses cannot reach the child.
- [ ] Settlement, cancellation, shutdown, or other terminal disposition invalidates pending interaction.
- [ ] A late response cannot reactivate or mutate a terminal task.
- [ ] #440/#448 remain the sole lifecycle and terminal-result authority.
- [ ] Pi remains the sole live conversation/session authority.
- [ ] No prompt, request, response, model output, reasoning, or tool data is stored in the task registry or activity projection.
- [ ] Existing non-managed subagent behavior remains unchanged.
- [ ] Existing peer messaging scope in #442 remains unchanged.
- [ ] Focused tests cover successful round trip, correlation, duplicate response, stale response, terminal race, cross-task isolation, and cleanup.

## Non-goals

- Peer-to-peer Gentle session messaging.
- Peer discovery, trust, authentication, or networking.
- Generic session-to-session messaging.
- Background scheduling or concurrency policy.
- Persistent messages, replay, recovery, or durable queues.
- New task lifecycle states.
- A second task/result authority.
- Direct mutation of Pi message history.
- Replacing #446's foreground executor.
- Changing existing legacy `subagent_run` behavior.
- UI or public peer tooling.

## Dependencies and delivery

This is a follow-up managed-runtime slice under #419.

It should build on the merged managed execution foundations rather than expand #446's bounded foreground PR.

Expected dependency order:

    #440 task registry
      -> #448 atomic settlement
      -> #449 foreground outcome classification
      -> #445 isolated AgentSession preparation
      -> #446 foreground executor
      -> this bounded parent-input interaction

Implementation should target current `main` only after the required managed-runtime foundations have merged.

## Duplicate analysis

This is not a duplicate of #440, which owns lifecycle state but no messaging or session interaction.

It is not a duplicate of #446, whose foreground executor explicitly excludes steering, follow-ups, queues, and interactive prompt behavior.

It is not a duplicate of #448/#449, which own terminal settlement and final-run classification.

It is not a duplicate of #442, which owns authenticated communication between separate peer sessions.

The missing capability is specifically the bridge between the existing `waiting-for-input` managed lifecycle state and a live process-local Pi `AgentSession` owned by that managed task.

## Review shape

Keep this as one bounded follow-up to the foreground executor.

If implementing correlation, lifecycle race handling, Pi delivery, and tests cannot fit within the repository's normal review-size limit, split the transport/delivery mechanism from lifecycle integration into separately approved children rather than widening this issue.

title: fix(review): reject duplicate execute bindings in v9 role submissions
body:
The v9 host-mediated role submission validation can fail to reject duplicated "execute" bindings.

For "review.capture-refuter" and "review.capture-validation", a submission descriptor must use "--materialize=true" and must not carry "--execute".

The current validation resolves an argument only when exactly one matching entry exists:

const argumentNamed = (argumentName: string): string | undefined => {
    const matches = argumentsList.filter((argument) => argument.name === argumentName);
    return matches.length === 1 ? matches[0]!.value : undefined;
};

if (argumentNamed("execute") !== undefined) {
    throw new TypeError(...);
}

With two "execute" entries, "argumentNamed("execute")" returns "undefined", so the incompatibility check does not detect that "execute" is present.

Reproduction

Use an otherwise valid v9 host-mediated role input with a submission descriptor and arguments equivalent to:

materialize=true
execute=true
execute=true

The same case applies to:

- "review.capture-refuter"
- "review.capture-validation"

Current behavior

A single "execute" binding is rejected, but duplicated "execute" bindings can bypass the presence check because multiple matches resolve to "undefined".

Expected behavior

Any "execute" binding must make the host-mediated submission invalid, regardless of its value or how many times it appears.

For example, the validation should reject all of these:

execute=true
execute=false
execute=true + execute=true
execute=false + execute=false

when a v9 role submission descriptor is present.

Proposed outcome

Check for the presence of any "execute" argument directly instead of using the helper that requires exactly one match.

Keep duplicate handling operation-specific rather than changing the shared argument decoder contract.

Regression coverage

Add tests for both role capture operations verifying that:

1. A valid submission with "materialize=true" remains accepted.
2. A submission with one "execute" binding is rejected.
3. A submission with duplicate "execute" bindings is rejected.
4. Duplicate "execute" bindings cannot bypass validation regardless of their values.

Regenerate the runtime artifact if required by the repository workflow.

Scope

Expected implementation scope is limited to the v9 role-submission validation and its regression tests. No change to the legacy self-contained "--execute" role path is intended.

title: fix(profiles): reconcile live thinking when an orchestrator omits it
body:
Problem

Applying a profile whose "orchestrator" defines a model but omits "thinking" can leave the running session on the previous thinking level, even though the persisted default no longer contains "defaultThinkingLevel".

This creates a split between the live session and the next session:

- the profile apply writes the new orchestrator model and removes "defaultThinkingLevel" from Pi's "settings.json";
- "switchLiveOrchestrator()" calls "setModel(...)", but returns immediately when "entry.thinking === undefined";
- Pi's model-switch resolution can reuse the current session thinking level when no default thinking level exists before falling back to its normal default.

So a profile without an explicit thinking level can inherit stale live state from the previously active profile/session.

Reproduction

1. Start with a session whose current model uses "thinking = high".
2. Save or create a profile with:

{
  "orchestrator": {
    "model": "nan/glm5.3"
  }
}

There is intentionally no "thinking" field.

3. Apply that profile from "/gentle:profiles".
4. Observe:
   - persisted settings contain the new provider/model and no "defaultThinkingLevel";
   - the running session can retain the previous "high" thinking level.
5. Start a fresh session from those persisted settings. The missing thinking level is resolved through Pi's normal default rather than the stale live value.

The mismatch can also be reproduced by applying profile A with an explicit thinking level and then profile B with an orchestrator model but no "thinking". Profile B should not silently inherit profile A's live thinking level.

Expected behavior

Applying a profile should leave the running session consistent with the profile's persisted orchestrator snapshot.

If the profile omits "thinking", the live session should resolve that omission the same way a fresh session would after "defaultThinkingLevel" has been removed, rather than preserving stale state from the previous profile/session.

Current code

"applyOrchestratorSettings()" removes the persisted default when thinking is omitted:

if (entry.thinking === undefined) delete next.defaultThinkingLevel;
else next.defaultThinkingLevel = entry.thinking;

But "switchLiveOrchestrator()" currently stops after switching the model:

if (entry.thinking === undefined)
    return `\nThis session now runs on ${label}.`;

The persisted and live orchestrator states can therefore diverge.

Proposed scope

Keep this as a narrow follow-up to #1220 / #1221 / #1224:

- reconcile the live thinking level when an applied orchestrator omits "thinking";
- preserve current behavior when "thinking" is explicit;
- preserve existing fail-closed/reporting behavior for unknown models, missing authentication, and rejected thinking levels;
- add regression coverage for "explicit thinking → omitted thinking".

Likely implementation scope:

- "extensions/gentle-ai.ts"
- "tests/gentle-ai.test.ts"

Acceptance criteria

- Applying an orchestrator with explicit "thinking" keeps current behavior.
- Applying one without "thinking" does not preserve stale live thinking from the previous profile/session.
- The live session and a fresh session started from the persisted settings resolve the omitted thinking level consistently.
- Unknown-model and authentication failures still leave the current live session untouched and are reported as today.
- Regression coverage demonstrates the transition from an explicit thinking profile to a profile with omitted thinking.

title: bug(review): session review consent re-prompts for every candidate when reviews run in per-PR throwaway clones (grant keyed to one canonical git common-dir identity)
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

The host consent action **"Review and allow this session"** is effectively unusable whenever reviews run against ephemeral review clones, because the standing session permission is keyed to one canonical Git common-directory identity (sha256 of `realpath(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)`).

In a single long session (17 review candidates over ~9 hours, RDD review enabled, consent dialogs answered with the session action every time), the orchestrating agent reviewed each PR in a fresh throwaway clone created with `rm -rf example-app-<n>-public-review && git clone ...`. Each clone has a different canonical common dir, therefore a different `repositoryIdentity`, therefore `hasReviewSessionPermission()` returns false on every new candidate and the three-action consent dialog is presented again. The user granted "reviews allowed for this session and this repository" 17 times and still got prompted on candidate 18.

Observations that isolate the cause:

- Re-STARTs against the **same** clone resolve without a new dialog (same repositoryIdentity), so the per-clone binding is confirmed.
- Sibling worktrees of one clone are covered as designed; fresh clones are not, and nothing in the dialog or the notify copy ("Reviews are allowed for this Pi session and this Git repository.") communicates that "repository" means "that exact clone".
- Secondary, same flow: a pending consent-binding expired after the 10-minute TTL while the model was still relaying, producing one blocked `answer-consent` that required a fresh START (`restart-for-fresh-consent`).

Impact: for the realistic multi-PR triage workflow (one review clone per PR), the standing permission never carries, consent fatigue sets in, and users reasonably read the repeated identical dialog as a bug.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Enable the review switch (RDD on) in an interactive Pi session in any Git repository.
2. Complete one consent dialog by choosing the host action "Review and allow this session". Status shows "reviews allowed for this session".
3. For a second candidate, run the review START with `workspaceRoot` pointing at a **freshly cloned** checkout of the same project (e.g. `rm -rf review-clone && git clone <url> review-clone`), not the session's own worktree and not a sibling worktree.
4. Observe the consent dialog appears again even though the session grant was just given and the project is the same.

Minimal check without a second candidate: grant the session action for clone A, then call the review START for clone B of the same repository content; the dialog reappears.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected: after choosing "Review and allow this session", later review candidates in the same interactive session are auto-consented, or at minimum the dialog explains why the existing grant does not apply (e.g. names the covered clone path and shows that this candidate lives in a different repository identity).

Actual: the identical three-action dialog reappears for every new review clone, with no indication that the previous grant was scoped to a different canonical common dir. 17 consent dialogs occurred in one observed session for 17 distinct per-PR review clones of one project.

Suggested directions (non-binding):

1. Name the exact clone path covered by the grant in the dialog/notify copy, so the per-clone scope is visible.
2. Offer an explicit, clearly-labeled broader action such as "allow reviews for any repository from this session" (the realistic scope for multi-PR triage).
3. When a standing grant exists for a different repositoryIdentity in the same session, include that fact in the dialog instead of showing an identical prompt.

### Pi version

0.85.1

title: bug(shell): NaN usage only works when the custom provider id is exactly "nan"
body:
## Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

## Problem

NaN Cloud subscription usage is gated on the provider **id string** being exactly `nan`, so a user who registers the same endpoint under any other id gets no usage at all — and no diagnostic explaining why.

Pi ships its own provider ids (`openai-codex`, `claude-bridge`), so keying those by id is safe. A NaN Cloud provider is created by the user in `models.json`, where the id is the user's own choice, and the integration still requires the literal `nan`:

```text
lib/shell-usage.ts:82      export const NAN_PROVIDER = "nan";
lib/shell-usage.ts:119     export const SUPPORTED_USAGE_PROVIDERS: readonly string[] = [CODEX_PROVIDER, ANTHROPIC_PROVIDER, NAN_PROVIDER];
lib/shell-usage.ts:125     const UNSUPPORTED_NOTE = "no subscription usage for this provider";
extensions/gentle-shell.ts:516   if (provider !== CODEX_PROVIDER && provider !== NAN_PROVIDER) return;
```

The gate returns before `fetchNanUsage` is reached, so `GET https://cloud-api.nan.builders/api/usage/quota` is never requested and the panel falls back to `UNSUPPORTED_NOTE`. Nothing about the credential, the network, or NaN is involved: the endpoint answers HTTP 200 for the same key with either id.

`pi auth check` is not a useful probe for this either — it reads `~/.pi/agent/auth.json` (empty in this setup) and ignores the `$ENV` interpolation `models.json` uses for `apiKey`, so it reports `not_ready` for every provider, including ones that work.

Impact: the feature added in #1177 (PR #1180) silently does nothing for a user whose provider id differs, and the NaN paragraphs in `docs/gentle-shell.md` never state the requirement, so the panel, the fallback note, and the documentation all leave it undiscoverable.

## Steps to reproduce

1. In `~/.pi/agent/models.json`, register NaN Cloud as a custom provider with an id other than `nan` (for example `nan-builders`), `baseUrl` `https://api.nan.builders/v1`, and an `apiKey` interpolated from the environment. Select one of its models in a session.
2. Open `/gentle:usage` (or read the bar): the panel shows `no subscription usage for this provider`.
3. Observe that `GET https://cloud-api.nan.builders/api/usage/quota` is never requested.
4. Rename the provider id to `nan` in `models.json`, restart pi, and repeat: the same session, the same key and the same endpoint now render the metered models (for example `deepseek-v4-flash 25.05%`). No other change was made.

Parsing itself is not the problem: calling `parseNanQuota` with the live payload yields 6 limits with the expected percentages.

## Expected and actual behavior

Expected: usage renders for a NaN Cloud provider regardless of the id the user chose for it, or the panel states that the provider was not recognized as NaN — either way the failure is diagnosable without reading `lib/shell-usage.ts`.

Actual: with any provider id other than `nan` the fetch is skipped and the panel prints the generic unsupported-provider note. A naming choice made in `models.json` silently disables a working integration, and no message distinguishes "this provider has no quota endpoint" from "this provider is not the one I was told to look for".

Possible direction, not prescribing an implementation: decide NaN support from the provider's `baseUrl` (`api.nan.builders`) instead of its id, or accept an explicit alias set, and cover it with a test that uses a provider id that is not `nan`.

## gentle-pi version

3.2.1

## Pi version

0.85.1

## Operating system

macOS

## Relevant logs or error output (optional)

```text
provider id "nan-builders"
  GET https://api.nan.builders/v1/models            -> HTTP 200
  GET https://cloud-api.nan.builders/api/usage/quota -> never requested
  /gentle:usage                                      -> "no subscription usage for this provider"

provider id renamed to "nan" (no other change)
  GET https://cloud-api.nan.builders/api/usage/quota -> HTTP 200
  /gentle:usage                                      -> 6 metered models, deepseek-v4-flash 25.05%
```

title: bug(agents): jd-judge-a/jd-judge-b ship unparseable tools frontmatter (folded block list)
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

`jd-judge-a` and `jd-judge-b` ship with an agent definition whose `tools:` frontmatter is not valid YAML. The installed copies under `~/.pi/agent/agents/` carry a block list that has been folded into a single line, and the leading `- "` of the first item was consumed:

```yaml
tools: *": false, read, grep, find, bash, mcp
```

The leading `*` opens a YAML alias, so the whole frontmatter fails to parse:

```text
yaml.scanner.ScannerError: while scanning an alias
  tools: *": false, read, grep, find, bash, mcp
```

The intended shape — and the shape the sibling read-only agents still have — is:

```yaml
tools:
  - "*": false
  - read
  - grep
  - find
  - bash
  - mcp
```

This is not caused by a user profile or by `/gentle:models`. It is present in the copies as installed, before any routing edit is applied: I captured a full backup of `~/.pi/agent/agents/` before touching anything, and both `jd-judge-*.md` files are already broken in that backup, while `review-refuter.md` and `review-validator.md` — the same `- "*": false` permission form, written as a block list — parse fine.

**Severity note, so this is not over- or under-stated:** it fails closed. I measured the effective tool set granted to a session loading the broken definition, and Pi grants 6 tools with `write` and `edit` absent:

```text
tools granted: 6   write: false   edit: false   bash: true
```

So the read-only guarantee of the Judgment Day judges still holds, and this is not a privilege escalation. It is still worth fixing because the declared intent (`read`, `grep`, `find`, `bash`, `mcp`) is not what is being applied — the parser discards the list — and because a YAML error in a shipped asset is the kind of thing that turns into a real defect the moment a runtime decides to fail closed on unparseable frontmatter instead of falling back to a default tool set.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install `gentle-pi` 2.6.0 with Pi subagents on a clean machine.
2. Inspect the installed definition:

```bash
sed -n '1,10p' ~/.pi/agent/agents/jd-judge-a.md
```

3. Observe the folded, unparseable `tools:` line.
4. Confirm it parses as invalid YAML (any parser, e.g. Python `yaml.safe_load` on the frontmatter block) while `review-refuter.md` parses as `[{'*': False}, 'read', 'grep', 'find']`.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected: `tools:` is a valid YAML block list, as it is in `review-refuter.md` and `review-validator.md`, and the agent receives the declared tool set.

Actual: the frontmatter is invalid YAML, the declared list is discarded, and the session falls back to a reduced tool set (6 tools, no `write`, no `edit`).

### gentle-pi version

2.6.0 (npm)

### Pi version

0.85.1

### Operating system

macOS

### Relevant logs or error output (optional)

```text
$ python3 -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open('/tmp/fm.yaml').read())"
yaml.scanner.ScannerError: while scanning an alias
  in "<unicode string>", line 5, column 8:
    tools: *": false, read, grep, find, bash, mcp
           ^
expected alphabetic or numeric character, but found '"'
```

Affected files on this install: `jd-judge-a.md`, `jd-judge-b.md`.

Related: #956 (`bug(agents): model routing breaks block scalar descriptions and empties them`) is the same family — the routing rewriter does not preserve frontmatter structure. This report is a distinct symptom (a folded `tools:` list rather than a broken `description:` block scalar) and, unlike #956, it is already present in the installed copies before any routing write.

title: bug(review): facade main rejects gentle-ai main's negotiated status/v8 — every review operation fails as schema-incompatible under the dev-binary override
body:
### Pre-flight Checks
- [x] I have searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand this issue needs `status:approved` before a PR can be opened

### 📝 Bug Description

With the gentle-pi dev-binary override pointing at a freshly built gentle-ai `main` binary, every native review operation through the Pi facade fails with `native-status-unavailable` / `schema-incompatible`. The facade on `main` decodes negotiated status schemas up to `gentle-ai.review-integration.status/v7`, while gentle-ai `main` now emits `status/v8`.

### 🔄 Steps to Reproduce

1. gentle-shell clone at `main` (`32e2416d`), loaded as the local-path package in pi settings.
2. Register the dev-binary override at `~/.pi/gentle-ai/dev-binary.json` pointing at a freshly built gentle-ai `main` binary (`d4187c1d`, reports `3.3.1-0.20260918235143-d4187c1d9967`).
3. Start a pi session and call the `gentle_review` tool with `{"operation":"inspect"}` on any repository.

### ✅ Expected Behavior

The facade decodes the negotiated status emitted by gentle-ai `main`, or fails with a version-incompatibility signal that names the schema gap.

### ❌ Actual Behavior

Every inspect/start/status call returns `blocked` with `outcome: "native-status-unavailable"`, `error_code: "schema-incompatible"`, `next_action: "require-complete-native-authority-inventory"`.

Evidence (the facade's exact spawn, captured from the live process):

```
gentle-ai review status --contract gentle-ai.review-integration/v2 \
  --cwd <repo> --projection workspace --agent pi --next-transition
```

- gentle-ai `main` (`d4187c1d`): emits `"schema": "gentle-ai.review-integration.status/v8"`
- pinned package-local 3.2.1: emits `"schema": "gentle-ai.review-integration.status/v7"` (works)

Facade side: `lib/review-integration-v2.ts` negotiates required status schemas up to `v7` (see the `v7`/`v6` decode chain around line 1931). v8 emission was introduced on the binary side by gentle-ai `15ea98ed` (#4765, "fix(review): relay provider-owned OpenCode lens tasks"), which merged to gentle-ai `main` without a matching facade release.

### 💡 Additional Context

- Workaround that restores native review today: remove the dev-binary override (or point it at the pinned release binary), so the extension uses the package-local `3.2.1` binary (v7).
- The four-lens group capture and the third-onwards single-slot captures are ALSO rejected (`collectBindings are unknown, expired, or belong to different session routes`) with the pinned 3.2.1 binary — that matches #4498 and is reported separately here only as context; this issue is strictly the v7/v8 dev-mode skew.

### Operating System
Linux (Arch/Manjaro)

### Versions
- gentle-shell `main` `32e2416d` (dev-mode local-path package, pi 0.85.1)
- gentle-ai `main` `d4187c1d` (`3.3.1-0.20260918235143-d4187c1d9967`, dev-binary override)
- package-local fallback: gentle-ai 3.2.1

title: bug(review): RECOVER drops committed-range baseRef before native recovery
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

`gentle_review` cannot recover an escalated committed-range (`base-diff`) lineage after the corrected candidate has changed.

Bound STATUS correctly recognizes the exact committed range and offers `action: recover`, but the facade drops the committed-only `baseRef` before invoking native `review recover`. Native then fails closed with `recovery base-ref does not match predecessor base`.

The predecessor remains escalated and the corrected candidate cannot enter a successor review authority through the supported Pi facade. This is a focused current-release follow-up to the broader committed-range recovery symptoms in #919 and the selector-retention defect class in #654.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start an ordinary review for a clean committed range using a full base commit and `committedOnly: true`.
2. Reach `correction_required`, apply and commit a corrected candidate, then have targeted validation reject the earlier correction so the predecessor becomes `escalated`.
3. Ensure the corrected HEAD differs from the predecessor authority target while retaining the same base commit.
4. Call bound STATUS with the predecessor lineage and the exact committed selector:

   ```json
   {
     "operation": "status",
     "lineageId": "review-<redacted>",
     "input": "{\"baseRef\":\"<full-base-commit>\",\"committedOnly\":true}"
   }
   ```

   STATUS correctly returns `applicability: current_target`, projection `base-diff`, the predecessor base tree, the corrected candidate tree, `action: recover`, and `action_disposition: escalated`.
5. Call facade RECOVER with the six documented fields and approve the fresh interactive authorization.
6. Observe native failure: `recovery base-ref does not match predecessor base`.
7. Re-query the same bound STATUS with the exact committed selector. It returns the unchanged escalated revision and the same RECOVER route; no successor exists and no mutation occurred.

This reproduced once on the previous matched pair (`gentle-pi 3.2.0` / Gentle AI `3.1.0`) and again after upgrading, fully restarting Pi, synchronizing managed assets, and restoring the exact committed selector on the current matched pair (`gentle-pi 3.2.1` / package-local Gentle AI `3.2.1`).

Source inspection corroborates the runtime evidence:

- the RECOVER branch includes `{ baseRef: frozenTarget.baseCommit, committedOnly: true }` in its pre-authorization `targetStatus` request;
- `executeNativeRecoveryRoute` then constructs `nativeReviewCli.recover({...})` without `baseRef` or `committedOnly`;
- the package-local native CLI advertises both `review recover --base-ref` and `--committed-only`.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected:

- After the exact range passes both fresh STATUS checks and the user authorizes RECOVER, the facade forwards the same committed-range selector to native recovery.
- Native creates one auditable successor authority for the corrected target while leaving the escalated predecessor untouched.

Actual:

- The facade validates and authorizes the correct `base-diff`, but invokes native recovery without its base selector.
- Native correctly refuses the mismatched implicit target with `recovery base-ref does not match predecessor base`.
- Reconciliation proves the predecessor revision and state are unchanged and no successor was created.

A regression should exercise a committed-range escalated predecessor through facade STATUS → authorized RECOVER and assert that `nativeReviewCli.recover` receives the canonical `baseRef` plus `committedOnly: true` used by the two status reads.

### gentle-pi version

3.2.1 (package-local Gentle AI 3.2.1)

### Pi version

0.85.1

### Operating system

Linux

### Relevant logs or error output (optional)

```text
STATUS before RECOVER:
applicability=current_target
projection.kind=base-diff
action=recover
action_disposition=escalated
authority.state=escalated
next_transition.reason_code=recovery_authorization_required

RECOVER:
operation=review/recover
error_code=non-zero
exit_code=1
stderr=Error: recovery base-ref does not match predecessor base
mutation_outcome=unknown
replayability=status_required

Required reconciliation STATUS with the same full baseRef:
authority.state=escalated
authority.revision=<unchanged>
action=recover
next_transition.reason_code=recovery_authorization_required
no successor authority present
```

title: bug(review): review-consent UI bypasses the Herdr blocked lifecycle and propagates silently
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

The native review consent envelope (`gentle-ai.review-integration.consent/v3`, rendered as "Review consent / Review this change / Skip this time / Review and allow this session") blocks the agent mid-turn inside a Herdr pane, but Herdr never learns about it: the pane keeps reporting `working` until the human happens to look at it. There is no `blocked` state and no attention signal, so a session can sit parked on a human decision indefinitely while every observer believes it is still working.

gentle-ai already owns the correct mechanism: `createHerdrConfirmationLifecycle` emits the deduplicated `herdr:blocked` event for three agent-initiated blockers:

- `ask_user_choice` (via `gentle-pi:ask-user-choice:blocked`)
- the RPIV questionnaire (via `rpiv:ask-user:blocked`)
- guarded command confirmations (`begin()`/`settle()` around `confirmCommand`)

The consent UI is not wired into that lifecycle. The call site awaits `presentReviewConsentUi(...)` directly (the `ReviewConsentComponent` shown via `ctx.ui.custom`), with no `begin()`/`settle()` and no blocked event. The Herdr pi bridge (`herdr-agent-state.ts`) therefore keeps reporting `working` (`agentActive` is still true because `agent_settled` has not fired while the tool call is pending).

This is the same pattern previously fixed for `ask_user_choice` (#472) and the questionnaire (#459). The broader "surface blocked-on-human status + unfocused-terminal notifications" UX ask is tracked separately in #1165; this report is the narrow consent-specific wiring gap that the existing lifecycle already knows how to close.

Suggested fix: wrap the `presentReviewConsentUi` call site with the existing `herdrLifecycle` (`begin()` before, `settle()` after, including the cancel path), with a blocker label such as "Review consent awaiting input". Also worth auditing any other agent-initiated `ctx.ui.*` blocker for the same omission (e.g. the SDD marker confirmation).

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run `pi` inside a Herdr pane with gentle-pi installed and receipt-driven review enabled.
2. Complete an authorized medium/high-risk source change and let the agent run the native review START until the consent envelope UI appears ("Review consent" with the three options).
3. Leave the prompt open and unanswered. From another pane run `herdr agent list`.
4. Observe the reported state of the agent in the consent pane.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected:

- While the consent UI is open, the agent is reported as `blocked` (e.g. "Review consent awaiting input"), so Herdr marks the pane and it participates in the blocked-agent attention queue.
- After answering, the state returns to `working`.

Actual:

- The agent reports `working` for the entire time the consent UI is open. No `blocked` state, no notification, no attention signal; the stall is only discovered by manually switching to the pane.

### gentle-pi version

3.2.0

### Pi version

0.85.1

### Operating system

Windows (WSL)

### Relevant logs or error output (optional)

_No response_

title: bug(guard): guarded-command matching ignores position, so a read-only search prompts or is blocked
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

The runtime guard classifies a shell command by matching the guarded phrase **anywhere in the command text**, with no notion of whether that phrase is a command about to run or an argument handed to something harmless. A read-only command that merely mentions the phrase is therefore treated as the guarded action and asks a human to confirm it.

Two consequences, and the second one blocks work rather than merely annoying:

- **Prompt fatigue.** The guard exists so a human reviews a risky action. When it also fires on a search, the human learns to answer Yes without reading — the opposite of the intent, and it erodes the value of every other prompt the guard raises.
- **A read-only command can be hard-blocked.** The hard-deny patterns include a forced push, so a command whose *text* contains that phrase is refused outright by the safety policy instead of merely confirmed.

### Steps to reproduce

Default configuration: no `runtime-guardrails.json` present, so `autonomousMode` is `false`.

1. Run a shell command whose text contains the guarded phrase in argument position, without invoking it as a command. Searching a source tree for the phrase is enough.
2. Observe the confirmation prompt, which names the guarded action as if a push were about to happen.

The command below is a literal search; nothing is pushed. The phrase appears only as the pattern given to the search tool:

```bash
grep -nE "git push" extensions/gentle-ai.ts
```

Same shape, and this one never reaches a prompt because it matches a hard-deny pattern:

```bash
grep -rn "git push --force" docs/
```

A commit message is affected the same way: passing a body that *describes* a push through a heredoc raises the prompt for the commit command.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected: no prompt and no block. The phrase is data passed to a search tool, not a command the shell is about to execute, and the guard should classify what is about to run.

Actual:

- The first command raises `Allow guarded git push?` and waits for a human.
- The second is blocked before any prompt: `Gentle AI safety policy blocked a destructive shell command. Ask the user for an explicit safer plan.`

### Evidence in 3.2.0

`extensions/gentle-ai.ts`:

```ts
const GIT_PUSH_RE = new RegExp(String.raw`\bgit${GIT_GLOBAL_FLAGS_SRC}(push)\b`);
```

`collectGuardedMatches` runs that expression over the whole command with `matchAll` and records `match.index`; nothing distinguishes an invocation from a mention. `DENIED_BASH_PATTERNS` holds the force-push expression that produces the hard block, and it is evaluated against the complete command independently of the guard classification.

The tests cover the real and compound cases — a plain push, `echo done || <guarded command>`, both force forms, and the configured action per mode — but there is **no case where the phrase appears as an argument**. That is why this reads as an unconsidered case rather than a deliberate trade-off.

### Suggested direction

Require the phrase in **command position**: at the start of a segment, or immediately after `;`, `&&`, `||`, `|`, or a newline. Every real case survives — `echo done || <guarded command>` still confirms, both force forms still block — while the false positives go away, and those are a search pattern, a commit message body, and an echoed string.

It stays a heuristic: `eval "<guarded command>"` would still pass, as it already does today, so this is not a regression. Position is simply evidence the current rule ignores and the cheapest signal available.

_Report prepared by an agent (el Gentleman, the harness this package installs, running on Pi) on the submitter's behalf. Both checkboxes above describe work that agent performed and verified: the open-and-closed issue search, and the redaction scan of this body._

3.2.0

### Pi version

0.85.1

### Operating system

Windows (WSL)

```text
Allow guarded git push?

 Yes
 No
```

title: bug(review): admission path scanner rejects reviewer evidence that cites the service endpoint/port — endpoint-touching candidates are unreviewable
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

Reviewer artifact admission deterministically rejects valid lens results whose **evidence prose cites the network endpoint or port of the service under review**. The admission path scanner classifies slash-bearing tokens such as an `host:port` publish string or an API route (`/v1/...`) as repository paths, fails to match them against the frozen path manifest, and refuses the payload:

```
reviewer artifact admission out_of_scope: reviewer evidence references a path outside the
frozen repository; admission_diagnostic={"code":"evidence_path_out_of_scope",
"location":"PublishPort=127.0.0.1:8100","reason":"unknown_or_malformed_repository_path"}
```

The reviewer cannot describe findings for a network-facing service without citing its endpoint — the endpoint string **is** the finding. This makes any candidate touching a published port, API base URL, or service route effectively unreviewable.

### Reproduction

1. Candidate adds a Quadlet service that publishes a port (e.g. `PublishPort=0.0.0.0:8100:8100`) and exposes HTTP endpoints (`/v1/audio/transcriptions`, `/v1/audio/diarize`).
2. Negotiated v2 START (high risk, 4 lenses), reviewer group capture via host relay.
3. The `review-risk` reviewer returns a completed, substantive result whose evidence cites the service endpoint and port (they appear verbatim in the diff: the `PublishPort` directive and the route constants).
4. Admission rejects the payload with `evidence_path_out_of_scope`; the lens slot is not consumed.
5. Retrying produces the same rejection: the reviewer's evidence legitimately needs the endpoint string. Two consecutive rejections per lineage; the slot can only be closed via `capture-unachievable`.

Observed triggering tokens across preserved payloads:

- `127.0.0.1:8100`
- `PublishPort=127.0.0.1:8100`
- `/v1/audio/diarize`
- `:8100/v1/audio/transcriptions`
- `Caddy/llama-swap` (a component name containing a slash)
- `os.environ/` (LiteLLM env-var indirection syntax)
- `LAN/VPN` (plain prose with a slash)

### Impact

Across three review lineages on one host, every attempt to review endpoint-touching candidates failed at admission (6+ preserved rejection payloads). Two candidates could only be closed by declaring all lens slots unachievable (`relay_transport_bound_exceeded`), so they carry no review verdict despite passing their other verification gates.

### Expected behavior

The admission path scanner should not treat arbitrary slash-bearing tokens in reviewer evidence prose as repository paths. Suggestions:

- Only consider a token a path reference if it matches a frozen manifest path or resolves to an existing path prefix (e.g. starts with a known top-level entry).
- Explicitly ignore well-formed `host:port`, URL path fragments (`/v1/...`), and `scheme://` tokens.
- Alternatively, restrict path validation to `inspection.paths` (which was correct in every rejection) and treat free-text evidence as prose.

### Environment

- gentle-ai native 3.2.1 (bundled at `gentle-pi/.gentle-ai/v3.2.1`) and 3.3.0; gentle-pi 3.2.1
- Transport: `pi_host_relay`, contract `gentle-ai.review-integration/v2`
- Related: #940 (same admission subsystem; different misread — that one treats a method-statement as an inspection failure)

title: bug(review): reviewer relay rejects the provider/model id it just listed as available (claude-bridge/claude-sonnet-5)
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

During an ordinary RDD review lineage (`gentle_review` start → `gentle_review_capture_group`), the reviewer relay deterministically fails to launch the `review-reliability` lens subprocess with `pi-host-relay-transport-failure`, because the relay invokes the `pi` binary with the fully-qualified model id `claude-bridge/claude-sonnet-5`, and `pi`'s own model resolver rejects it with `Model "claude-bridge/claude-sonnet-5" not found` — even though `pi --list-models` on the exact same machine lists that model as available (as `claude-bridge  claude-sonnet-5`, without the provider prefix). This makes it impossible to complete the review-capture step for any change on an affected install, blocking the RDD lifecycle entirely regardless of the change's content or risk tier.

Separately, and likely relevant context for triage: the Gentle AI harness skill (`gentle-ai` SKILL.md, "Compact Rules") documents strict TDD (RED, GREEN, TRIANGULATE, REFACTOR) and review-workload forecasting as mandatory harness discipline, but neither is enforced by any hook, lint, or gate in the installed tool surface — the calling agent has to proactively call `gentle_review inspect`/`start` itself, and nothing blocks progress or reminds the agent if it skips straight to implementation and testing without RED-first TDD or an RDD review. In this session, the agent implemented and tested a multi-file frontend change, then only started an RDD review after the human operator explicitly asked why no review had run; TDD's RED-first step was never used at all. Flagging this so maintainers can decide whether the "automatic contract" language should be backed by an active gate/reminder, or whether documentation should be corrected to state it is opt-in.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install gentle-pi 3.2.1 with Pi 0.85.1 on macOS (arm64), inside a git repository with an ordinary uncommitted multi-file change (in this case: 4 files, ~268 changed lines, TSX/React).
2. Resolve review authority: `gentle_review` `operation: "inspect"` → if blocked on `intended_untracked_selection_required`, resolve with `operation: "inspect"`, `untrackedScope: "exclude"` → if blocked on `managed_assets_outdated`, run the returned `gentle-ai sync --agent pi` command, then re-inspect until `status: "ready"`.
3. Start the review: `gentle_review` `operation: "start"`, `input: {"mode":"ordinary"}`. Confirms `state: "reviewing"`, `risk_tier: "medium"`, `selected_lenses: ["review-reliability"]`.
4. Call `gentle_review` `operation: "status"` with the returned `lineageId`. It returns `next_transition.kind: "collect"`, `reason_code: "reviewer_results_required"`, plus a `collectBindings[0].collectBinding` for the `review-reliability` lens.
5. Call `gentle_review_capture_group` with that exact `lineageId`, `collectBindings: [<the exact collectBinding string from step 4>]`, `reviewerRunAcknowledged: true`.
6. Observe the failure below. Re-fetching a fresh `status` and resubmitting the freshly reoffered binding (per the tool's own `next_action` instruction) reproduces the identical failure every time — tried 3 times across a few minutes, byte-identical `stderr`.

Independently confirm the model actually exists on the same machine:

```
$ pi --list-models
provider       model              context  max-out  thinking  images
claude-bridge  claude-fable-5     1M       128K     yes       yes
claude-bridge  claude-haiku-4-5   200K     64K      yes       yes
claude-bridge  claude-opus-4-6    200K     128K     yes       yes
claude-bridge  claude-opus-4-7    1M       128K     yes       yes
claude-bridge  claude-opus-4-8    1M       128K     yes       yes
claude-bridge  claude-opus-5      1M       128K     yes       yes
claude-bridge  claude-sonnet-4-6  200K     128K     yes       yes
claude-bridge  claude-sonnet-5    1M       128K     yes       yes
```

`claude-sonnet-5` is listed under provider `claude-bridge`, but the relay's subprocess invocation uses the slash-joined form `claude-bridge/claude-sonnet-5` as a single model argument, which `pi`'s CLI model resolver does not accept.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected:
The reviewer subprocess for the `review-reliability` lens launches successfully (or, if the specific model is genuinely unavailable for a legitimate reason, the relay surfaces a config-correctable message and/or falls back to another configured model), so the RDD review lineage can progress past `collect`.

Actual:
Every capture attempt returns the same transport failure and the lineage stays stuck at `next_transition.kind: "collect"` / `reason_code: "reviewer_results_required"` indefinitely:

```json
{
  "tool": "gentle_review_capture_group",
  "status": "blocked",
  "outcome": "pi-host-relay-transport-failure",
  "reason": "pi subprocess failed",
  "failure": {
    "kind": "pi-failed",
    "stage": "pi",
    "exit_code": 1,
    "timed_out": false,
    "elapsed_ms": 155,
    "timeout_ms": 925684,
    "stderr": "Error: Model \"claude-bridge/claude-sonnet-5\" not found. Use --list-models to see available models.\n"
  },
  "prepared_reviewers": 0,
  "submitted_reviewers": 0,
  "host_relay": { "transport": "pi_host_relay", "reviewers": [] },
  "mutation_performed": false,
  "mutation_outcome": "none",
  "next_action": "Call fresh STATUS and submit only an exact reoffered one-slot binding; never replay this capture from transcript inference."
}
```

### gentle-pi version

3.2.1

### Pi version

0.85.1

### Operating system

macOS

### Relevant logs or error output (optional)

```text
Error: Model "claude-bridge/claude-sonnet-5" not found. Use --list-models to see available models.
```

No other stack trace was surfaced to the calling agent; `stage: "pi"` and `exit_code: 1` are the only additional signal in the tool's structured failure payload.

title: bug(hermes): Engram writes dead-end without a runtime session ID
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

The Gentle AI Hermes adapter installs an Engram protocol that requires mutations to use an authoritative runtime session ID, forbids the agent from calling `mem_session_start`, and tells it to omit `session_id` when the runtime does not provide one.

Hermes does not register an Engram session automatically, and its default launch path keeps `pass_session_id` disabled. When more than one active Engram session matches the same project and directory, Hermes can read memory but every write that omits `session_id` fails closed as ambiguous. This leaves no permitted continuation: the managed protocol requires a pre-registered identity that the runtime never supplies.

Cleaning historical sessions cannot fix the root cause because the same ambiguity returns whenever concurrent agents or abandoned sessions exist.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install Hermes Agent v0.21.3 on WSL.
2. Install Gentle AI 3.2.1 for the Hermes agent with the `full-gentleman` preset.
3. Configure Engram 2.0.0 as the Hermes MCP memory server.
4. Ensure Engram has multiple active session candidates for one project/directory, as can happen after ordinary multi-agent use.
5. Start Hermes normally, without the optional `--pass-session-id` flag.
6. Ask Hermes to persist a memory.
7. Observe that the managed SOUL protocol omits `session_id` because none was supplied, and Engram rejects the write as ambiguous.

Relevant implementation facts:

- Hermes defaults `pass_session_id` to false.
- Hermes can expose its native ID through `--pass-session-id` or `HERMES_TUI_PASS_SESSION_ID=1`.
- Engram mutations accept an explicit `session_id`.
- Engram exposes `mem_session_start` and `mem_session_end`, but the installed Hermes protocol says not to call `mem_session_start` because registration is assumed to be runtime-owned.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected:

The Hermes integration owns one complete session lifecycle. A fresh Hermes session should expose its native ID, register that exact ID with Engram once, pass it to all mutations, and end it on clean shutdown. It must remain able to write when other historical or concurrent sessions exist.

Actual:

The runtime does not register or expose an Engram session by default, while the managed protocol prohibits agent-owned registration. Reads work, but writes without `session_id` are blocked by session ambiguity.

Suggested acceptance coverage:

- A fresh Gentle AI-managed Hermes session can save memory while multiple active candidates already exist for the same project/directory.
- The native Hermes session ID is registered exactly once and is reused for every Engram mutation.
- Clean shutdown ends the same session.
- No ID is invented or inferred from unrelated active sessions.
- Re-running the installer preserves the working lifecycle contract.

### gentle-pi version

gentle-ai 3.2.1 / gentle-pi 3.2.1

### Pi version

0.85.1

### Operating system

Windows (WSL)

### Relevant logs or error output (optional)

```text
Engram write blocked: multiple active runtime sessions match the same project and directory when session_id is omitted.
```

title: bug(review): the prompt-size-derived reviewer relay timeout has ~0% margin, so lens runs are killed 16-18ms over the bound
body:
### Problem

The reviewer relay's timeout is derived from the materialized prompt size, and on this host that derived bound sits **within milliseconds below** the reviewer's real wall time. The bound is then hit repeatedly, each attempt re-spending all four lens runs, and a group can be left partially submitted.

The derivation lives in `lib/review-host-relay.ts`:

```
REVIEW_HOST_RELAY_PI_TIMEOUT_FLOOR_MS        = 900_000
REVIEW_HOST_RELAY_PI_TIMEOUT_PER_MEBIBYTE_MS = 900_000
bound = min(900_000 + ceil(bytes / 1MiB * 900_000), 7_200_000)
```

Two things stand out:

1. **The per-MiB term does not model model latency.** A ~60 KB prompt gets ~15.9 minutes, and the reviewer consistently needs roughly that. The term is effectively a fixed budget with a rounding sliver on top, not a size-scaled one.
2. **There is no margin.** Four group attempts across three lineages were killed 16–18 ms over the bound, i.e. the reviewer was **finishing** when the kill landed.

### Steps to reproduce

Environment: macOS arm64, `gentle-pi` 3.2.0 (global npm), Pi runtime with RDD enabled, `GENTLE_PI_REVIEW_RELAY_PI_TIMEOUT_MS` **unset** (so the derived bound applies). Candidates were high tier with ~20 changed files / ~300 changed lines, materialized lens prompts ~60–66 KB.

1. `gentle_review inspect` → offers `review.start`; run START; resolve consent; the lineage enters `reviewing` with four lenses.
2. `gentle_review status` → offers the complete four-slot reviewer group.
3. Call `gentle_review_capture_group` (forecast first, then `reviewerRunAcknowledged: true`).

### Expected and actual behavior

**Expected:** a lens run that is about to finish is not killed; or, when the bound is genuinely too small for the offered prompt, the failure distinguishes "the reviewer needed more time" from "the reviewer produced nothing", and the sanctioned retry is not a coin flip.

**Actual:** verbatim failures observed on this host:

```
pi reviewer subprocess exceeded the relay bound: killed after 952873ms
against a 952857ms limit for a 61582-byte materialized prompt.
Relaunching the same slot unchanged reaches the same wall.
```

```
pi reviewer subprocess exceeded the relay bound: killed after 953256ms
against a 953238ms limit for a 62026-byte materialized prompt.
```

| # | lineage | outcome | elapsed / limit | prompt bytes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `review-66d1aa9556f30c2e` | `pi-host-relay-timeout` | 952 873 / 952 857 (**+16 ms**) | 61 582 |
| 2 | `review-88505c898f090636` | `pi-host-relay-timeout` | 953 256 / 953 238 (**+18 ms**) | 62 026 |
| 3 | same lineage, retry | `native-operation-failed`, `mutation_outcome: partial_unknown`, **3 of 4 submitted** | 4th lens (`review-reliability`) timed out; successful siblings 62 001 / 62 015 / 62 047 B | — |
| 4 | `review-88505c898f090636` predecessor lineage | `native-operation-failed`, **3 of 4 submitted** | 4th lens timed out | — |

Three points worth separating:

- **The failure message is actively misleading here.** "Relaunching the same slot unchanged reaches the same wall" is not what happened: retries of lineages 1 and 3 succeeded, and the successful runs finished comfortably. The wall is variance, not a fixed ceiling — so the field guidance sends the human away from the retry that works.
- **A partial group is a worse outcome than a clean failure.** `submitted_reviewers: 3` with `mutation_outcome: partial_unknown` forces STATUS reconciliation, and the following STATUS escalated terminally (`native_stop_required`, `unknown_causality`) because the partial set left a finding unclassifiable. That escalation is what ended the review cycle, not a code defect.
- **Killing a run milliseconds before it finishes wastes the entire lens.** With four lenses per group and a near-miss every other attempt, the effective cost of a review roughly doubles.

### Why this is not #367 or #578

- **#367** (closed) was the *hardcoded 600 000 ms* constant with no override; its stated fix #1 was "make the relay `pi` timeout configurable … **or scale it with materialized prompt bytes**". This report is about the **calibration of the size-derived bound that replaced it** — it is now configurable (`GENTLE_PI_REVIEW_RELAY_PI_TIMEOUT_MS`) but the default has no margin.
- **#578** (open) is **documentation**: it notes the observed default "~1000s … too low for high-tier lens runs with ~200KB materialized prompts". The prompts here were 60–66 KB, i.e. *far below* the case #578 describes, and the miss was 16–18 ms, not minutes. That points at the formula, not the docs.

### Suggested fixes

1. **Give the derived bound real margin.** Either raise `REVIEW_HOST_RELAY_PI_TIMEOUT_PER_MEBIBYTE_MS`, add a percentage headroom (e.g. +25%), or raise the floor. The measured miss is tiny, so any of these removes the class.
2. **Do not kill a reporter that is still producing output.** If the child is streaming tokens when the timer fires, the process is alive and progressing; a wall-clock kill is the wrong instrument there. A stall detector (no output for N seconds) would fail fast *and* let slow-but-live runs finish.
3. **Admit per-slot results as they arrive inside one group capture.** Today one late lens discards the group and leaves `partial_unknown`, which is what produced the terminal escalation above. Already suggested as #367 fix #4 and still relevant.
4. **Correct the retry guidance for this failure code.** Since retries demonstrably succeed, the message should say so instead of asserting the same wall will be hit.
5. **If the intended answer is "set the env var", say the number.** The message suggests raising `GENTLE_PI_REVIEW_RELAY_PI_TIMEOUT_MS` without noting that it is only read at Pi process launch, so it cannot be adopted from inside the running session that just failed.

### gentle-pi version

3.2.0 (global npm install). `gentle-ai` binary resolved by the package pin. Repo: `Gentleman-Programming/gentle-shell`.
