title: feat(orchestrator): route implementation tasks to specialized workers
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a request for this feature.
- [x] I reviewed this request and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem or opportunity

Gentle Pi currently routes bounded non-SDD implementation work to the generic `gentle-ai-worker`. Gentle Agents already discovers user- and project-defined workers, but the orchestrator does not prefer a more specific worker when one clearly matches the task.

Specifications and derived tasks normally define the outcome, scope, acceptance criteria, and checks—not every implementation decision. A generic worker must therefore rediscover basic domain conventions, relevant skills, safe defaults, and suitable validation for each task. This adds context and tool calls while making implementation quality less consistent.

Specialized workers can carry a small amount of durable domain “flavor”: the constraints and practices that repeatedly matter in that ecosystem. The root still owns scope and governance, while the implementation worker starts with better defaults.

### Proposed outcome

Let the root orchestrator select the most specific available implementation worker for each bounded work unit, using discovered worker names/descriptions and the task domain. Fall back to `gentle-ai-worker` when no clear specialist matches or the task is genuinely mixed.

The root should continue to inject the shared execution contract:

- exact allowed edit surfaces;
- task outcome and acceptance criteria;
- effective TDD mode and exact checks;
- applicable skill paths;
- single-writer and permission boundaries.

Specialist workers should remain leaves. They need only domain-specific guidance, tool preferences, safety constraints, and a compact handoff containing status, changed paths, decisions, observed checks, and remaining risks. They should not duplicate the full ODD, RDD, review, Git, memory, or user-interaction contract.

The root remains responsible for synthesis, SDD/RDD, review, permissions, Git/worktrees, user decisions, and delivery. This proposal does not require nested delegation or child `subagent_*` tools.

#### Example

A generated task may say:

> Add a Terraform module input for retention settings, preserve existing resource addresses, and add focused tests.

That defines the required outcome but leaves important implementation choices open. A generic worker must first rediscover Terraform-specific concerns. A Terraform-focused worker can begin with durable guidance to:

- preserve resource addresses and stable `for_each` keys;
- avoid implicit replacement and index churn;
- model types, nullability, defaults, and validation explicitly;
- separate static source validation from provider-backed operations;
- never run `apply`, `destroy`, `import`, or mutate state without explicit authority;
- use Terraform-specific formatting, validation, and test commands when authorized.

The same pattern improves React accessibility, Firebase security, TypeScript module boundaries, Flutter state handling, and portable Bash work.

#### Expected benefits

- **Higher code quality:** recurring domain hazards and testing practices are present before implementation begins.
- **Lower context and tool cost:** workers do not repeatedly search for baseline skills and conventions.
- **More consistent changes:** similar tasks use the same ecosystem-specific defaults.
- **Better tool selection:** workers can prefer domain-appropriate navigation, diagnostics, and checks.
- **User extensibility:** teams can add or override specialist workers without changing Gentle Pi.
- **Preserved governance:** the root retains all authority and one writer owns each work unit.

A minimal first version can be implemented in the orchestrator prompt assets and package contract tests; no new scheduler or nested-agent runtime is required.

### Alternatives considered

- **Always use `gentle-ai-worker`:** simple, but forces repeated domain discovery and produces less consistent implementation choices.
- **Copy the full generic contract into every specialist:** functional but bloated, expensive, and difficult to keep synchronized.
- **Let `gentle-ai-worker` launch specialists:** requires nested delegation and additional authority/runtime machinery without improving the common direct-routing case.
- **Use specialists only as advisers:** adds another model pass even when one specialist can safely own the bounded implementation directly.

### Additional context

The intended routing shape is:

```text
root orchestrator
  ├─ clear domain match → specialized leaf worker
  └─ mixed or unclear   → gentle-ai-worker
```

For mixed features, the root can split genuinely independent work units and route each separately while preserving the existing single-writer rule per checkout and work unit.

bug(orchestrator): all-worktree cleanup misses recursive submodule Git common directories
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

When a user asks Gentle Pi to inventory or clean up all worktrees in a repository tree, an inventory based only on the superproject's `git worktree list` silently misses worktrees owned by recursive submodules or nested Git common directories.

Each Git common directory owns an independent worktree registry. A superproject command cannot see linked worktrees registered by a submodule. In a real agent session, an “all worktrees” cleanup initially omitted one submodule-owned worktree and still appeared complete until the user found it manually.

A controlled local fixture reproduced the underlying topology deterministically: the superproject inventory reported one worktree, while a recursive oracle reported three checkout roots across two Git common directories. The missing issue-relevant record was a real linked worktree owned by the submodule.

Gentle Pi currently has intentionally common-dir-scoped session/change tracking, but no explicit orchestration contract for exhaustive cleanup. This report concerns natural-language requests whose scope is explicitly “all”, not changing the deliberate scope of `/gentle:changes`.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create an isolated local superproject on `main`.
2. Add a local Git repository as a submodule at `deps/sub`.
3. From the submodule checkout, create a linked worktree at `<fixture>/sub-linked`.
4. Run `git worktree list --porcelain` from the superproject.
5. Observe one record: the superproject checkout only.
6. Enumerate the superproject plus recursive submodule roots, resolve each root with `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` and `git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir`, deduplicate common directories, and run `git worktree list --porcelain` once per unique common directory.
7. Observe three normalized checkout roots across two common directories: the superproject, the submodule checkout, and the submodule-linked worktree.
8. Ask the orchestrator to inventory or clean up “all worktrees”. A root-only procedure omits the linked worktree even though the requested scope is exhaustive.

The fixture is filesystem-local and can be removed at the directory boundary. Reproduction requires no network, remote service, or destructive worktree cleanup command.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected:
- For an explicit “all worktrees” or equivalent cleanup request, the orchestrator discovers the repository root, recursive submodules, and explicitly relevant nested repositories before claiming the inventory is complete.
- It canonicalizes and deduplicates Git common directories, then inventories each one exactly once.
- Cleanup safety still applies independently: dirty or unique worktrees are not deleted without the required authorization.
- Branch and remote-branch cleanup remain separate scopes unless the user explicitly includes them.
- After an authorized cleanup, the same recursive inventory is repeated before reporting completion.

Actual:
- The superproject inventory exposed one checkout only.
- The recursive oracle exposed three checkout roots across two Git common directories.
- The submodule checkout and its linked worktree were invisible to the root-only inventory.
- An agent can therefore omit a real worktree while claiming an “all worktrees” cleanup is complete.

Related but not duplicate: #710 deliberately scoped session changes to registered worktrees in one repository/common directory, and #765 concerns session-baseline diffs across repositories. Neither defines exhaustive recursive inventory before cleanup.

title: bug(orchestrator): prompt-granted multi-action requests fragment at runtime authorization gates
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

A direct user instruction that explicitly names several actions is not retained as authorization for the complete sequence when execution reaches Gentle Pi's runtime safety guard in a headless host.

In a controlled local-only reproduction, the user explicitly requested four actions: commit the staged change, push the branch, create a named tag, and push the tag. The compound command was blocked before execution because interactive confirmation was unavailable. The model then completed the unguarded commit separately, but the branch push was blocked again and the final response asked the user to confirm publishing. The tag steps were never attempted.

This fragments one explicit A-B-C-D request into repeated authorization gates and leaves the requested operation partially complete. The problem is broader than commit/push: authorization for actions explicitly named in the active user request should survive planning, tool boundaries, reviews, subagents, retries, and completion of earlier steps.

This does not propose bypassing provider-owned consent, approving review verdicts, force-pushing, overwriting tags, or authorizing operations that the user did not request. Those remain separate decisions.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create an isolated local Git repository on `main` with a filesystem-local bare `origin` and one staged file modification.
2. Run Pi in a noninteractive/headless host with Gentle Pi loaded, RDD effectively off, and no manual answers available.
3. Send this exact user message:

   `Commit the staged change with message fix: demo, push main to origin, create tag demo-1, and push the tag.`

4. Let the agent execute normally with tools enabled.
5. Observe that the agent first submits the whole sequence as one shell call. The runtime blocks it because interactive confirmation is required.
6. Observe that the agent then commits separately, retries the branch push, receives the same runtime block, and asks the user to confirm publishing. The tag is not created or pushed.

The reproduction used a local bare remote only. It made no network or GitHub mutation.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected:
- The active user message is recognized as authorization for every explicitly named action and exact target in that message.
- Generic runtime safety confirmation is not requested again solely because execution advances from A to B to C.
- Authorization survives successful completion of an earlier step and ordinary orchestration boundaries.
- A new decision is requested only if scope changes, a new operation is proposed, destructive remediation such as force-push becomes necessary, or a separate provider-owned consent contract requires it.
- If a technical gate cannot consume prompt-granted authorization, the flow stops once before partial execution with one actionable explanation rather than committing A and then re-requesting permission for B/C/D.

Actual:
- The compound A-B-C-D call was blocked before execution.
- The agent executed A (commit) separately.
- B (branch push) was blocked again.
- The agent requested new publishing confirmation and left C/D unattempted.
- The local commit existed while the remote branch and both local/remote tags remained unchanged.

Related but not duplicate: #469 concerns a valid `interaction_required` answer that cannot be delivered after a background subagent becomes terminal. This report concerns direct parent-turn authorization that is already present before execution and is not consumable by the headless runtime guard.

### gentle-pi version

3.2.0 (source revision `2b579c80824e83442b8ae9f7bfad629a52f9f711`)

### Pi version

0.85.1

### Operating system

Linux

### Relevant logs or error output (optional)

```text
User request:
Commit the staged change with message fix: demo, push main to origin, create tag demo-1, and push the tag.

First attempted tool call:
git commit -m "fix: demo" && git push origin main && git tag demo-1 && git push origin demo-1

Runtime result:
Gentle AI safety policy requires interactive confirmation before this command.

Commit-only retry:
git commit -m "fix: demo"
Result: success

Push retry:
git push origin main
Runtime result:
Gentle AI safety policy requires interactive confirmation before this command.

Final assistant response:
The runtime blocked git push origin main pending interactive confirmation, so the tag was not created. Please confirm publishing the commit and demo-1 tag.
```

title: Orchestrator invents bash `sleep 295` to wait for background subagents, delaying result delivery (model-agnostic)
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

When the orchestrator launches a `gentle-ai-worker` (or any subagent) in background mode, it frequently does not end its turn as the delegation contract requires ("Wait for it: end the turn once launches and any non-overlapping work are done. Never poll, sleep..."). Instead, it invents a wait primitive through the bash tool:

```
bash: sleep 295; echo waited   (timeout: 330s)
```

This defeats the background design in two ways:

1. **The completion notification is delayed.** `gentle-agents.result` only starts a new turn if the session is idle. While the `sleep` tool call is in flight, the session is not idle, so the message is queued. A worker that settles in ~40s is not delivered to the parent for up to ~5 minutes, and if the parent re-checks and finds the task still running, it issues another `sleep 295`. In one observed session this repeated 7 times.
2. **It is model-agnostic, which points to a design gap rather than model quality.** The exact same invented `sleep 295` pattern was observed with two different orchestrator models (DeepSeek 4.1 Flash and MiniMax M3). I verified that no asset in gentle-pi v3.2.0, no pi-subagents runtime file, and no user/project config instructs sleeping — the models converge on this behavior on their own.

Root-cause hypothesis (two compounding factors):

- The contract forbids polling/sleeping but there is **no sanctioned wait primitive** for the case where the parent must not end the turn. The only tool available for "waiting" is bash, so models invent `sleep`.
- The ODD workflow requires the parent to close by *"reporting the verified outcome"*, which pulls against ending the turn with a pending child. Models resolve this conflict by holding the turn open — via bash sleep.

Related but distinct reports: #1028 (no blocking wait primitive for headless `pi -p`) and #1092 (unread background completion during a long parent tool call). This report adds the missing upstream cause: the long parent tool call is very often a self-invented `sleep`, produced by any model, because no sanctioned alternative exists and the delegation contract alone does not hold.

### Steps to reproduce

1. gentle-pi v3.2.0 on Pi, interactive session, background subagent policy `on` (global policy file).
2. Run a delegated flow where the parent must continue after the worker finishes (e.g., SDD/ODD apply: parent authorizes worker surfaces, launches the worker, then needs the result to proceed).
3. Launch the worker with `subagent_run` (default background mode).
4. Observe the next parent tool call: instead of ending the turn, the parent runs `bash sleep 295; echo waited` with a ~330s timeout.
5. Let the worker finish well before the sleep expires; observe that the result notification is only delivered after the sleep completes, and that the parent may issue additional `sleep 295` calls if the task was still running when it woke.

Observed with at least two different orchestrator models, suggesting reproducibility is not model-dependent.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected:
- After launching a background worker, the parent ends its turn; the `gentle-agents.result` message starts a new turn immediately when the child settles (typically seconds later).
- If the parent genuinely cannot end the turn, there should be a sanctioned way to wait that does not occupy the tool-call slot and keeps the session idle-eligible for the completion notification.

Actual:
- The parent invents `bash sleep 295`, keeping the session non-idle for up to ~5 minutes per call, delaying delivery of the already-finished child's result, and directly contradicting the "Never poll, sleep" clause of its own delegation contract.

### gentle-pi version

3.2.0

### Pi version

0.85.1

### Operating system

macOS

### Relevant logs or error output (optional)

```text
❀ agent run · gentle-ai-worker
Started gentle-ai-worker in the background as task <task-id>.

$ sleep 295; echo waited   (timeout 330s)
waited

❀ agent result · <task-id>
Task <task-id> is still running (last: bash).

$ sleep 295; echo waited   (timeout 330s)
```

Session transcript excerpt (tool call immediately after the background launch, with no intervening user input):

```json
{"type":"toolCall","name":"bash","arguments":{"command":"sleep 295; echo waited","timeout":330}}
```

The same literal command appeared 7 times across one session, and with the same shape (295s sleep / 330s timeout) under a different orchestrator model in a second session.

title: review: session report — 37k-line staged set split into 19 units, full remediation, and 2 committed-range CLI reviews (4+1 lenses) approved/burned
body:
### Problem

Field report from a full RDD cycle on a large staged decomposition (continuing the session-report series #577 / #581 / #919). Two committed-range reviews completed end-to-end through the direct CLI route — one HIGH (4 lenses), one MEDIUM (1 lens), both approved and acknowledged with zero corrections — while the compact facade could not start the committed-range candidate at all, and the review-* host dispatch lane rejected every envelope for the CLI-created lineage.

Also included: remediation data for 3 P1 + 16 P2 + 5 WARNING findings across a 37k-line staged decomposition, since several later review warnings point at exactly those fixes.

### Steps to reproduce

1. 182-file staged change (+31,027/−6,020) split into 19 pathspec work-unit commits on a feature branch; 61-file fix stack (`27515a01..643a6e3`) selected as the review candidate (base `723dd77a`, committed-only).
2. Compact facade: `inspect` → intended-untracked exclusion → START attempts carrying `baseRef`/`committedOnly` in `input`. Every attempt returned `start does not accept intendedUntracked` while the same envelope also re-emitted that field — seven byte-identical rejections, no lineage created.
3. Facade `capture` of the pre-START `select_base_ref` binding using the target identity as lineage: rejected (`capture-binding-rejected`, "belongs to a different session route"). A later `status` call with the same id failed safely: `lineage_id must be a canonical lowercase kebab-case identifier`.
4. Direct CLI route: selectorless `review status --next-transition` → negotiated START command extracted from the refusal prose → consent envelope relayed and granted → 4 × (`capture-result --materialize` → host-executed lens task → `capture-result --input`) → `acknowledge-approved` → `gentle-ai.review-acknowledged/v1`, authority burned.
5. Second candidate (11 files, 585 lines, MEDIUM): same CLI route; medium tier selected a single reliability lens; approved on the last admitted event; acknowledged; burned.

Host-relay dispatch detail (both reviews): dispatching the installed `review-*` agents with the materialized task was rejected at every envelope variant — with/without `mode`, with the exact `GENTLE_AI_REVIEW_BINDING` line as the task prefix — always ending in `review subagent dispatch has no current controller-owned candidate view lineage binding` (pre-START variants: `requires mode task`, `unsupported input field`). Lens execution therefore ran through generic read-only agents that read the materialized task file and returned the reviewer JSON, which `capture-result --input` admitted without friction.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected:
- The compact facade either expresses committed-range candidates itself (baseRef reachable on START) or hands off to the CLI route with a typed, non-dead-end transition.
- Once a lineage exists (created via CLI or facade), the host relay accepts host-executed materialized lens tasks bound to that lineage — the binding prefix and lineage are unambiguous.
- Identical repeated rejected STARTs return a typed replay/circuit-breaker signal instead of the same opaque failure, so agents do not loop.

Actual:
- Seven byte-identical facade START rejections (`start does not accept intendedUntracked`) with no typed replay signal.
- Facade capture of any binding after the CLI lineage went live: `capture-binding-rejected ... belongs to a different session route` — facade and CLI maintain disjoint session routes for the same repository.
- Review-agent dispatch rejected in all shapes for the CLI lineage; only generic-agent execution of the materialized file worked.
- The CLI route itself was fully completable: both reviews approved and burned, zero corrections.

### gentle-pi version

3.2.0 (source)

### Pi version

0.85.1

### Operating system

macOS

### Relevant logs or error output (optional)

```
facade START (x7, identical): start does not accept intendedUntracked; it is accepted only by inspect with untrackedScope select
facade capture: capture-binding-rejected — collectBinding is unknown, expired, or belongs to a different session route
facade status: lineage_id must be a canonical lowercase kebab-case identifier of at most 128 bytes
dispatch (all shapes): review subagent dispatch has no current controller-owned candidate view lineage binding
CLI success: {"schema":"gentle-ai.review-acknowledged/v1","action":"acknowledged","authority":"burned"} (x2)
```

title: bug(review): candidate view checkout-index fails on Windows at MAX_PATH
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

On native Windows, review candidate materialization fails before START when the candidate-view root plus a tracked repository path reaches the legacy `MAX_PATH` boundary. The facade reports only `candidate-view Git command checkout-index failed`.

A faithful reproduction using the same candidate tree and 16,384-byte checkout batches failed with `Filename too long`. Repeating the same operation with invocation-scoped `-c core.longpaths=true` completed all 39 batches. Applying repository-local `core.longpaths=true` also allowed the previously blocked native review to start and close approved.

This is distinct from #670 (committed symlinks) and #673 (executable-mode verification).

### Steps to reproduce

1. On native Windows, use a repository with enough tracked path depth that `<candidate-view-root>/<tracked-path>` reaches 260 characters.
2. Leave `core.longpaths` unset or false.
3. Start native review for any workspace change.
4. Candidate materialization fails during `checkout-index` before lineage creation.
5. Repeat checkout materialization with `git -c core.longpaths=true checkout-index ...`; it succeeds.

Observed fixture: 7,540 tracked paths, longest tracked path 171 characters, no committed symlinks, `core.autocrlf=false`, and `core.symlinks=false`.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected: Candidate-view materialization handles valid long tracked paths on Windows without requiring users to mutate repository or global Git configuration.

Actual: Batched `checkout-index` fails with `Filename too long`; the facade omits the underlying stderr and reports only a generic Git-command failure.

Suggested fix: invoke candidate-view Git materialization with invocation-scoped `-c core.longpaths=true` on Windows, while preserving existing candidate identity and safety checks. Also retain sanitized stderr or a bounded reason code sufficient to distinguish long-path failures.

`3.1.1-0.20260917180601-eae8fadd5ece`

### Pi version

`0.85.1`

### Operating system

Windows

### Relevant logs or error output (optional)

error: unable to create file <long-tracked-path>: Filename too long

Without core.longpaths: checkout-index failed
With -c core.longpaths=true: SUCCESS, 39 batches

title: feat(agents): añadir enrutamiento automático de subagentes con investigación revisada
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a request for this feature.
- [x] I reviewed this request and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem or opportunity

El enrutamiento actual de subagentes depende de perfiles estáticos: no puede elegir automáticamente el proveedor, modelo y nivel de razonamiento adecuados para la tarea completa. Una selección opaca de una sola llamada tampoco aporta suficiente trazabilidad ni permite distinguir capacidad, esfuerzo y evidencia del modelo.

Además, la información sobre modelos cambia. Investigar durante cada dispatch introduciría red, latencia y evidencia mutable en una ruta sensible. La solución debe mantener el dispatch sin red, preservar la privacidad de las operaciones posteriores y no modificar el modelo padre, las herramientas, los permisos ni el flujo de trabajo.

### Proposed outcome

Añadir enrutamiento TypeSafe opcional para cada lanzamiento de subagente:

- `/gentle:models` permite refrescar explícitamente la investigación desde fuentes públicas estructuradas y permitidas, persistiendo tarjetas de afirmaciones por alcance con contenido canónico y hash.
- La revisión humana muestra la evidencia y exige aprobación `routing` para el hash exacto. La persona usuaria conserva autoridad exclusiva sobre cada par exacto `modelo + thinking`; las recomendaciones, exclusiones y esfuerzos sugeridos son evidencia visible, no vetos sobre el pool.
- Cada dispatch habilitado valida offline el pool completo, el alcance de sesión, las capacidades informadas por Pi y las aprobaciones del mismo alcance antes de credenciales, SDK, historial, directorios o spawn.
- La primera operación clasifica el texto completo de la tarea en nueve dimensiones tipadas. Una segunda operación selecciona un ID exacto del pool usando la clasificación y las tarjetas revisadas. Si la confianza provisional es menor que `0.70`, una tercera operación adjudica solamente entre las dos mejores rutas.
- Las operaciones posteriores nunca reciben el texto crudo de la tarea. No existen truncamiento silencioso, sustitución de rutas, degradación estática ni investigación de red durante el dispatch.
- Tarjetas desconocidas, sin política, malformadas, desactualizadas, con hash o alcance incorrectos, o aprobadas solamente para `shadow`, fallan de forma cerrada.

### Alternatives considered

- Mantener solamente perfiles estáticos: preserva previsibilidad, pero exige selección manual para cada clase de tarea.
- Usar una sola elección TypeSafe con texto truncado: resultó opaca y poco estable para separar capacidad y esfuerzo.
- Permitir que la política del paquete agregue, elimine o vete rutas: se descartó porque el pool exacto debe pertenecer a la persona usuaria.
- Investigar modelos en cada dispatch: se descartó por privacidad, latencia, costo y mutabilidad de la evidencia.

### Additional context

La validación incluyó un refresco real de las dos fuentes permitidas, ocho casos de shadow routing con 21 operaciones lógicas y dos comparaciones ciegas entre niveles adyacentes en un proyecto externo. En esas dos tareas, `Terra/high` igualó sustancialmente la calidad de `Luna/max` y terminó aproximadamente 5,3× y 1,9× más rápido; esto se conserva como evidencia, no como autoridad sobre el pool.

La candidata corregida pasó 444 pruebas focalizadas y la suite completa con 2828 aprobadas, 38 omitidas y 0 fallidas. La validación de probabilidades acepta precisión arbitraria solamente cuando el vector está normalizado; cualquier tolerancia no normalizada exige valores en la grilla de centésimas y el límite observable estricto. También pasaron contrato del proveedor, runtime nativo, módulos generados, verificación de paquete, ratchet de tipos, paquete instalado en modo offline y controles de whitespace. La verificación independiente no encontró bloqueos.

title: review host relay: pi-empty-output carries no diagnosis, and the default thinking level can end a review
body:
## Context

While reviewing a candidate in a local repository, the review host relay failed three times in a row with its typed `pi-empty-output` transport failure: `stage: pi`, `exit_code: 0`, `timed_out: false`, ~60 s, zero bytes on stdout and stderr. The typed failure and its continuation were exactly right — I re-queried negotiated STATUS and relaunched only the exact re-offered slot, nothing was admitted and no authority was burned.

The underlying cause is in `pi`, not in the relay, and it is filed upstream with a minimal reproduction: **earendil-works/pi#9718**. Short version: the reviewer's strict-JSON prompt over a code diff makes the model spend its whole output budget on reasoning (13 951 `thinking_delta` events, final message `"stopReason":"length"`, no text), so `pi --print` has nothing to print, exits `0` and emits nothing at all. Empty stdin reproduces the same zero-byte output but in ~0.4 s instead of ~60 s.

## Two suggestions

1. **Carry the diagnosis in the operator line.** `pi-empty-output` today cannot be told apart from "the provider materialized an empty prompt" without measuring wall time by hand (0.4 s versus ~60 s). The relay already measures `elapsed_ms`; surfacing it, plus the stop reason once `pi` exposes one, would let an operator classify the failure without repeating the investigation. Right now the only way to reach the root cause was to spawn the relay's argv by hand outside the harness.

2. **Document the inherited model and thinking level.** The relay deliberately passes no `--model` ("model/provider/profile selection stays user-owned"), so a reviewer run uses the user's default model and `defaultThinkingLevel`. On a model with a ~32K output budget at a high thinking level, a candidate whose diff triggers a long reasoning chain exhausts the budget and produces nothing — which is how a 14-file, 545-line candidate failed while 79- and 239-line candidates passed through the same relay on the same day. A sentence in the docs stating that the lever is candidate scope or the default model/thinking level — never a retry — would have saved this investigation.

## Measured, same prompt and model, varying only the thinking level

| Thinking level | Wall time | `stopReason` | stdout |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `high` (one run) | 5.8 s | `stop` | text produced |
| `medium` | 62.9 s | `length` | **no text** |
| `low` | 39.4 s | `stop` | text produced |
| settings default (`high`) | 59.3-60.8 s, three times | `length` | **no text** |

Verified before reporting: the relay's argv with a trivial prompt works (exit 0, `OK`), so the argv, the scratch directory and the environment are not at fault; and the reviewed change itself was independently verified (`safe to accept`, 52 files / 518 tests, typecheck clean, browser check of the loading state), so nothing here reflects on the candidate under review.

title: /gentle:changes corrupts CRLF session diff rendering on Windows
body: ### Before submitting - [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem. - [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data. ### Problem On Windows, `/gentle:changes` renders a captured CRLF diff with scattered vertical bars, overwritten text, and apparently corrupted removed/added lines. Git reports the underlying commit correctly, so the corruption is limited to the fullscreen session-diff renderer. The current implementation preserves CRLF snapshot text, then splits rendered diff text on `\n` without removing the remaining `\r`. Diff content is rendered without terminal-text sanitization. A retained carriage return can therefore move the terminal cursor and overwrite previously rendered content. The changes panel can also display `detached` for a session-captured worktree even when Git is on a named branch, because session change models do not populate the optional branch field. This is secondary to the rendering defect but makes diagnosis confusing. ### Steps to reproduce 1. On Windows, use a repository containing a text file with CRLF line endings. 2. Modify the file through an agent write/edit operation so the session captures before and after snapshots. 3. Open `/gentle:changes`. 4. Expand the captured worktree and select the CRLF file. 5. Compare the rendered session diff with `git diff` or `git show`. In the observed case, Git reported two insertions and zero deletions, while `/gentle:changes` displayed scattered colored bars and overlapping fragments across unchanged and removed lines. The file contained only valid CRLF endings and no isolated carriage returns. ### Expected and actual behavior Expected: `/gentle:changes` renders CRLF and LF session diffs equivalently, without interpreting file carriage returns as terminal cursor controls. The worktree label should not claim `detached` when branch metadata was simply not captured. Actual: CRLF diff lines can retain `\r`, causing terminal cursor movement and visually corrupted output. Session-captured worktrees without branch metadata are labeled `detached` even when the repository is on a named branch. ### gentle-pi version 3.1.1-0.20260917180601-eae8fadd5ece ### Pi version 0.85.1 ### Operating system Windows ### Relevant logs or error output (optional) ```text Git status: clean, named branch Git numstat for the observed commit: 2 insertions, 0 deletions Captured file endings: valid CRLF; no isolated carriage returns ```

title: feat(shell): surface blocked-on-human status and notifications when the agent stalls
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a request for this feature.
- [x] I reviewed this request and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem or opportunity

On long autonomous runs the session can silently stop and wait for the human at several points: a command permission prompt, a `gentle_review` consent envelope, an RDD stop, or an ask-question prompt. When that happens nothing marks the session as blocked: the status keeps looking like normal work in progress, and no signal reaches an unfocused terminal. The operator keeps assuming the agent is working and discovers the stall only after returning to the pane, losing wall-clock time.

Current mechanisms do not close this gap: `ctx.ui.notify` toasts are transient and only visible while watching the terminal, and the RDD status line is text injected into the orchestrator prompt, not a live UI state.

### Proposed outcome

- A persistent, clearly distinguishable "blocked / waiting on you" agent status whenever the session is stalled on human input (command approval, review consent, RDD stop, ask-question), instead of the ordinary working presentation.
- The blocked status should state why it is blocked (permission needed / review consent / RDD stop reason) so a glance is enough to act.
- An attention signal that works when the terminal is unfocused: terminal bell and/or an OSC 9/777 desktop notification emitted when the agent enters the blocked state, so the human can safely context-switch while the run is parked.

### Alternatives considered

Keeping the terminal visible and polling it manually, or relying on transient `ctx.ui.notify` toasts. Both require the operator to already be watching the pane, which is exactly what fails on long unattended runs.

### Additional context

The blocking points already have distinct sources that could feed this status: the command-permission and ask-question prompts from the Pi host, the `gentle_review` consent envelope, and RDD stop reason codes. The prompt-side RDD status line already tracks review mode; this would be its user-visible complement for "the agent is stopped and waiting".

title: bug(review): review.capture-validation fails deterministically in preflight — the validator transport produces no final message
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this specific symptom.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Environment

| Component | Version |
| --- | --- |
| Pi | `0.85.1` |
| Node | `v26.0.0` |
| gentle-ai (package-local, Go CLI) | `3.1.0` |
| gentle-pi (npm) | `3.2.0` |
| OS | macOS 26.5 (`darwin`, `arm64`) |
| Review transport | `pi_host_relay` |

### Problem

A candidate whose reviewer result was captured and whose finding was corroborated by a provider refuter batch reaches `correction_required`. The bounded correction is declared and applied, fresh `STATUS` reoffers the **targeted-validation** slot — and submitting that exact binding fails in preflight before any work is attributed:

```json
{
  "native_failure": {
    "schema": "gentle-ai.review-integration.failure/v2",
    "operation": "review.capture-validation",
    "phase": "preflight",
    "code": "invalid_request",
    "message": "The negotiated review request is invalid.",
    "mutation_outcome": "not_started",
    "authority_applicability": "not_evaluated",
    "retry_safe": true,
    "cause": "invoke provider targeted validator: pi reviewer transport produced no final message"
  },
  "mutation_performed": false,
  "mutation_outcome": "none",
  "next_action": "correct_request",
  "retry_discipline": "Call fresh STATUS and execute only the exact one-slot role vector it reoffers; never relaunch from transcript inference."
}
```

`retry_safe: true` invites a retry, and the retry discipline says to re-query STATUS and execute only the reoffered vector — which is exactly what was done. A fresh `STATUS` reoffered the slot with the **identical** `validation_request.request_hash`, and the verbatim resubmission reproduced the failure byte for byte. So on this host it is **not** intermittent.

What makes the "correct_request" action unreachable: `required_inputs` is empty, there is no additional input the caller can supply (the binding is submitted verbatim), and nothing in the diagnostic names an input that was malformed. As far as the caller can tell, the request it submitted is the one the provider just rendered.

The **reviewer** role is healthy on the same host, session and transport: six ordinary reviews approved in the same working period, on candidates of 197, 287, 345, 504, 722 and 847 changed lines, plus one reviewer slot that hit the relay's wall-clock bound and approved on the retry after the unachievable slot was withdrawn. Only the validator role fails, and it fails the same way every time.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Drive an ordinary review to `correction_required` on a candidate whose finding is **inferential** and was confirmed by a refuter batch (the slot was reoffered as `targeted_validation_required` after a deterministic correction plan was accepted).
2. Declare the correction plan (`correction_lines` inside the provider bounds) and apply the bounded edit while the candidate is bound.
3. Query bound `STATUS`: it reoffers `review.capture-validation` with a `validation_request`.
4. Submit that exact `collectBinding` unchanged.
5. Observe the preflight failure above, with `mutation_outcome: not_started`.
6. Query `STATUS` again: the same slot is reoffered with the **same** `request_hash`; resubmitting reproduces it exactly.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected: either the validator run completes and produces a verdict, or the failure names a concrete input the caller can correct — since the caller is told `next_action: "correct_request"`.

Actual: the failure is reported in `phase: preflight` as `invalid_request`, blames the validator transport ("produced no final message"), consumes no correction budget and mutates nothing, and gives the caller nothing to correct. Because the contract forbids retrying anything other than the reoffered vector, the only remaining moves are to abandon the lineage (see the separate blocker in #1159) or to start a fresh review of the corrected candidate.

### Workaround that worked

A fresh review of the **corrected** candidate. The controller offered a fresh `START` for the new target, and that review approved on the first attempt with no validator needed. So the correction itself was never validated in place; it was re-reviewed as a new candidate.

### What this report does not determine

The validator child's own stderr and transcript. The relay does not surface them and no session transcript was left behind, so I cannot say whether this is the provisioning class of #936, the empty-output class of #1140, or something specific to how the validator role is spawned or prompted. I am reporting the observed symptom and the fact that it is deterministic here, not a root cause.

### Impact

On this host, any candidate whose reviewer marks a CRITICAL or BLOCKER finding cannot complete the lifecycle: the correction route leads to a validator slot that can never return a verdict, so the only ways forward are an unaudited workaround (a fresh review) or an audited abandonment that the facade currently cannot perform.

title: feat(odd): derive a feature index so `odd/tasks/` never has to be read in full
body:
### Before submitting
- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

ODD maintains one canonical document per feature (`odd/tasks/<feature>.md`) plus an Engram mirror under topic `odd/<feature>/tasks`, but the contract defines **no index, rollup, rotation, or archive layer**. `assets/orchestrator-memory.md` requires, on resume, reading the *actual task file* — so with N features a session either reads all N documents or guesses which one is active. There is no cheap way to answer "which features exist, what state are they in, and which one is live" without reading the corpus.

Evidence that no navigation layer exists in gentle-pi 3.2.0 — searching the four assets that define ODD for `index|rollup|archive|compact|rotat|ledger|manifest`:

- `orchestrator-memory.md:33` — the SDD `archive` phase row (not ODD).
- `orchestrator-delegation.md:148` — the Judgment Day frozen ledger (not ODD).
- Remaining hits are incidental uses of "indexed" / "answer".

Lines matching a navigation keyword **and** `odd`: **0**.

### Measured cost

One real repository after two features (sizes are `wc -c`):

| Document | Bytes |
| --- | --- |
| `odd/tasks/s1-foundation.md` | 32,589 |
| `odd/tasks/repo-hygiene.md` | 22,446 |
| **canonical total** | **55,035** (average 27,518/doc) |
| `odd/` on disk, 4 files (includes `.es.md` mirrors) | 113,763 |

At ~27.5 KB/doc (~7k tokens at a rough 4 bytes/token), a 200k context window holds **~28 documents**. The wall is reachable at roughly **20 features** — not at 1,000. Projected to 1,000 features the tree is ~27.5 MB canonical (~55 MB with mirrors), but that number is irrelevant: the binding constraint is the context window, and it binds an order of magnitude earlier.

### Why compaction is not available

The same contract forbids an exhaustive decision journal and requires observed evidence. A feature document is the memory of record, so it cannot be summarised away, rewritten, or rotated into a digest without breaking verifiability. The only remaining option is a **derived navigation layer** that is additive and mechanically checkable.

### Proposal

1. `odd/state.jsonl` — one object per feature: `name`, `status`, `tasks_done`, `tasks_total`, `last_commit`, `open_decisions`, `blockers`, `doc_path`, `generated_at_sha`.
2. `odd/INDEX.md` — generated, O(N) lines, not O(bytes).
3. Rotation of closed features into `odd/tasks/archive/`.
4. Verifiable freshness — regenerate and `git diff --exit-code` in CI.
5. Minimal YAML front-matter (`status`, `tasks_done`, `tasks_total`) so derivation is mechanical rather than prose parsing. A document without front-matter degrades to `status: unknown` and must not break the rollup.
6. Engram mirrors the rollup under **one** topic (`odd/index`), not N.

Explicitly **not** proposed: LLM-generated digests or summary chains (they drift and cannot be verified); compacting or rewriting journals.

### Where it would land

`assets/orchestrator-memory.md:7` · `assets/orchestrator.md` · `assets/orchestrator-delegation.md` (only if the index feeds routing) · `docs/readme-reference.md:24` · `README.md:123` · a generator in `scripts/`.

### Acceptance criteria

- Derivation is deterministic: re-running produces byte-identical output.
- The index is O(N) lines, not O(bytes of features).
- Staleness is detectable in one command and fail-able in CI.
- A document without front-matter degrades to `status: unknown` without breaking the rollup.
- Engram mirrors the rollup under a single topic.

### Open questions for maintainers

- Does the package ship the generator, or is the convention enough?
- `odd/state.jsonl`, or fold this into the existing status surface?
- Prescribed rotation, or repository policy?
- Who owns the front-matter schema version?

### Deduplication performed before filing

14 searches across this repository for this concern (`ODD index`, `odd/tasks index`, `feature index rollup`, `ODD resume handoff`, `progressive disclosure`, `ODD context budget`, `odd/state.jsonl`, `odd/ manifest`, `ODD rollup archive rotate`, `engram odd index`, `ODD scale`, `odd/ navigation`, `ODD memory growth`, `ODD feature document size`): **0 results**.

Related but distinct: #1114 (keep task artifacts out of existing project trees), #1079 (ODD always-on mandatory), #1035 and #1146 (organic workflow parity), #545 (backlog survey dashboard).

### Environment

gentle-pi 3.2.0 · gentle-ai 3.1.0 · Pi on Windows · git 2.49.0

title: bug(review): audited abandon requires discarded-work inputs the facade cannot expose
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

The `gentle_review` facade cannot complete an audited `abandon` request when the caller has only facade-authorized data.

`abandon` requires the exact `expectedRevision`, `snapshotIdentity`, `capturedLensResults`, and `findingsPresent` values. The negotiated `inspect` and lineage-bound `status` operations do not expose the authority inventory's `entries[].discarded_work` projection, and the facade has no read-only inventory operation. The only adapter that decodes that projection is `NativeReviewCli.reviewStatus()`, which invokes plain native `review status`; the mirrored orchestration contract prohibits the caller from replacing bound facade STATUS with raw shell STATUS.

This leaves a non-terminal compact-v2 lineage that is natively eligible for audited abandonment with no facade-only way to construct the exact authorization input. The caller must not infer the discarded-work summary from admitted role results or persisted state.

This appears distinct from #631, which fixed decoding `discarded_work`, #466, which fixed relaying the eight-line authorization, and #846, which concerns stale lineage reuse after a successful abandonment.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start an ordinary review and let it reach a non-terminal state with captured reviewer results, such as `correction_required`.
2. Decide to discard that review through the audited maintenance route.
3. Call `gentle_review` with `operation: "abandon"`, the lineage ID, and no invented maintenance fields.
4. Observe `native-input-required` for the exact revision, snapshot identity, captured lens results, and findings-presence value.
5. Call facade `inspect` and lineage-bound facade `status`.
6. Observe that these negotiated target-status responses do not publish `entries[].discarded_work`, and that no facade inventory operation exists.
7. Inspect the current implementation: `NativeReviewCli.reviewStatus()` decodes the required native inventory, but the ABANDON controller path requires the caller to supply those decoded fields instead of deriving them for the caller-specified lineage.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected:

For a caller-specified eligible non-terminal lineage, the facade should freshly read the native authority inventory, locate exactly one matching entry, derive its revision, snapshot identity, and discarded-work summary, then display the exact authorization binding for fresh interactive approval. Alternatively, it should expose a schema-validated read-only inventory operation explicitly permitted by the orchestration contract.

Actual:

The facade requires the exact inventory-derived fields as caller input but provides no permitted facade operation that returns them. Audited abandonment is therefore unreachable without violating the facade-only lifecycle contract or fabricating authority data. The lineage remains unchanged and no mutation occurs.

### gentle-pi version

3.2.0

### Pi version

0.85.1

### Operating system

Linux

### Relevant logs or error output (optional)

```text
operation: abandon
status: blocked
outcome: native-input-required
missing_input:
  - expectedRevision
  - snapshotIdentity
  - actor
  - reason
  - capturedLensResults
  - findingsPresent
mutation_performed: false
mutation_outcome: none
next_action: resubmit-with-exact-native-maintenance-input
```

title: bug(tests): wall-clock deadline assertion cancels all rdd-status-line tests in local full-suite runs
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

Running the full test suite locally (`node --experimental-strip-types --test tests/*.test.ts`, or `pnpm test`) cancels all tests of `tests/rdd-status-line.test.ts` on a loaded machine, while CI stays green. This is pre-existing on `main` — reproduced on a pristine `main` checkout with no local changes — and invisible to CI because shared runners do not hit the same CPU contention.

Root cause: the deadline test below asserts wall-clock elapsed time under a stubbed never-settling reader. It measures machine responsiveness rather than code correctness, so any loaded local run breaks it, and a process-level cascade cancels the remaining tests of the file. The rest of the file already uses the right patterns (stubbed native reader, injected virtual clock in the memoization tests), so the fix is narrow: virtualize the timer in the deadline test or replace the `elapsed` bound with a structural assertion (did it resolve, without the underlying reader settling). The test protects an important invariant — a hung `reviewMode` read must never stall the session — so it should be made deterministic, not deleted.

I am volunteering to fix this if the issue is approved — happy to submit the PR.

### Steps to reproduce

1. On a loaded Linux dev machine, from a clean checkout of `main`:

```bash
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
node --experimental-strip-types --test tests/*.test.ts
```

2. Observe `# fail 0` but `# cancelled 10`, with the first `not ok` being `resolveRddModeStatus resolves to undefined within the deadline when reviewMode never settles`, followed by the remaining tests of the same file cancelled.
3. Run the file in isolation:

```bash
node --experimental-strip-types --test tests/rdd-status-line.test.ts
```

It passes 7/7, both on `main` and on feature branches.

The wall-clock assertion in question (the `neverSettling` deadline test in `tests/rdd-status-line.test.ts`):

```text
const neverSettling = fakeReviewMode(() => new Promise<never>(() => {}));
const deadlineMs = 150;
const status = await resolveRddModeStatus(neverSettling, "/repo-hung", AbortSignal.timeout(deadlineMs));
assert.ok(elapsed < deadlineMs + 1000, `expected the read to resolve near the ${deadlineMs}ms deadline, took ${elapsed}ms`);
```

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected: the full suite is green locally exactly as on CI, with no test depending on wall-clock responsiveness.

Actual: the deadline test breaks its `elapsed < deadlineMs + 1000` bound under load (the event loop is starved past ~1.15 s while dozens of test-file processes compete), and the runner cancels the remaining tests of the file — `# pass 2628 / # fail 0 / # cancelled 10` on pristine `main`. Every developer who runs the full suite locally then has to spend time proving the cancellation was not caused by their own change.

### gentle-pi version

From source: `main` @ 2b579c80 (also reproduced on the base of PR #1144, c3ae6fed).

### Pi version

Pi coding agent 0.85.1 (the repo `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` devDependency).

### Operating system

Linux

### Relevant logs or error output (optional)

```text
not ok 1301 - resolveRddModeStatus resolves to undefined within the deadline when reviewMode never settles
not ok 1302 - resolveRddModeStatus memoizes a resolved status per cwd for RDD_STATUS_MEMO_TTL_MS
not ok 1303 - resolveRddModeStatus re-reads once the memoized status expires
not ok 1304 - resolveRddModeStatus memoizes independently per cwd
not ok 1305 - resolveRddStatusLine renders on, off, and unavailable from the stubbed native reader
not ok 1306 - RDD_STATUS_TIMEOUT_MS is a small, positive bounded-deadline constant
not ok 1307 - getOrchestratorPrompt renders the resolved RDD status line next to the background policy line
not ok 1308 - getOrchestratorPrompt defaults to the worst-case unknown RDD status line (budget-critical path)
not ok 1309 - the prompt cache key distinguishes on, off, and unknown so each renders a distinct prompt
not ok 1310 - the on and off renders are never longer than the unknown (worst-case) render
# pass 2628
# fail 0
# cancelled 10
```

title: fix(usage): display remaining Codex quota like official clients
body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find a report of this problem.
- [x] I reviewed this report and removed credentials, tokens, private paths, hostnames, and other sensitive data.

### Problem

Gentle Shell displays the raw consumed percentage for Codex rate-limit windows without indicating that the value means "used." ChatGPT and the official Codex client display the complementary percentage as quota remaining (`% left`).

When both interfaces are checked at the same time, the values appear inconsistent even though they describe the same backend state:

- ChatGPT: 46% left; Gentle Shell: 54%
- ChatGPT: 59% left; Gentle Shell: 41%

Gentle Shell correctly parses the backend's `used_percent` field, but rendering it without a semantic label makes the UI misleading and diverges from the official clients.

The official Codex TUI converts the transport value at the presentation boundary with `(100.0 - percent_used).clamp(0.0, 100.0)` and formats it as `% left`:

- https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/eaf81d3f/codex-rs/codex-api/src/rate_limits.rs
- https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/27c05a52/codex-rs/tui/src/status/rate_limits.rs
- https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/f1affbac/codex-rs/tui/src/status/card.rs

### Steps to reproduce

1. Use an OpenAI Codex subscription through Gentle Shell.
2. Open the Gentle Shell status bar or `/gentle:usage` panel.
3. Open the ChatGPT plan-limits page at the same time.
4. Compare the 5-hour and weekly percentages.

### Expected and actual behavior

Expected:

Gentle Shell should present remaining quota consistently with ChatGPT and the official Codex client. The internal model may continue storing `used_percent`, but the bar, percentage text, panel, gauge semantics, tests, and documentation should consistently describe the rendered value as remaining.

Actual:

`renderUsageBar` and `renderUsagePanel` pass `usedPercent` directly to the gauge and print it without a `used` label. This produces the exact complement of the percentages labeled `left` by OpenAI.
